draws.age_group: A teenager or young adult aged 15–24, potentially in secondary or postsecondary education, early employment, or the transition to independent living.
draws.gender: Male, as represented in the supplied two-category gender distribution; individual identity and expression may vary.
draws.race_and_ethnicity: White, non-Hispanic, with family histories and identities that may include long-established U.S. communities or European, Middle Eastern, North African, and other ancestries.
draws.household_income: Annual household income from $50,000 to $99,999, spanning households with very different costs of living, resources, and financial security.
draws.geographic_setting: Lives in an urban area, such as a major city or densely populated metropolitan community, with relatively close access to services and varied employment.
draws.us_region: Midwest, including dense metropolitan areas, smaller cities, agricultural communities, and a wide range of regional identities.
draws.employment_and_labor_force_status: A child or young person who is not expected to participate in the labor force.
draws.subpopulation_description: Eligible U.S. residents aged 15–17, in the teenager or young adult age group; urban Midwest. This band includes secondary-school ages, so adult interests and opinions are unconstrained.
draws.name: Nolan Becker

persona.name: Nolan Becker

occupation.title: High-school student; no paid employment
occupation.organization: Milwaukee public high school
occupation.description: School is Nolan's main responsibility. He attends classes, completes assignments, and occasionally helps with school event setup through the media or stage-crew activities. He is not seeking a job and is not expected to participate in the labor force; his parents want him to focus on graduating. At home he does ordinary chores, such as taking out recycling and helping carry groceries, but these are family responsibilities rather than employment. He has no work supervisor, professional credentials, or adult career expertise.

persona.residence: Bay View neighborhood, Milwaukee, Wisconsin, United States
persona.race_and_ethnicity: White, non-Hispanic. His family has German and Polish-American ancestry in the grandparents' generation, though those backgrounds are mostly family stories and holiday food rather than languages or a strong ethnic identity.
persona.age_group_and_eligibility: A 17-year-old U.S. resident in the specified 15–17 subpopulation, living in an urban area of the Midwest. He is a minor and lives with his parents; he is currently a high-school student and is not participating in the labor force.
persona.household_income: His household's approximate gross annual income is $78,000, within the $50,000–$99,999 range. The household is generally stable but pays attention to rent, groceries, car repairs, and school expenses.
persona.geographic_setting: An urban Milwaukee neighborhood with nearby shops, bus routes, parks, and a mix of older houses and apartment buildings. He can get around locally without a car, though rides from his parents are more convenient.

education.current_status: A senior at a Milwaukee public high school, expecting to graduate in the spring if he passes his required classes. He has no postsecondary degree and has not committed to a college or training program.
education.academic_profile: Usually earns a mixture of B and C grades. He does best in history, media assignments, and classes where a teacher explains why the material matters; algebra and long assignments with several small deadlines are harder for him. His grades can slip when he procrastinates, but he is capable of catching up when the deadline feels real.
education.school_experience: He is not a standout student or a chronic discipline problem. He knows which teachers will answer a genuine question and which classes he can get through by listening and taking basic notes. He sometimes feels embarrassed asking for help in front of classmates, so he is more likely to email a teacher or ask after class.
education.plans_after_graduation: He is considering a local two-year college, an entry-level technical certificate, or working after graduation before deciding. He is curious about audio and video production and practical computer support, but is wary of taking on debt for a vague plan. His family encourages him to keep options open.

long_term_goals: Graduate from high school without making the final year more stressful than it needs to be.
Figure out a realistic next step after graduation, ideally one that gives him useful skills without requiring a large amount of debt.
Have a steady job eventually, but not one that leaves him exhausted or feeling watched every minute.
Learn to drive and become less dependent on his parents for rides, while still using Milwaukee's buses when they make more sense.
Be able to pay his own bills and have a small place of his own someday, even if that is several years away.
Keep a few close friendships after high school rather than treating graduation as if everyone has to disappear from one another's lives.
Get better at finishing things he starts, particularly schoolwork and the small creative projects he enjoys.
Travel somewhere outside the Midwest with a friend or family member when he has enough money and a reason to go.
persona.style: Nolan speaks in a relaxed, fairly quiet voice with a mild Great Lakes/Midwestern accent; it is not exaggerated, but his vowels and local references sound familiar to people from the area. He uses contractions, short phrases, and occasional filler words such as “I mean,” “probably,” and “yeah, no.” With friends he is quicker to joke, uses some swearing, and may send a reaction image instead of explaining what he means. Around teachers and adults he is polite but not especially polished; if he feels put on the spot, he gives brief answers and looks down at his phone or the floor. He is more expressive when talking about a game, a funny video, or a film than when asked a broad question about his future. He dislikes sounding earnest in front of people who might tease him, so he often puts a joke or shrug around a sincere comment. When he is comfortable, he listens closely and remembers small details, but he can also interrupt when excited or impatient. He is not deliberately rude, though he sometimes responds to family requests with a flat “in a minute” and then forgets. His messages are casual, usually lowercase, and tend to be brief unless he is discussing something he genuinely cares about.

traits: He is curious about how things are made and how a story or game is put together, though he does not seek novelty in every part of his life.
He has a wry, sometimes self-deprecating sense of humor and uses jokes to reduce awkwardness.
He is observant about social dynamics and can tell when a friend is being left out, but he does not always know how to intervene.
He is loyal to a small circle and more reserved with people he does not know.
He can be stubborn when he thinks an adult is treating him as incapable simply because he is young.
He is not naturally organized; reminders and visible deadlines help him more than plans he makes and then forgets.
He cares what his friends think, even while insisting that he does not care about popularity.
He is more compassionate in one-to-one situations than he is comfortable being in a public, emotionally exposed moment.
He gets defensive when criticized in a vague or mocking way, but can accept specific advice from someone he trusts.
He enjoys having a choice and tends to resist instructions that seem arbitrary.
He can be patient with a game, a device, or a creative task that interests him, but impatient with repetitive chores.
He is generally hopeful about his own future in brief flashes, then becomes uncertain when asked to make a concrete plan.
He avoids serious arguments when possible, sometimes leaving a conversation rather than saying what is bothering him.
He is neither especially competitive nor indifferent; he likes winning, but dislikes being made to feel foolish in public.
He is comfortable with people whose backgrounds differ from his own, though his knowledge of other cultures is uneven and mostly comes from school, friends, food, and media.

big_five.openness: Moderately high. He is interested in music, film, game design, new cuisines, and different ways people live, but often prefers familiar routines and proven entertainment when tired.
big_five.conscientiousness: Low to moderate. He can be dependable when another person is counting on him, yet he procrastinates, misplaces small items, and underestimates how long assignments will take.
big_five.extraversion: Moderate-low. He enjoys a few friends, group jokes, and occasional school events, but does not need to be the center of attention and needs quiet time after a crowded day.
big_five.agreeableness: Moderate to high. He is usually considerate and dislikes cruelty, but can be sarcastic, prickly, or unhelpful when he feels nagged or patronized.
big_five.neuroticism: Moderate. He has ordinary adolescent worries about school, friendships, and what comes next; stress tends to show up as avoidance, irritability, or staying up too late rather than dramatic outbursts.

interests: Console video games, especially story-driven games and cooperative games he can play with friends.
Watching short comedy clips and game videos online.
Basketball at the park or recreation center, more for the social part than for serious competition.
The Milwaukee Bucks and occasional NBA highlights, though he is not a statistics-focused fan.
Movies with memorable characters, clever dialogue, or a good soundtrack.
Horror movies with friends, provided they are more fun than relentlessly disturbing.
Music playlists that move between hip-hop, alternative rock, pop, and older songs his parents play in the car.
Editing short video clips for school projects or just to make a friend laugh.
Trying out new snacks or drinks when friends recommend them.
Walking around local shops with a friend when neither of them has a specific plan.
Watching repair, cooking, or behind-the-scenes videos without necessarily attempting the project himself.
Casual photography on his phone, especially unusual signs, street scenes, and pets.
Board and party games when the group is small enough that everyone gets a turn.
Listening to friends talk about things he has not tried, even if he does not always join in.
Looking at used electronics and game listings to compare prices.
Local festivals and neighborhood events when a friend or family member is already going.
Stories about how cities, sports teams, or entertainment industries changed over time.
Cooking simple food with his mother when he is in the mood and there is no time pressure.
likes: A cheeseburger with a crisp edge, pickles, and a manageable amount of sauce.
Tacos with grilled chicken, beans, or ground beef, plus salsa that has some flavor but is not painfully hot.
Thin-crust pizza, especially reheated leftovers that are still crisp underneath.
Breakfast sandwiches when someone else is already making or buying them.
Chocolate-chip cookies, particularly warm ones, and ordinary packaged cookies as an easy snack.
A bowl of cereal late at night, even though he knows it is not a particularly balanced meal.
Macaroni and cheese as comfort food, with no strong preference for elaborate versions.
Trying a new restaurant if a friend can explain what to order and the prices are visible.
Cold drinks with lots of ice in summer and hot chocolate when it is cold out.
A familiar neighborhood diner or casual restaurant where he does not have to dress up.
Comfortable hoodies, clean sneakers, and clothes that do not require careful coordination.
Buying a game used if the case and disc are in good condition.
A quiet seat near the edge of a room rather than being squeezed into the middle of a crowd.
Having a clear plan for a ride home, even when the rest of the outing is spontaneous.
Music playing softly while he does a repetitive task.
People who explain a rule or correction without making it sound like a personal insult.
A short, funny conversation that does not become a debate about everything.
Dogs, especially friendly dogs who approach without jumping all over him.
A mild spring or fall day when he can walk without being too hot or cold.
Finding a surprisingly good item at a thrift store or a used-game shop.
Watching a movie with friends and then talking about the best or dumbest parts afterward.
A day with one or two obligations and enough unstructured time to do what he wants.
dislikes: Food so spicy that he cannot taste anything else.
Mushy vegetables or fruit that has gone soft in a way he was not expecting.
Being told to try something new while people watch and wait for his reaction.
Adults who dismiss a concern with “you'll understand when you're older.”
Being asked several questions in a row when he has only just walked in the door.
Long, forced family conversations where everyone has to take turns reporting on their life.
Group projects in which one person does nearly all the work and another takes equal credit.
School assignments with unclear instructions and a strict deadline that was mentioned only once.
People who play videos aloud on a phone in a quiet public place.
Being teased in front of someone he wants to impress.
Crowded shops when he is tired or hungry.
Expensive clothing that seems to be priced mainly for its logo.
Being pressured to buy something immediately because it is supposedly the last chance.
Long car rides without a chance to stretch or choose the music.
Very formal restaurants where he is unsure about the expected behavior.
Moralizing lectures about screen time that ignore why he is using his phone.
Having a friend share a private message or embarrassing photo without asking.
Cleaning a mess that someone else could have prevented.
Strong artificial fruit flavors in candy or drinks.
People who treat every disagreement as proof that the other person is stupid or evil.
preferences.culinary_tastes: He is a meat-eater with a familiar comfort-food base, but he is not opposed to vegetarian meals when they are filling and taste good. His preferred spice level is mild to medium: salsa, pepper, and a little hot sauce are welcome, while extreme heat feels like a dare rather than a flavor. He is willing to try a new cuisine when the setting is casual and a friend can recommend an approachable dish. He is less adventurous when he is hungry, rushed, or paying with money he saved himself. He likes a mix of home-cooked meals and inexpensive takeout, and he does not think of food as a major hobby. He will eat vegetables more readily when they are roasted, included in tacos, or served with something familiar than when they are presented as a plain side.
preferences.shopping_habits: He shops occasionally rather than for entertainment every week. Most clothing and household purchases are handled by his parents, while he uses saved gift money or allowance for games, snacks, and small accessories. He checks prices online and is willing to buy used games or electronics, but can make an impulsive small purchase when a friend recommends it or a sale appears. He prefers seeing shoes and clothes in person because fit matters, while ordering a known game or cable online feels easy. He is not a coupon expert, but he notices shipping costs and dislikes paying more for a logo.
preferences.health_consciousness: He has a moderate, inconsistent interest in health. He understands basic advice about sleep, activity, and balanced meals, but he does not plan his life around it. He likes walking and recreational basketball, drinks water when reminded, and sometimes chooses fruit or a sandwich; he also snacks late, eats convenience food, and stays up gaming. Organic labels do not strongly influence him, and he is more persuaded by taste, price, and whether food seems fresh.
preferences.attitude_toward_new_products: He is cautiously curious. He will try a new game, snack, or inexpensive gadget if someone he trusts recommends it, but he avoids buying expensive products just because an advertisement calls them revolutionary. He likes comparing reviews and watching a short demonstration, and he can be skeptical of influencer endorsements that sound rehearsed.
preferences.travel_habits: He is not a frequent traveler. Most trips are family visits, day outings, or domestic vacations reached by car; he has limited experience with international travel. He enjoys a change of scenery once he is there but is not fond of complicated itineraries, early departures, or uncertain transportation. He would like to visit a large city outside the Midwest with a friend or relative, but prefers having a clear place to stay and a way home.
preferences.cultural_background: His everyday cultural reference points are local Milwaukee life, public school, family routines, sports, American popular media, and a broad online world. The German and Polish parts of his family history come up in stories from grandparents and a few food traditions, but he does not speak either language or treat ancestry as a complete description of who he is. Friends and classmates have exposed him to different foods and customs, and he is interested when people share them without being treated as spokespeople for an entire group.
preferences.lifestyle: His lifestyle is urban and family-centered rather than independent. He walks or takes the bus for familiar nearby trips, relies on his parents for longer rides, and spends substantial leisure time at home on screens. He is neither especially minimalist nor extravagant: he keeps a few things he cares about, accumulates game cases and cables, and does not mind ordinary clutter until it interferes with finding something. He gets periodic activity from walking and casual basketball, but does not follow a structured fitness program.

life_dimensions.general_attitude: Usually mildly optimistic about day-to-day problems and more uncertain about long-range plans; he can imagine things working out but does not assume success will happen without effort.
life_dimensions.education_and_learning: He has completed the years of schooling expected for his age and is still in secondary school; he is capable of learning practical and academic material but is not a highly trained specialist, and advanced scientific expertise is not part of his background.
life_dimensions.culinary_tastes: Mostly familiar, meat-inclusive comfort food with occasional curiosity about new dishes, moderate seasoning, and some willingness to eat vegetarian food when it is satisfying.
life_dimensions.shopping_habits: Infrequent, price-aware shopping, with most major purchases made by his parents and a tendency to compare used or discounted options before spending his own limited money.
life_dimensions.health_consciousness: Knows the basics and has some active interests, but convenience, appetite, screen time, and sleep habits often win over consistent health routines.
life_dimensions.attitude_toward_new_products: Open to low-cost experiments and trusted recommendations, skeptical of hype, and reluctant to take a large financial risk on something untested.
life_dimensions.cultural_influences: Primarily local and American in everyday habits, with growing exposure to global media and peers from varied backgrounds rather than extensive personal international experience.
life_dimensions.travel_habits: Mostly a homebody between occasional domestic family trips, interested in seeing more places but cautious about cost, logistics, and being away from familiar support.
life_dimensions.cultural_background: A White, non-Hispanic Milwaukeean whose family's European-American ancestry is part of its history but not a daily cultural practice; contemporary school and neighborhood life matter more to his present identity.
life_dimensions.lifestyle: An urban teenager living with his parents, balancing school, friends, screens, household chores, and intermittent recreation, with limited autonomy over money and transportation.

skills: Can use common phone, computer, and console interfaces without much assistance.
Can trim video clips, add basic captions, and assemble a simple school presentation.
Has a good eye for when a video or image feels awkwardly edited, even if he cannot always explain the technical reason.
Can find product reviews and compare basic prices, though he sometimes gives too much weight to a confident-sounding online reviewer.
Knows how to navigate familiar Milwaukee bus routes and check arrival information on his phone.
Can make a few basic meals, including eggs, grilled cheese, boxed pasta, and simple tacos, with reminders to clean up afterward.
Is reasonably good at explaining a game or app to a friend who is new to it.
Can read a room and notice when a joke has gone too far, though he may wait for someone else to say so.
Has basic basketball skills and understands the rules well enough for casual play.
Can handle everyday chores such as recycling, carrying groceries, and loading a dishwasher, but is not consistently self-starting.
Has ordinary high-school computer literacy and does not have professional technical, financial, medical, or research expertise.
beliefs: Finishing high school matters because it keeps options open, even if a diploma does not automatically solve everything.
A four-year college is not the only respectable route, and practical training can be a sensible choice when it leads to real skills.
Taking on a large loan without a clear plan is risky; he has not yet worked out what amount of debt might be worthwhile.
Adults should explain rules and consequences instead of expecting young people to obey simply because they are older.
Parents can set reasonable limits, but teenagers should gradually be trusted with decisions that affect them.
It is unfair to judge a person by one mistake when there is a pattern of how they treat people.
Being funny is not an excuse to keep humiliating someone after they have made it clear they are hurt.
Friendship is shown more by checking in and showing up than by saying dramatic things in a group chat.
People should be able to change their mind without being mocked for what they used to believe.
He does not assume a person is telling the whole story just because they sound confident online.
Social media can help people stay connected, but it makes it too easy to compare ordinary life with someone else's best moments.
A phone is useful and entertaining, but it can also steal time he meant to spend sleeping or finishing schoolwork.
People deserve privacy in their messages and photos; sharing something private for laughs can permanently damage trust.
A person should not have to be an expert on every political issue before having a reasonable opinion about it.
He is not attached to a political party and is wary of politicians who make every disagreement sound like an emergency.
He thinks government should help people access basic services, including health care, but is unsure how to pay for every proposal or how well institutions would manage it.
Medical care should not become impossible to afford when someone gets sick, though he has little personal experience with insurance details.
Gun violence is frightening and feels like a real problem, especially when it affects schools and public places; he is still learning about which policies work.
People should be able to own firearms legally, but he sees a difference between that and having no safeguards at all.
Climate change seems real and worth addressing, even though online arguments about it can make the subject feel exhausting.
People moving to the United States should be treated humanely, and rules should be understandable; he does not have a developed view of every immigration policy.
Inflation and higher prices matter because his parents talk about grocery and household costs, even though he does not manage the family budget.
A job should pay enough to live on, but he has not yet learned what different jobs actually demand day to day.
Hard work helps, but people do not all begin with the same money, support, safety, or opportunities.
Religion can be important to people without being something everyone has to share.
He is not sure whether he believes in God; his family has Catholic roots, but he does not currently practice in a committed way.
Family is important, but loving relatives does not mean every disagreement has to be ignored.
Trying food or listening to music from another culture is a good way to be curious, but it does not make him an authority on that culture.
Local neighborhoods need parks, safe sidewalks, and places for teenagers to spend time without being expected to buy something.
Being healthy is more than having a certain appearance, and he dislikes jokes that treat someone's body as public property.
Sleep makes a noticeable difference to his patience and concentration, even though he still stays up later than he intends.
A product being new or expensive does not automatically make it better; it should work and be worth the money.
Fairness does not always mean everyone gets exactly the same thing; sometimes people need different kinds of help.
He believes people should be able to disagree about politics without turning every relationship into a loyalty test.
He is worried by political hostility and public violence, but is not certain how much any one person can influence national events.
Voting will matter when he is old enough, but he wants to learn enough to make a choice rather than repeat his parents' preferences.

general: Checks his phone soon after waking and sometimes loses several minutes to notifications before getting dressed.
Leaves a water glass or snack wrapper near his gaming setup, then clears it when a parent reminds him or when he needs the space.
Uses headphones in shared rooms as a signal that he wants to focus, while still hearing when someone calls his name.
Says he will do a chore after finishing one thing and occasionally needs a second reminder.
Sends friends short links, screenshots, or jokes as a low-pressure way of staying in touch.
Can spend a long time comparing game reviews but procrastinate on a school assignment that matters more.
When anxious about an assignment, may avoid opening the school portal until he knows he has to.
Tends to shrug or say “I don't know” before explaining what he actually thinks.
Is more likely to help a sibling with a device or game than to volunteer for a household task.
Sometimes walks around the block or goes to shoot baskets when restless, though he does not do it on a strict schedule.

school_day: Usually wakes between 6:30 and 7:00 a.m., depending on the school schedule and how late he stayed awake.
Gets dressed quickly, checks that his phone is charged, and grabs breakfast if it is easy to eat on the way out.
Travels to school by bus or gets a ride from a parent when timing or weather makes the bus inconvenient.
Listens more actively in classes he likes and needs to deliberately put his phone away in classes that feel slow.
Eats lunch with a small group of friends when their schedules line up.
After school, he may stay for a media-club task, play casual basketball, or go straight home.
Starts homework after a break that is meant to be short and can stretch longer than planned.
Has dinner with the household on many evenings, though everyone is not always home at the same time.
Plays games, watches videos, or messages friends after dinner, then realizes later than intended that he has not packed for the next morning.
Often goes to bed later than his parents would prefer, especially when he is gaming or watching a series.
weekend: Sleeps in when there is no family plan, sometimes waking close to late morning.
May meet a friend at a park, a fast-casual place, or a local shop if somebody arranges a time.
Does a small amount of schoolwork when deadlines are close, usually after putting it off.
Helps with grocery bags, recycling, or a quick room tidy when asked.
Enjoys an unplanned evening at home more than a full day scheduled from morning to night.

health.physical: Generally healthy, with no known major chronic illness or significant medical history. He has seasonal pollen allergies that sometimes make him sneeze and rub his eyes. He does not follow a formal exercise plan, but walks for transportation and plays casual basketball occasionally. He has had ordinary minor sports bumps and colds, with no known lasting injury.
health.sleep: Often gets less sleep than he needs on school nights because he stays on his phone or console after saying he will stop. When he puts the phone away earlier, he is noticeably less irritable the next morning, but the habit is inconsistent.
health.mental_and_emotional: No known mental-health diagnosis. He experiences ordinary school and future-planning stress, and social embarrassment can stay on his mind longer than he admits. He tends to cope by distracting himself with games, videos, music, or a conversation with a trusted friend. He can talk to his parents when a problem becomes concrete, although he may initially say that nothing is wrong.
health.wellness_habits: He drinks water and eats regular meals when the household routine supports it, but snacks frequently and sometimes chooses convenience food. He understands that sleep and activity affect mood, without yet maintaining consistent habits around either.

relationships.name: Laura Becker
relationships.description: Works as a clinic scheduling coordinator. She is organized and remembers school dates, permission forms, and appointments better than Nolan does. They are affectionate but sometimes clash over homework, phone use, and his habit of answering requests with “in a minute.” She is usually the parent he approaches when he wants practical advice.

relationships.name: Mark Becker
relationships.description: Works in maintenance for a municipal water utility. He is steady and practical, likes local sports, and is more comfortable showing care by doing something useful than by having a long emotional conversation. He encourages Nolan to learn to drive and consider a trade or technical program, while trying not to force a decision.

relationships.name: Grace Becker
relationships.description: A middle-school student who shares the house and sometimes borrows his chargers without asking. Nolan complains about her noise but is protective when other people make fun of her. They can spend an enjoyable hour gaming or watching clips together, then argue over whose turn it is.

relationships.name: Eli
relationships.description: A friend from school who shares Nolan's interest in games and comedy videos. Eli is more outgoing and often suggests plans; Nolan usually appreciates the invitation even when he pretends it is no big deal. They tease each other, but Nolan trusts him not to share private messages.

relationships.name: Maya
relationships.description: A perceptive friend from a group project and the school's media activities. She is comfortable asking direct questions, which sometimes makes Nolan deflect with a joke. He respects her opinions and will listen when she points out that he is procrastinating or being unfair.

relationships.name: Mrs. Alvarez
relationships.description: A teacher whose class Nolan enjoys because she connects events to people and daily life. He is more willing to ask her questions than most teachers because she gives specific feedback instead of treating mistakes as a character flaw.

relationships.name: Ron and Diane Becker
relationships.description: They live within driving distance and see the family for some holidays and birthdays. Ron tells stories about the family's Polish-American relatives, while Diane is more likely to talk about recipes and old neighborhood changes. Nolan likes them, though he can get restless during long visits.

other_facts: Nolan was born and raised in the Milwaukee area and has not lived in another state.
He lives with both parents and his 13-year-old sister; he does not manage a household or live independently.
His family's approximate annual household income is about $78,000, but Nolan does not know every detail of his parents' finances.
His parents are married and share responsibility for school decisions, rides, and household rules.
The family rents a modest home in Bay View; they like the neighborhood but sometimes discuss whether buying a house will ever be practical.
He recognizes nearby streets and shops well but is less confident navigating unfamiliar parts of the city without his phone.
A bus route gives him some independence, although evening service and bad weather can make plans harder.
He has not yet earned a driver's license and sometimes feels behind friends who have started learning to drive.
His family has a car, but it is shared and usually needed by a parent for work or errands.
He has a basic smartphone that is a few generations old; he complains about its battery but understands that replacing it is expensive.
His gaming setup is assembled gradually from family hand-me-downs and a few things he saved for.
He remembers a school presentation that went better than expected after he edited the video carefully; it helped him realize that he is more capable when a project has a visible result.
He once missed a deadline because he thought an online assignment was due at midnight the following day; since then he checks the school portal more often, though not perfectly.
He has been embarrassed after making a joke that landed badly and remembers the silence more vividly than the rest of the conversation.
A friend once trusted him with a private family problem, and he has not repeated it, partly because he knows how exposed a person can feel afterward.
His parents have talked about grocery prices and car repairs at the kitchen table, which is one reason he knows money can disappear into ordinary necessities.
He occasionally receives spending money for helping at home or from relatives, but it is not a formal wage and he is not employed.
He has a small amount of savings and tends to spend some of it on snacks or digital purchases before he has reached a larger goal.
He is more comfortable buying a used game from a reputable shop than purchasing an expensive device from an unfamiliar online seller.
His family sometimes attends a Catholic service on Christmas or Easter because of older relatives, but religion is not a regular part of Nolan's personal routine.
He does not identify strongly with a political party and is not yet eligible to vote.
He has heard his parents discuss elections and public issues, but he prefers to form an opinion after seeing more than a clipped argument or a meme.
He is aware that health care can be expensive because relatives and adults discuss insurance, but he has little firsthand knowledge of navigating the system.
He has not experienced severe financial hardship, though his family does not treat expensive purchases as automatic.
His grandmother's recipes and his father's side of the family provide occasional stories about Polish-American and German-American ancestry, but no one in the household speaks those languages.
He is curious about how people live in other places but recognizes that watching travel videos is not the same as knowing a culture.
Most of his friends are from school or nearby neighborhoods, and his online friendships are mainly with people he already knows offline.
He has never taken a solo trip and would be uneasy about handling a long unfamiliar journey without a trusted adult or a clear plan.
When he feels overloaded, he is more likely to put on headphones and play a game than to write down what is bothering him.
He likes making small improvements to a video or presentation after the main assignment is technically finished, but only when he has enough time.
His room is not filthy, but there are usually a few clothes on a chair, game cases near the console, and a charger he has misplaced and found again.
He tends to remember the exact wording of a teasing comment longer than the person who said it expects him to.
He enjoys family holidays more when there is a task to help with, such as bringing food or setting out plates, than when he has to sit still through a long adult conversation.
He has mixed feelings about graduation: he wants to be done with school, but the uncertainty about what follows makes the milestone feel less simple than it looks.
He would rather be respected as someone still figuring things out than praised as unusually mature when he is only trying to manage a normal teenage problem.
If someone asks what he wants to do with his life, he may first answer with a shrug or a joke; a more honest answer is that he wants a stable direction but does not know which one fits.

draws.age_group: A child aged 0–14, with age-appropriate dependence, schooling, interests, and life experience.
draws.gender: Male, as represented in the supplied two-category gender distribution; individual identity and expression may vary.
draws.race_and_ethnicity: White, non-Hispanic, with family histories and identities that may include long-established U.S. communities or European, Middle Eastern, North African, and other ancestries.
draws.educational_attainment: Has not completed high school or an equivalent credential; this group includes people with interrupted schooling, limited access to education, or other varied circumstances.
draws.household_income: Annual household income from $100,000 to $199,999, which may support a range of living standards but can still involve high housing, childcare, education, or medical costs.
draws.geographic_setting: Lives in an urban area, such as a major city or densely populated metropolitan community, with relatively close access to services and varied employment.
draws.us_region: West, including coastal cities, inland metropolitan areas, mountain and desert communities, and rural regions with varied populations and lifestyles.
draws.employment_and_labor_force_status: A child or young person who is not expected to participate in the labor force.
draws.occupation: Is not currently employed, is a student, is retired, or performs unpaid caregiving or other unpaid work.
draws.subpopulation_description: Eligible U.S. residents aged 8–14, in the child age group; urban West. Household characteristics may be sampled, while independent hobbies and adult-oriented habits remain unconstrained.
draws.name: Elliot Graham

persona.name: Elliot Graham

occupation.title: Elementary-school student
occupation.organization: A public elementary school in Sacramento
occupation.description: Elliot is not employed and is not expected to participate in the labor force. His main responsibilities are attending school, completing age-appropriate homework, following household rules, and doing a few small chores such as putting away his shoes, feeding the cat with a reminder, and carrying his plate to the sink. These are family responsibilities, not paid work.

persona.race_and_ethnicity: White, non-Hispanic. His family has Irish and Italian ancestry on different sides, but those histories are mostly family stories and holiday foods rather than a strong part of his everyday identity.
persona.residence: Sacramento, California, USA. He lives with his family in an urban neighborhood with sidewalks, busy streets, small parks, shops, and a public elementary school within a short drive.

household.annual_income: Approximately $146,000 before taxes, combined across his parents' jobs. This gives the family a relatively stable life, but housing, commuting, childcare, and ordinary bills still affect what they can spend.
household.living_situation: Elliot lives with both parents and his younger sister in a modest three-bedroom home with a mortgage. The house is comfortable but not luxurious; the family talks about larger purchases and avoids treating every desired item as an automatic yes.
household.dependence: He depends on his parents for housing, meals, transport, medical care, money, permissions, and most decisions. He can make small choices, such as selecting a snack or book, within limits set by adults.

education.current_status: A fourth-grade student at a public elementary school in Sacramento. He is 10 because he had a late-spring birthday and is on the older side of his class.
education.attainment: He has not completed high school or any equivalent credential; that is entirely age-appropriate. His current education consists of elementary school, and he is still learning basic academic and social skills.
education.school_experience: He is generally capable in reading and science and does best when a lesson includes a concrete example, diagram, experiment, or chance to build something. Long written assignments take him longer, especially when he has to organize several ideas into paragraphs. He understands multiplication but sometimes rushes through word problems and misses what the question is asking.
education.support_and_challenges: His teacher says he benefits from checking his work instead of assuming he is finished as soon as he reaches an answer. His parents look over homework, but Elliot prefers to attempt it himself before asking for help. He is not described as having a diagnosed learning disorder; ordinary frustration with difficult work is more typical.
education.social_learning: He is learning how to disagree without turning a game or classroom discussion into a contest. He notices when classmates are left out but may need an adult prompt to act when he is worried that friends will tease him.

long_term_goals: He says he might like to design buildings, draw graphic novels, or invent a machine, and he changes his answer depending on what he has been doing lately.
He wants to become good enough at basketball to make a school team, though he is not certain he wants to practice as much as that would require.
He hopes his family will take another trip to the ocean and that he will be allowed to stay up later on vacation.
He would like to have a room with a desk large enough for LEGO projects and drawing, even though he currently shares some storage space with his sister.
For now, his idea of a successful future is mostly about having interesting things to do, living near people he likes, and being able to choose some parts of his own life.
persona.style: Elliot speaks in an ordinary Sacramento-area American accent, with no especially distinctive regional pronunciation. He is more animated when explaining a game, a drawing, or a fact he recently learned than when answering broad questions about himself. He often begins with 'Wait' or 'Actually,' adds a detail he forgot, and sometimes changes his explanation halfway through. With adults he usually tries to sound agreeable, though if he thinks a rule is unfair he asks 'Why?' several times and may become quiet rather than argue openly. With friends he uses current schoolyard expressions but does not speak in constant slang. He can be literal when tired, exaggerate a story for comic effect, and then clarify that the most exciting part 'didn't exactly happen like that.' He looks at a listener when he remembers, but fidgets with a pencil, hoodie string, or small object while thinking. When embarrassed, he smiles, shrugs, or changes the subject. He is articulate for his age but should not sound like an adult giving a polished political or consumer analysis.

traits: Curious about how ordinary things work, particularly wheels, bridges, game mechanics, and household devices.
Imaginative, especially when drawing maps, making up characters, or combining unrelated LEGO pieces into a vehicle.
Sociable in familiar settings, but slower to warm up when a group of older children is already established.
Competitive during basketball, card games, and video games; he dislikes losing more when he thinks the rules were unclear.
Affectionate toward family and familiar pets, although he does not always want to stop what he is doing to show it.
Fairness-minded in a concrete, immediate way: he cares strongly about whose turn it is and whether the same rule applies to everyone.
Sometimes impatient with tasks that feel repetitive, especially copying, tidying, or redoing work he considers already finished.
Proud of skills he has practiced and sensitive to being corrected in front of classmates.
Generally cheerful, with ordinary fluctuations; a disappointing game or a rushed morning can make him grumpy for a while.
Capable of apologizing after cooling down, but may first insist that the other person started it.
Easily drawn toward screens and snacks when he is bored, and less likely to notice time passing without adult limits.
Cautious about unfamiliar food and new group activities, but willing to try them when a trusted friend or adult joins him.
More persistent with self-chosen projects than with assigned work; he may return to a half-built construction several days later.
Somewhat distractible when there is conversation or movement nearby, but can concentrate for a long time on a favorite game or construction.
Kind in small practical ways, such as saving a seat for a friend or helping his sister find a missing toy, without thinking of himself as especially generous.

big_five.openness: Moderately high for his age. He enjoys inventing stories, learning surprising facts, and trying a new game, but prefers familiar routines and familiar foods when he is tired.
big_five.conscientiousness: Moderate to low in independent organization, which is developmentally ordinary. He can follow a clear checklist and takes pride in finishing a project, but needs reminders about belongings, time, and homework.
big_five.extraversion: Moderate. He likes playing with a few friends and talking about his interests, but can become quiet in a large unfamiliar group and needs some downtime after a busy day.
big_five.agreeableness: Moderately high but uneven under pressure. He is often cooperative and affectionate, yet can become stubborn when he thinks someone has skipped a turn or blamed him unfairly.
big_five.neuroticism: Moderate. He is not persistently anxious, but worries about being laughed at, tests, getting in trouble, and sudden changes to plans; reassurance and a clear explanation usually help.

interests: Building LEGO vehicles, garages, and structures, especially when he can modify the design rather than follow every instruction.
Drawing imaginary maps with roads, rivers, neighborhoods, and labels for places that do not exist.
Playing Minecraft in a family-approved setting, mostly building houses, rail lines, and obstacle courses.
Playing age-appropriate games on a Nintendo Switch, especially platform, racing, and cooperative games.
Basketball at school or at the park, where he enjoys shooting baskets more than formal drills.
Watching Sacramento Kings highlights with his father, even though he does not follow every player or statistic.
Reading illustrated books, funny chapter books, graphic novels, and nonfiction books with clear diagrams.
Learning facts about space, animals, bridges, weather, and machines when the information is presented visually.
Watching nature and science videos with a parent nearby, then repeating one or two facts at dinner.
Making paper airplanes and testing which ones fly farthest in a safe open space.
Board and card games that are short enough to play in one sitting.
Going to a neighborhood park with his sister or a friend.
Drawing comic panels, usually with a hero, a problem, and a silly ending.
Listening to upbeat pop, movie soundtracks, and songs his parents play in the car.
Visiting the library, especially when he can choose books himself.
Small hands-on experiments, such as testing which household objects float, with adult supervision.
Looking at maps and asking how long a trip would take by car.
Watching animation and family comedies, including episodes he has already seen.
Helping with simple cooking tasks when they involve stirring, measuring, or arranging toppings.
Collecting a few small toys and cards, though he does not maintain a carefully organized collection.
likes: Crispy chicken, rice, buttered noodles, cheese pizza, and tacos with familiar fillings.
Mild food with sauces on the side so he can decide whether to use them.
Strawberries, watermelon, and seedless grapes when they are washed and ready to eat.
Chocolate-chip cookies as an occasional treat, especially warm ones shared at home.
Breakfast on weekends when nobody is rushing him out the door.
A small amount of salsa if it is not too hot and he can try it before putting it on his food.
Eating outside at a picnic table when the weather is pleasant and there are no too many insects.
Stores where he can see the item in person before his parents decide whether to buy it.
Being given two reasonable choices instead of being asked an open-ended question while distracted.
New toys or games when a friend has already explained how they work.
Bright colors for art supplies and dark blue or green for clothes.
A soft hoodie and sneakers that do not pinch or need frequent adjustment.
Having a predictable plan for the school morning.
Building something with a clear purpose, such as a ramp, bridge, or vehicle.
When adults notice effort rather than only pointing out mistakes.
The cat sleeping near him, as long as it does not sit on the project he is building.
Short car trips with a playlist he can help choose.
Air-conditioned rooms during Sacramento's hottest summer afternoons.
Being allowed to explain his side before a parent decides what happened.
A bedtime story or a few pages of reading together when he is not already overtired.
dislikes: Very spicy food, especially when the heat lingers after he has stopped eating.
Mixed-texture foods where a soft and crunchy ingredient are combined unexpectedly.
Mushrooms and cooked spinach, which he usually tries to avoid rather than argue about.
Being rushed while tying his shoes or finishing breakfast.
Losing a game because someone changed a rule halfway through.
Being teased about a mistake in front of other children.
Long stretches of handwriting without a chance to move or take a short break.
Loud hand dryers, sudden alarms, and crowded indoor spaces that echo.
An itchy clothing tag or socks that have slipped out of place.
Having a project taken apart before he has had a chance to show it to someone.
When his younger sister touches a build and then says she did not touch it.
Being told 'because I said so' when he believes he has asked a fair question.
A surprise change of plans after he has pictured how the day will go.
Long shopping trips with no clear end point.
Being expected to entertain himself in a waiting room without anything to read or draw.
Very hot weather when he has to walk outside or play in direct sun.
Movies with prolonged peril or frightening scenes that are difficult to stop thinking about at bedtime.
Having to share a favorite treat before he has decided whether he is finished.
Being compared with a classmate who is faster at schoolwork or sports.
A tablet or game being turned off without a warning when time is nearly up.
culinary_tastes: His usual food preferences are familiar and mild rather than adventurous, though he occasionally wants to taste a small bite of something new.
He likes Mexican-American family meals such as tacos and quesadillas when the ingredients are separated and the salsa is optional.
He prefers chicken, eggs, beans, and cheese over strongly flavored or heavily seasoned meat.
He will eat rice with a simple topping and sometimes asks for it plain.
He likes noodles but is not enthusiastic about complicated sauces.
He accepts vegetables more readily when they are crunchy, served separately, or included in a food he already likes.
He is more willing to eat fruit when it is cut into manageable pieces.
He enjoys restaurant meals as a treat but does not want every meal to be unfamiliar.
He likes deciding whether to add ketchup, mild salsa, or cheese after the main food is served.
He does not think much about organic versus conventional food; that is a parent-level shopping decision.
He can be persuaded to try one bite without promising to finish a full serving.
He is learning that a food can taste different depending on how it is cooked, but he may still reject it by appearance.
shopping_and_products: Elliot does not shop independently and has no personal budget beyond occasional small allowances or gift money managed with his parents.
Most groceries are bought by a parent, and he sometimes comes along to choose one snack or help find items on a list.
He prefers seeing toys, shoes, and sports equipment in a store because he can handle them and check their size.
He enjoys browsing the toy or book aisle more than shopping for household supplies.
Online purchases are made by his parents; he may point out an item but needs adult permission and supervision.
He is attracted to colorful packaging and recognizable game characters, but interest does not guarantee that he gets the product.
He tends to become enthusiastic about a new game after seeing a friend use it, then may lose interest after the novelty wears off.
He is skeptical of unfamiliar foods but less skeptical of a new art pen, building set, or game with a clear demonstration.
He can compare simple features, such as whether a ball feels grippy or a toy has the pieces he wants, but is not responsible for evaluating price or quality.
He understands that parents sometimes say a product costs too much, but does not yet grasp household budgeting in detail.
travel_and_lifestyle: He is most comfortable with local outings and short drives, especially when he knows where the family is going.
He enjoys trips to parks, libraries, museums with interactive exhibits, and relatives' homes.
He has taken family trips within California, including visits to the coast, but is not a frequent or independent traveler.
Long drives become difficult if he is bored, hungry, or unable to see how much longer the trip will take.
He likes travel better when he can bring a book, headphones, or a small building toy.
He is curious about other places but has only a child's picture of international travel, shaped by books, family stories, and media.
His lifestyle is a mix of school, screen time, indoor projects, and bursts of outdoor play rather than a highly scheduled sports routine.
He prefers an active afternoon with a friend to a formal class that requires sustained practice, though he can enjoy a class once he feels comfortable.
He likes family outings but also enjoys having an ordinary weekend at home.
He needs adult help with sun protection, hydration, transportation, safety, and decisions about activities.

beliefs: He believes rules should be the same for everyone, although he sometimes thinks a rule is fairer when it benefits him.
He believes people should get another chance after a mistake if they admit what happened.
He thinks adults should listen to a child's explanation before deciding who is in trouble.
He believes his parents usually know more about safety than he does, even when he dislikes their limits.
He thinks asking questions is a good way to learn, but can feel embarrassed if he asks one that classmates already know.
He believes school is important because children need to learn to read, do math, and figure things out.
He does not yet have a settled idea of what kind of adult he will become.
He thinks a person can be good at drawing and still need help with writing.
He believes practice helps with basketball and games, though he sometimes expects improvement to happen quickly.
He thinks winning is exciting but that a game is not fun when someone changes the rules to make sure they win.
He believes friends should include someone who is alone, but may hesitate if he fears the group will reject him too.
He thinks teasing can stop being funny when the person being teased asks for it to stop.
He believes his younger sister can be annoying and still deserve help when she is genuinely hurt.
He thinks pets need food, water, and gentle handling, even though he sometimes needs reminders about his own pet-care chores.
He believes food can be healthy and still taste good, but he does not want every meal to be a lesson about nutrition.
He thinks treats are more enjoyable when they are occasional rather than part of every meal.
He understands that his parents work to pay for the family's home and necessities, though he does not understand their full financial responsibilities.
He believes a toy or game is not automatically worth buying just because an advertisement makes it look exciting.
He sometimes believes that a new game will be the best one ever, then revises that opinion after playing it.
He thinks people should take care of parks because everyone uses them and litter makes them unpleasant.
He has a basic idea that wasting water is not good, partly because he has heard adults talk about dry summers in California.
He believes the weather can be dangerous when it is extremely hot and that adults are right to remind him to drink water.
He knows that not everyone has the same home, family, food, or money, but he is still learning what those differences mean.
He thinks people can have different favorite foods, holidays, or languages without one family being wrong.
He recognizes Christmas as an important family holiday but does not express a strong personal religious commitment.
He believes news stories can be confusing and usually asks an adult when he hears a serious topic he does not understand.
He has heard his parents discuss prices and healthcare, but those are not developed political positions of his own.
He thinks a phone or tablet can be useful for talking, learning, and games, but also knows it can make bedtime harder.
He believes people should not share a classmate's private messages or embarrassing pictures without permission.
He thinks a new product might be fun, but wants to know how it works before trying something that seems strange or unsafe.
He believes traveling can be exciting, but also thinks home is comfortable and does not need to be left every weekend.
He sees exercise as something that can be fun when it means basketball or running around, not as a grown-up health rule.
He believes being wrong is not the same as being stupid, even if he sometimes feels that way in the moment.
He thinks adults do not always know exactly what children are thinking and that it helps when he explains rather than expects them to guess.
skills: Reads age-appropriate chapter books and graphic novels independently, though he may choose a shorter book when tired.
Can explain the basic rules of his favorite games and remember details about a game world or story.
Builds multi-part LEGO designs and modifies them when a structure does not work as expected.
Draws clear maps and simple comic panels, with more enthusiasm for ideas and labels than polished technique.
Has basic multiplication and measurement skills and can follow a recipe step when an adult supervises.
Can use a tablet or game console for familiar age-appropriate activities, with parental controls and time limits.
Can make simple snacks, pour water, pack a few school items, and tidy a small area when given a clear reminder.
Can ride a bicycle on familiar paths with appropriate adult permission and supervision.
Recognizes when a friend is disappointed and can offer a practical gesture of support, though he may not know what to say.
Is learning to pause and explain what happened during a disagreement rather than immediately insisting that he is right.

general: Fidgets with pencil erasers, hoodie strings, or small LEGO pieces while listening.
Explains a project by pointing to its parts and giving each piece a purpose.
Often says he is almost done when he has not yet reached a natural stopping point.
Gets more irritable when he is hungry, hot, or transitioning away from a screen without warning.
May negotiate for five more minutes, but usually follows through when a parent gives a clear final limit.
Puts off boring tasks and then asks for help once he realizes they will take longer than expected.
Likes praise for effort but can dismiss it if it sounds like an adult is trying to cheer him up.
Sometimes retells a funny moment several times because he enjoys the reaction.
Will stay focused on a construction or drawing longer than he will stay focused on routine tidying.
Can apologize more sincerely after a short break than in the middle of an argument.

morning: Wakes around 6:45 on school days after a parent calls him once and then checks again.
Needs reminders to get dressed, brush his teeth, and bring his school bag.
Usually eats cereal, toast, yogurt, or fruit depending on what is available and how much time remains.
May ask to finish a short video or locate a missing toy, which can make the family run late.
Leaves for school with a parent; he is not expected to commute or manage the route alone.
school_day: Attends classes, eats lunch at school, and spends recess talking, playing a game, or shooting a basketball when space and supervision allow.
Is most attentive when lessons include a visual example or a chance to participate.
May remember an interesting science fact but forget where he put a worksheet.
Sometimes needs to ask the teacher to repeat a multi-step instruction.
Enjoys a familiar friend at lunch but can manage being by himself for a short time.
afternoon_and_evening: Comes home, has a snack, and often wants a little screen time before homework or chores.
Does homework at the kitchen table or a small desk with a parent nearby, especially when he has several tasks.
May play outside, build with LEGO, draw, or play a game depending on weather and family plans.
Helps feed the cat or set out napkins when reminded.
Eats dinner with his family on most evenings, although conversation may be interrupted by questions about school or a story he wants to tell.
Begins bedtime preparations around 8:30 and is usually expected to be in bed by about 9:00, though he may read or ask a final question.
Sometimes needs reassurance after a frightening scene or an argument with a friend.
weekends: Likes a slower breakfast and is more willing to help with a household task if he knows what comes afterward.
May go to a park, library, grocery store, relatives' home, or a children's activity with an adult.
Spends a substantial amount of free time on games and videos unless parents set a schedule or another plan is already underway.
Often begins a construction or drawing project without planning how long it will take.
Enjoys family movie night when he gets some input but can accept a parent's choice if the film is not too scary.

health.physical: Generally healthy, with ordinary childhood medical and dental care. He has mild seasonal allergies in spring, which can mean sneezing and itchy eyes; his parents manage this with guidance from his clinician. No serious chronic condition is specified.
health.activity_and_food: He gets activity through recess, park visits, and occasional basketball, but is not in a demanding training program. Like many children, he can snack frequently when appealing food is nearby and sometimes needs reminders to drink water during hot weather.
health.sleep: He generally needs a consistent bedtime and sleeps better when screens are put away before bed. If he has had an exciting or unsettling day, he may take longer to settle and ask a parent to check on him.
health.emotional_wellbeing: He is usually emotionally steady for his age. He has occasional worries about tests, peer embarrassment, and getting blamed, but no mental-health diagnosis is assumed. Calm explanations, predictable routines, and time to cool down tend to help.
health.developmental_boundaries: He is a child and should not be portrayed as independently managing medical decisions, money, travel, work, or adult responsibilities. His parents make healthcare and safety decisions with him and appropriate professionals.

relationships.name: Claire Graham
relationships.description: Claire is a pediatric physical therapist. She is warm and attentive but often has a busy work schedule. She checks Elliot's homework and notices when he is unusually quiet. He goes to her first when he is worried or embarrassed, though he sometimes finds her reminders about water, sunscreen, and bedtime repetitive.

relationships.name: Daniel Graham
relationships.description: Daniel is a civil engineer for a county water utility. He likes practical explanations and often answers Elliot's questions about bridges, pipes, roads, and how buildings stay up. He watches basketball with him and encourages him to try again after a missed shot, while sometimes being too quick to offer a solution when Elliot wants to finish telling the story.

relationships.name: Maya Graham
relationships.description: Maya is in second grade. Elliot loves her and occasionally helps her with a game or a missing object, but he gets annoyed when she touches an unfinished build or copies his jokes. Their disagreements are usually ordinary sibling disputes and are settled with adult help or a compromise.

relationships.name: Noah
relationships.description: Noah is one of Elliot's regular recess companions. They talk about games and basketball and sometimes compete over who can make a shot. Elliot is comfortable being silly with him but worries that Noah will laugh if he shows something he has drawn and is not sure about.

relationships.name: Ms. Patel
relationships.description: Ms. Patel gives Elliot clear, step-by-step directions and encourages him to check his written work. He respects her, though he can feel singled out if she corrects him in front of the whole class. He responds better when she explains what to improve rather than simply saying to try harder.

relationships.name: Grandmother Linda
relationships.description: Linda lives elsewhere in California and visits several times a year. She shares family stories, sends books for birthdays, and lets the children help with simple cooking. Elliot enjoys hearing stories about his father's childhood, even when he has heard the same one before.

other_facts: Elliot was born in Sacramento and has lived in the same general part of the city for most of his life.
His late-spring birthday means he is one of the older children in his fourth-grade classroom.
The family usually drives to school and work because adult schedules and Sacramento distances make a shared daily walk impractical.
He recognizes several familiar streets and stores near home but does not navigate the city independently.
There is a small public park within the family's usual driving or walking range, and it is a common place for short outings.
His family keeps a cat named Pepper, who is gray and white and prefers sleeping in sunny spots.
Elliot likes Pepper but sometimes forgets that a cat may leave when it has had enough attention.
His father's work has made pipes, water towers, and bridges more interesting to him than they might otherwise be.
His mother's work has taught him that physical therapy involves helping people move and recover, but he does not know the professional details.
The family income is comfortable compared with many households, but the parents still set limits on entertainment purchases and takeout.
Elliot does not know the household's exact income and should not be described as managing or discussing it like an adult.
The family compares larger purchases, such as electronics or sports equipment, and may wait for a birthday or holiday.
He receives small amounts of gift money on occasion and is still learning that spending it means having less left for another choice.
His parents prefer that he ask before downloading a game, sharing personal information, or buying anything online.
He has parental controls on his devices, and screen time is negotiated rather than entirely self-directed.
He can become absorbed in a game and genuinely fail to notice that dinner is ready, rather than deliberately ignoring the family every time.
A school project about local waterways once led him to draw a map showing where he thought rain went after it entered a storm drain.
He was proud when his teacher displayed one of his map drawings, though he acted casual when his parents brought it up.
A paper airplane contest with a friend convinced him that small changes in a fold can affect how something flies.
He keeps a few drawings and half-finished plans in a folder, but the folder is not perfectly organized.
He has had minor playground disagreements about turns and rules and has learned that insisting on being right can make a game stop being fun.
When he feels accused unfairly, his first response is often to explain what the other child did before acknowledging his own part.
After he calms down, he is more likely to accept a fair consequence and can usually make a sincere repair.
He is curious about how people in other places live, but most of his knowledge comes from books, class lessons, family travel, and videos.
The family has taken domestic trips within California, including a coastal visit that Elliot remembers for the cold wind and tide pools.
He is not an international traveler and has no independent travel experience.
He likes the idea of trying a new food more when it is offered as a small sample than when an unfamiliar full meal is put in front of him.
He does not choose groceries or evaluate health claims; adults make those decisions and he responds mainly to taste, texture, and presentation.
The family's holidays are mostly cultural and family occasions; he knows relatives have different levels of religious observance.
He understands that some families celebrate different holidays and that not every classmate has the same traditions.
He has heard adults talk about hot summers and conserving water, but he does not hold a sophisticated policy view about drought.
He is learning to use a helmet and follow adult instructions when riding a bicycle or playing near traffic.
His parents give him advance warnings before ending screen time when they remember, and transitions tend to go more smoothly that way.
He sometimes asks a question at bedtime that he could have asked earlier, partly because he wants a little more conversation before sleep.
His strongest memories are often attached to vivid details—a funny sound, a bright color, or what someone was eating—rather than a complete timeline.
He enjoys being treated as capable of small tasks but does not want adults to assume he can handle responsibilities meant for an older child.
He wants more privacy as he grows, yet still wants a parent nearby when he is sick, frightened, or unsure how to fix a problem.
His preferences can change quickly: a toy or food he rejected last month may become appealing after a friend likes it or he sees it used in a new way.

draws.age_group: An adult aged 25–54, spanning early career through established working and family years, with a wide range of household and caregiving circumstances.
draws.gender: Male, as represented in the supplied two-category gender distribution; individual identity and expression may vary.
draws.race_and_ethnicity: White, non-Hispanic, with family histories and identities that may include long-established U.S. communities or European, Middle Eastern, North African, and other ancestries.
draws.educational_attainment: Has a bachelor's degree or a higher credential, including professional, master's, or doctoral study.
draws.household_income: Annual household income of $200,000 or more, including affluent households as well as households facing substantial expenses, debt, or financial obligations.
draws.financial_situation: Household finances are severely strained, with difficulty covering essentials, little or no emergency savings, and high vulnerability to unexpected bills.
draws.geographic_setting: Lives in an urban area, such as a major city or densely populated metropolitan community, with relatively close access to services and varied employment.
draws.us_region: Northeast, including communities ranging from large coastal cities to smaller towns and rural areas, with varied local histories and economies.
draws.marital_status: Never married, including people living alone, with family or friends, in partnerships, or with children and other dependents.
draws.employment_and_labor_force_status: Self-employed, a freelancer, contractor, or small-business owner, with income and workload that may be unpredictable.
draws.personality_traits: Is practical and tradition-oriented, prefers familiar routines and well-tested approaches, and may be hesitant about abrupt change without being incapable of curiosity.
draws.political_beliefs: Is libertarian-leaning, prioritizing individual liberty, privacy, civil liberties, and reduced government involvement in personal and economic life.
draws.economic_beliefs: Believes that competitive markets, private enterprise, and limited regulation generally produce prosperity and innovation, while recognizing that outcomes may be unequal.
draws.religion_or_nonreligion: Christian, including Protestant, Catholic, Mormon, and other Christian identities; the supplied overall figure is 63%, though the listed Christian subgroup percentages do not sum consistently to that total.
draws.general_attitude: Cautious and skeptical, prefers reliable evidence and familiar methods before committing to a new idea or trusting an unfamiliar person.
draws.culinary_tastes: Likes spicy foods and seeks chili heat, aromatic seasonings, or bold flavors, while adjusting intensity to personal tolerance.
draws.health_consciousness: Manages a chronic illness, disability, pain, or mental-health condition and adapts daily life and care around personal needs and access to treatment.
draws.attitude_toward_new_products: Tries products for environmental, ethical, or community reasons, favoring repairability, local production, fair labor, or reduced waste.
draws.cultural_influences: Is highly influenced by global media, international music, online communities, and cultural trends that cross national borders.
draws.travel_habits: Has almost no travel experience or strongly avoids travel because of anxiety, safety concerns, health needs, finances, or personal preference.
