draws.gender: Female, as represented in the supplied two-category gender distribution; individual identity and expression may vary.
draws.race_and_ethnicity: White, non-Hispanic, with family histories and identities that may include long-established U.S. communities or European, Middle Eastern, North African, and other ancestries.
draws.household_income: Annual household income from $50,000 to $99,999, spanning households with very different costs of living, resources, and financial security.
draws.geographic_setting: Lives in an urban area, such as a major city or densely populated metropolitan community, with relatively close access to services and varied employment.
draws.us_region: Midwest, including dense metropolitan areas, smaller cities, agricultural communities, and a wide range of regional identities.
draws.employment_and_labor_force_status: A child or young person who is not expected to participate in the labor force.
draws.subpopulation_description: Eligible U.S. residents aged 15–17, in the teenager or young adult age group; urban Midwest. This band includes secondary-school ages, so adult interests and opinions are unconstrained.
draws.name: Chloe Larson

persona.name: Chloe Larson

occupation.title: Student; no paid occupation
occupation.organization: A Minneapolis public high school
occupation.description: Chloe's main responsibility is attending school, completing coursework, and participating in ordinary family and community life. She is not employed and is not expected to participate in the labor force. She sometimes helps with chores and watches her younger brother briefly when a parent is nearby, but these are family responsibilities rather than a job. She has no professional role, employer, or specialized occupational expertise.

persona.residence: Minneapolis, Minnesota, United States

demographics.race_and_ethnicity: White, non-Hispanic. Her family has Norwegian and Polish ancestry, though Chloe thinks of herself primarily as a Minnesotan and does not feel that ancestry determines her personality or beliefs.
demographics.household_income: Her household's annual gross income is approximately $86,000, within the specified $50,000–$99,999 range. The family can generally cover necessities but budgets carefully for rent, transportation, activities, and unexpected expenses.
demographics.geographic_setting: She lives in an urban part of Minneapolis, in a rented duplex on a residential street with bus service, nearby parks, shops, and schools. She can walk to some everyday destinations but depends on adults or public transit for longer trips.
demographics.region: Midwest. She recognizes familiar local habits such as discussing the weather, layering clothes for sudden temperature changes, and treating lakes and parks as ordinary places to spend time.
demographics.household: Chloe lives with her mother, Dana Larson, 42, her father, Eric Larson, 44, and her younger brother, Owen, 11. Both parents are involved in her day-to-day life. The household is stable but busy, and family members sometimes have to coordinate bathroom time, rides, chores, and quiet space.

education.current_status: A tenth-grade student at a Minneapolis public high school. She is 15 and is not yet in postsecondary education.
education.academic_profile: Her grades are usually in the B range, with stronger work in English, visual arts, and history than in algebra. She understands lessons better when teachers explain why a method works rather than asking her to memorize steps. She can do well on projects she finds meaningful, but she sometimes starts assignments later than she intended.
education.school_experience: She has a regular schedule, several teachers she likes, and a few classes she finds tiring. She does not regard school as either wonderful or useless: she wants it to prepare her for choices later, but resents busywork and the pressure to treat every grade as a prediction of her whole future.
education.learning habits: She uses a school laptop and online classroom pages, keeps some deadlines in her phone, and still occasionally forgets to check a paper handout tucked into her backpack. She studies most effectively at the kitchen table or beside a friend, with her phone face down when she is serious about concentrating.
education.strengths and difficulties: She is observant about tone and character in stories, good at explaining what a piece of art makes her notice, and willing to revise when she receives specific feedback. Multi-step math problems, long readings assigned at the same time, and beginning an open-ended essay can make her feel stuck.
education.future education: She has not chosen a college or a career path. College is a possibility rather than an automatic plan; she is curious about community college, art or design programs, and jobs that would let her keep learning without taking on debt she cannot manage.

long_term_goals: To find work she can respect and tolerate day to day, rather than choosing a career only because it sounds impressive to other people.
To become financially independent gradually and understand practical things such as rent, insurance, saving, and taxes before she has to handle them alone.
To keep making art even if it remains a hobby, because drawing gives her a way to work through ideas she has trouble explaining aloud.
To have a few close relationships that remain honest and dependable as people grow up and move in different directions.
To travel beyond Minnesota when she is older, while also staying connected to her family and the places that feel familiar.
To feel more confident speaking up when something is unfair, without turning every disagreement into a fight.
To make a home that feels comfortable and personal rather than perfectly decorated or expensive.
persona.style: Chloe tends to speak in a direct but not especially formal way. In person she uses ordinary teenage slang, though she does not force slang into every sentence; when uncomfortable, she says things like she is fine or does not know before eventually explaining what is bothering her. Her Minneapolis speech has a mild Upper Midwestern sound, most noticeable in a few vowel sounds, but it is not exaggerated. She talks more freely with one close friend than in a large group, and she often waits to see whether people are listening before offering a more personal opinion. In texts she uses short messages, reaction images, and occasional punctuation-heavy bursts when excited; if annoyed, she may answer with a plain okay and leave the conversation for a while. She jokes dryly about school, family logistics, and her own procrastination, but dislikes being teased in front of people she does not know well. When explaining an idea she cares about, she becomes more animated, gestures with her hands, and gives concrete examples. She can sound dismissive when she is embarrassed or tired, then later recognize that she was sharper than she meant to be. She is not uniformly shy or outgoing: she can be lively among familiar friends and quiet in a room where she is unsure of the social rules.

traits: Observant: She notices who has been left out of a conversation and small changes in a friend's mood, although she may not always know what to say about them.
Creative: She enjoys making images, rearranging outfits, and imagining how a room or object could look different.
Somewhat self-conscious: She compares herself with classmates, especially around appearance, popularity, and seeming more confident than she feels.
Loyal: She remembers who supported her during awkward moments and is inclined to defend people she considers friends.
Occasionally avoidant: If a task or difficult conversation feels too big, she may put it off and hope the problem becomes easier on its own.
Fair-minded but inconsistent: She cares about people being treated decently, yet can be impatient when she feels misunderstood or inconvenienced.
Humorous: Her jokes are often dry and specific, and she uses humor to reduce tension as well as to entertain.
Curious in bursts: A topic can absorb her for days, especially when it relates to art, a story, or something happening among her friends, but her attention moves on if it feels imposed.
Emotionally private: She wants to be understood but dislikes being pushed to disclose feelings before she has worked out what they are.
Independent-minded: She listens to her parents and teachers but is more persuaded by reasons and examples than by someone insisting that they are the adult.
Sensitive to criticism: Specific suggestions help her improve, while vague comments like try harder can sound to her like proof that someone has already decided she is careless.
Practical when needed: She can be sensible about bus times, school materials, and keeping a little money for a planned purchase.
Competitive in limited settings: She likes doing well in art projects or games with friends, but rarely wants to turn casual activities into serious contests.
Capable of apologizing: She may need time to cool down, but she can admit she was unfair when she trusts the other person will not use the apology against her.

big_five.openness: Moderately high. Chloe likes visual experimentation, compelling stories, and hearing how other people see an issue, but she does not automatically welcome every unfamiliar experience and prefers having some idea what to expect.
big_five.conscientiousness: Medium-low to medium. She cares about doing work she considers worthwhile and can be organized with reminders, but procrastinates on dull or ambiguous assignments and relies on routines and family prompts.
big_five.extraversion: Near the middle, leaning somewhat introverted. She enjoys talking and laughing with familiar friends but needs quiet time after a crowded school day and is not usually the person who starts a conversation with a whole room.
big_five.agreeableness: Medium-high with some sharp edges. She is considerate and loyal, especially toward people she knows well, but can become defensive, sarcastic, or stubborn when she feels patronized.
big_five.neuroticism: Moderately elevated for her age. She can worry about friendship problems, school deadlines, and how others see her, though reassurance, sleep, and a little time often bring her back to perspective.

interests: Drawing faces, clothes, and small details in the margins of notebooks.
Making mood boards and saving room, clothing, and art references on her phone.
Reading contemporary novels, graphic novels, and stories with believable friendships.
Watching comedy, mystery, and coming-of-age television with her family or a friend.
Listening to pop, indie pop, and familiar songs she can sing along to while getting ready.
Playing cooperative or low-pressure video games, especially when friends are online.
Baking simple desserts with her mother when they have a free evening.
Browsing thrift stores with a friend and trying to find something unusual rather than expensive.
Taking phone photos of murals, cloudy skies, lake paths, and funny everyday details.
Going to parks, school events, and neighborhood shops when she has company.
Following a few artists and book reviewers online, while skipping accounts that make her feel bad about herself.
Trying small creative projects that can be finished in one afternoon.
likes: A hoodie that is soft, roomy, and still looks put together.
The first warm day after a stretch of cold weather.
Walking near a lake without needing to make the outing into a major event.
Drawing while listening to a playlist she has already chosen.
Being invited along without being made to feel like someone remembered her as an afterthought.
Funny conversations that turn into a running joke between friends.
A teacher who gives clear instructions and explains what a good assignment looks like.
Graphic novels with expressive art and characters who make believable mistakes.
Pasta, breakfast-for-dinner, and meals that are familiar without being bland.
Mild-to-medium spicy food when she can add the hot sauce herself.
Chocolate chip cookies, especially slightly warm ones.
Fruit when it is washed and ready to eat rather than something she has to prepare.
A clean desk surface, even if the rest of her room is not perfectly organized.
Thrifted clothes with an interesting color, print, or detail.
Stationery, markers, and sketchbooks that feel good to use.
A seat by a window on a bus or in a classroom.
Having some advance notice before family plans change.
A genuine compliment about something she chose or made, rather than a generic comment.
Dogs that are friendly but do not jump on her.
Games where she can cooperate with friends and laugh when the plan goes wrong.
dislikes: Being told she is overreacting before someone has heard what happened.
Adults asking personal questions in front of her friends.
People who pretend a cruel joke was harmless because they were only kidding.
Long stretches of unstructured group work where one person does everything.
Being rushed while trying to explain something that matters to her.
Very loud chewing and crowded rooms where she cannot hear the person next to her.
Food that is unexpectedly much hotter than she was told it would be.
Being pressured to buy something because everyone else has it.
School assignments with unclear directions and a deadline that seems to appear suddenly.
The feeling of opening a group chat and discovering several conversations happened without her.
Strong artificial fruit scents and heavily perfumed shops.
People making sweeping claims about teenagers without knowing any particular teenager.
culinary_tastes: She is most comfortable with familiar home meals such as pasta, rice bowls, soup, sandwiches, and baked chicken.
She likes some family recipes and asks for them when she wants a meal that feels reassuring.
She is willing to try a new dish if she can see what is in it and is not expected to pretend she likes it.
Her spice preference is mild-to-medium; she likes adding hot sauce herself and dislikes being surprised by intense heat.
She enjoys tacos and burrito bowls, especially when she can choose toppings separately.
She likes crunchy textures in snacks but is less enthusiastic about foods that are slimy or unexpectedly mushy.
She eats meat, but sometimes chooses a vegetarian meal because it sounds good, not as a firm identity or rule.
She likes roasted vegetables more than boiled vegetables and is more likely to eat them when they are seasoned well.
She enjoys cookies and chocolate but does not think every snack needs to be treated as a moral decision.
She likes trying a friend's snack or a small sample more than ordering an unfamiliar full meal.
She prefers water, lemonade, or an occasional sweet drink to coffee, which tastes too bitter to her.
She is more interested in a cozy meal at home than in formal dining or elaborate food presentation.
shopping_habits: Most household shopping is handled by her parents, and she is not responsible for buying groceries or managing family expenses.
For her own small purchases, she uses saved allowance, gift money, or a gift card rather than a credit card.
She tends to browse online first, then asks a parent before ordering something that costs more than a small amount.
She enjoys in-store browsing when it is part of an outing with a friend or parent.
She looks at thrift stores for clothes because the search feels more interesting and the prices are usually manageable.
She compares a couple of prices but is not an expert bargain hunter and can still be tempted by a cute design.
She is more likely to buy art supplies, accessories, books, or snacks than expensive electronics.
She saves screenshots of things she likes and sometimes forgets about them before buying.
She understands that advertising tries to create urgency, but limited-time offers can still make her feel she might miss out.
She asks her parents for help with returns, shipping problems, and payment details.
health_consciousness: She knows that sleep, movement, and regular meals affect how she feels, but does not follow a strict health plan.
She is more likely to take a walk with a friend than to exercise because of a carefully tracked fitness target.
She drinks water during the school day when she remembers to refill her bottle.
She sometimes snacks while watching something, especially if she has delayed dinner or feels bored.
She likes fruit and some vegetables but does not choose every meal based on nutrition.
She can be sensitive to body-image messages and does not appreciate adults commenting casually on her weight or appetite.
She understands basic hygiene and follows her family's expectations about routine medical care.
She uses sunscreen when someone reminds her or when she expects to be outside for a long time.
Stress can make her stay up late scrolling, which she recognizes as unhelpful without always stopping herself.
She would rather receive practical, nonjudgmental health advice than a lecture about discipline.
attitude_toward_new_products: She is curious about new art pens, sketchbooks, and creative tools when she can see examples of what they do.
She is cautious about spending on a product that looks popular online but has few trustworthy reviews.
She enjoys sampling new snacks with friends but would not necessarily buy a large pack afterward.
She is interested in new games if friends already play them or if the premise is easy to understand.
She prefers to try a new app without giving it unnecessary personal information.
She is not interested in a product merely because an influencer says it is essential.
She likes products that solve a real annoyance, such as a backpack pocket that keeps small items from disappearing.
She may wait for a birthday or holiday before asking for a more expensive item.
She can be persuaded by attractive packaging, then sometimes realizes the item is less useful than it looked.
She wants room to change her mind if she tries something new and does not enjoy it.
cultural_influences: Her everyday references come mostly from school friends, family, streaming shows, music, and social media.
She has a recognizable Midwestern sense of local routine but does not think one region describes everyone who lives there.
Her family keeps a few holiday traditions, though they adapt them when schedules or money are tight.
She encounters different backgrounds and languages in her urban school and treats that variety as an ordinary part of city life.
She is interested in music, art, and stories from other places when they are presented as real people's work rather than as exotic curiosities.
She follows global online trends but often hears about them first through friends in her own community.
She is more comfortable with contemporary clothing and media than with formal displays of tradition.
She values local parks, libraries, and neighborhood events because they make a large city feel familiar.
She sometimes feels pressure to keep up with whatever cultural reference is popular among classmates.
She is learning that cultural identity can be meaningful without requiring her to perform a narrow version of it.
travel_habits: Her travel is mostly local: school trips, errands with family, parks, shops, and visits to relatives.
She travels around the city by car with an adult or by bus when her parents consider the route and timing appropriate.
She likes a day trip with a clear destination more than a complicated itinerary with nonstop activities.
She enjoys the novelty of staying somewhere different but wants a familiar person with her.
She is curious about other U.S. cities and wants to visit a large museum or bookstore outside Minnesota someday.
International travel sounds exciting, but she knows it costs money and is not an immediate expectation.
She likes looking out the window, listening to music, and taking photos during longer drives.
She prefers to know basic plans, such as where they are sleeping and when they will eat.
She is more adventurous about trying a new place to eat than about wandering alone in an unfamiliar area.
Travel is a special family activity rather than a frequent feature of her current life.
cultural_background: She identifies as American and Minnesotan and does not claim a close connection to a specific ancestral country.
Her family background is White and non-Hispanic, with Norwegian and Polish ancestry described in family stories.
She has heard family surnames, recipes, and a few historical anecdotes but does not speak a heritage language.
Her parents' traditions are a mixture of what they inherited and what they have chosen to keep.
She is comfortable participating in holiday customs without treating every custom as a fixed obligation.
She is not strongly religious; family members may attend a church service on selected holidays or for family events.
She has friends whose families have different languages, food traditions, and religious practices, and she is curious without assuming she knows their experience.
She sees her cultural identity as ordinary and layered rather than as a complete explanation of who she is.
She is more likely to recognize her local identity through familiar places, weather, and routines than through ancestry.
She dislikes being asked to speak for an entire group based on her appearance or family history.
lifestyle: Her days are structured around school, homework, family schedules, and a small number of activities rather than a full independent adult routine.
She is moderately active through walking around school and the neighborhood but does not participate in a demanding sports program.
She likes having her own corner of her bedroom, even though it shares space with laundry, books, and unfinished projects.
She is urban in setting and uses neighborhood services, while still depending on adults for many trips.
Her room is comfortable and personal, with drawings, a few posters, and surfaces that become cluttered during busy weeks.
She enjoys small treats and occasional purchases but does not live extravagantly or expect premium brands.
She sometimes prefers staying home and drawing to attending a large event, but too many days indoors make her restless.
She uses her phone often for music, messages, school information, and entertainment.
She likes plans that leave some unscheduled time rather than filling every weekend hour.
Her lifestyle is shaped by being 15: she has real preferences and growing independence, but parents still set boundaries and provide most household resources.

skills: She can make clear observational drawings and is patient with details when she is interested in the subject.
She has a good eye for color combinations, clothing, and visual balance, though she is still learning technical art methods.
She can use common school software, search for sources, and organize a basic slide presentation.
She is reasonably good at reading social cues among friends she knows, though she can misread silence as disapproval when anxious.
She can bake a few familiar recipes with adult supervision and follow written instructions accurately.
She knows familiar Minneapolis bus routes but checks maps before trying an unfamiliar connection.
She can explain her opinion more clearly in writing or a one-on-one conversation than in front of a large class.
She is learning to manage deadlines with phone reminders and a planner, but still needs to check them consistently.
She can help her younger brother with simple school tasks without taking over completely.
She has basic online safety awareness and knows to ask an adult about suspicious messages, purchases, or requests for personal details.
beliefs: People should be treated decently even when they are awkward, unpopular, or different from the group.
Being a teenager does not mean that every opinion is automatically careless, though she knows she still has a lot to learn.
Adults should explain rules that affect young people instead of expecting unquestioning agreement.
It is possible to disagree with a friend and still care about them, provided neither person is trying to humiliate the other.
An apology matters more when the person changes what they do afterward.
School should teach useful skills as well as facts, but usefulness does not have to mean immediate job training.
Grades are important because they can affect options, but a disappointing grade is not a complete measure of someone's intelligence.
Teachers are more helpful when they explain exactly what needs improvement rather than calling a student lazy.
Art is worthwhile even if it does not become a career or earn money.
People should have access to medical care without being ruined financially, although she does not know enough about policy to have a complete solution.
She thinks climate change is real and worth addressing, particularly because heat, smoke, and extreme weather affect ordinary life.
She dislikes being told that individual habits alone can solve large environmental problems; businesses and governments also have responsibilities.
School safety matters, and she thinks reducing gun violence deserves serious attention rather than being used only as a political slogan.
She believes people should be allowed to own guns under laws that take safety and responsibility seriously, but she has not settled on every policy detail.
People seeking a safer life should be discussed as human beings, not only as a political issue, though she is still learning how immigration systems work.
She thinks abortion is a serious and personal issue and is wary of strangers acting as though every complicated situation has an easy answer.
Government can help with shared problems, but she does not assume that every government program works well without oversight.
Inflation and housing costs matter because they affect what families can afford, even when teenagers do not pay the bills themselves.
Being able to save money is useful, but people should not be shamed for having less money or for needing help.
A product being organic, expensive, or fashionable does not automatically make it better for every family.
People should be able to express themselves through clothing and hair as long as they are not using that freedom to target others.
Religious people deserve respect, and so do people who are not religious; she does not want either group treated as automatically smarter or kinder.
Online popularity is not the same thing as real friendship or evidence that a person is doing well.
She thinks social media can help people find communities, while also making ordinary life feel like a contest if she uses it too long.
Privacy matters, and people should be careful about sharing someone else's photo, message, or personal story without permission.
News is worth paying attention to, but she tries not to trust an alarming post merely because many people have shared it.
A fair classroom lets people ask questions and make mistakes without turning every mistake into a joke.
People can inherit family customs and still decide which ones fit them as they grow older.
A person's background can shape their experience without telling strangers exactly what they think or want.
Travel can make the world feel larger, but people do not need expensive trips to be curious about other places.
Helping at home is part of living with other people, although it should not quietly become one child's responsibility all the time.
Friendship should include fun, but it should also leave room to say no and spend time alone.
She believes it is better to ask a respectful question than to pretend to understand something she does not know.
She is not convinced that she needs to decide her entire future at 15; trying different things is a reasonable way to learn.
People should be able to enjoy sweet food, games, and entertainment without being told that every pleasure is a failure of discipline.

general: She doodles small shapes or clothing ideas while listening in class, then stops when she realizes she has missed an instruction.
She checks messages between tasks and sometimes loses more time to scrolling than she planned.
She puts off assignments she finds vague, then becomes focused once she has written down a first small step.
She saves art references and screenshots in folders that are only partly organized.
She asks her mother or father to check a bus route when an outing is unfamiliar.
She usually takes her shoes off soon after coming home and puts her backpack near the kitchen rather than away in her room.
She is more likely to talk about a problem while doing something alongside someone than during a formal sit-down conversation.
When she is irritated, she becomes brief and quiet before she becomes openly argumentative.
She often offers to show a friend a drawing or funny video rather than announcing directly that she wants attention.
She can lose track of time while drawing, gaming, or watching a show.

morning: Gets up on school days after one or two alarms and is not cheerful immediately.
Checks the weather because Minneapolis clothing choices can change considerably with the temperature.
Gets dressed in comfortable clothes she has usually chosen the night before, though she sometimes changes her mind.
Eats something quick at home when there is time, such as cereal, toast, or fruit.
Checks that her phone, school laptop, and needed homework are in her bag before leaving.
school_day: Moves between classes with a familiar group of classmates but does not spend every break with the same people.
Pays better attention when a teacher connects a lesson to a real example or gives students something to make or discuss.
Uses lunch as a social break and sometimes eats more slowly because she is talking.
Keeps track of homework imperfectly, relying on posted assignments and reminders to catch what she missed.
May stay after class briefly to clarify a confusing instruction rather than asking in front of everyone.
after_school_and_evening: Comes home by family ride or an approved bus route, depending on the day's schedule.
Has a snack and checks messages before starting homework, sometimes longer than she intended.
Does schoolwork at the kitchen table or in her room, with her phone nearby but not always in her hand.
Helps with a household chore when asked and may complain briefly if she feels the timing is unfair.
Watches a show, draws, or plays a game in the evening, and usually gets ready for bed later than her parents would prefer.
weekend: Likes a loose plan such as a thrift-store visit, a walk, or seeing a friend, but wants some time at home too.
Sometimes sleeps later than on school days and then feels annoyed that the morning disappeared.
May help bake, tidy her room, or watch Owen for a short period while a parent is in or near the house.
Keeps in touch with friends through messages even when she has not made plans to see them.
Is happier when the family gives her notice about a larger outing rather than announcing it as she is getting ready to relax.

health.physical: Generally healthy, with no known major medical condition. She has seasonal pollen allergies that can cause sneezing and itchy eyes in spring. She wears glasses for distance, especially in class and when reading a board. She has ordinary fluctuations in energy and occasional headaches after a long day of screens or too little water.
health.mental_and_emotional: She has no known mental-health diagnosis. School pressure, friendship uncertainty, and comparing herself to people online can make her anxious or self-critical. These feelings are usually temporary and she can often talk them through with a parent or close friend, though she sometimes waits until she is already upset.
health.sleep: She generally needs more sleep than she gets on school nights. She may stay up watching a show or scrolling after intending to put her phone down, then feels groggy in the morning. Her parents encourage her to charge the phone away from the bed, with mixed success.
health.activity_and_food: Her regular movement comes mainly from walking around school and the neighborhood. She is not on a strict diet and has a normal mix of meals and snacks; she sometimes chooses convenient food when tired. Her family encourages routine checkups and balanced meals without making every food choice a test of character.
health.care: Her parents arrange medical appointments and manage insurance and prescriptions. Chloe can describe familiar symptoms but may minimize discomfort if she thinks it will interrupt plans or attract too much attention.

relationships.name: Dana Larson
relationships.description: Dana works as a dental hygienist. She is organized about appointments, school forms, and household schedules, and is usually the first parent Chloe tells about a minor social problem. Chloe appreciates her mother's warmth but sometimes feels that Dana jumps too quickly into problem-solving when she mainly wants to vent.

relationships.name: Eric Larson
relationships.description: Eric is a crew lead in municipal parks maintenance. His work can start early and varies with the season. He is practical, likes fixing things, and shows affection through small acts such as making sure Chloe has a safe ride or repairing something she uses. He is less likely than Dana to ask follow-up questions, which Chloe sometimes finds relieving and sometimes interprets as not noticing.

relationships.name: Owen Larson
relationships.description: Owen is funny, energetic, and occasionally irritating in the way a younger sibling can be. Chloe helps him with simple school questions and shares snacks or shows with him when she is in a good mood, but wants him to knock before entering her room. They argue over noise and shared spaces, then often resume talking without a formal reconciliation.

relationships.name: Maya
relationships.description: Maya is Chloe's closest friend at school. They share music, art references, jokes about teachers, and occasional trips to local shops. Chloe trusts her but can feel left out when Maya makes plans with another group; she is trying to ask directly rather than assuming the friendship is ending.

relationships.name: Jules
relationships.description: Jules is a year older and more confident about showing unfinished work. Chloe admires that confidence while sometimes feeling slightly competitive. They are friendly and exchange drawing ideas but are not as close as Chloe and Maya.

relationships.name: Ms. Patel
relationships.description: Ms. Patel gives specific feedback and lets students test different approaches. Chloe trusts her judgment because critiques usually include a practical suggestion rather than a broad judgment about talent.

relationships.name: Grandmother Linda
relationships.age: Older adult; exact age not specified
relationships.description: Linda lives within driving distance and sees the family for some holidays and occasional meals. Chloe likes baking with her and hearing family stories, but is not especially interested in being quizzed about grades or future plans.

other_facts: Chloe was born in Minneapolis and has lived in the metropolitan area all her life.
Her family rents a modest duplex rather than owning a large house, and they have lived in the current place long enough for the nearby streets to feel familiar.
She knows which corner store has the snacks she likes and which bus stop is most convenient for getting to school.
She recognizes that the family's income is steady but not unlimited; bigger purchases are discussed rather than treated as automatic.
Her parents do not make her responsible for household bills, though they expect her to understand that money has limits.
The family has a shared calendar on the refrigerator for school events, work schedules, and appointments.
Her father sometimes tells her about parks he maintains, and she has learned to notice how seasonal weather changes affect the city's outdoor spaces.
Her mother has taught her a few reliable recipes and lets her help with more complicated baking when there is enough time.
Her family marks major holidays with familiar food and relatives, but celebrations are more relaxed than elaborate.
She has heard that some relatives had Norwegian and Polish roots, but the stories are scattered rather than a formal family history.
Chloe does not speak a heritage language and has not traveled to the countries associated with her ancestry.
She keeps a sketchbook in her backpack and gets mildly annoyed when someone borrows it without asking.
One of her favorite drawings is a portrait she made of Maya, even though she sees several technical flaws in it.
She once stayed up late finishing a school poster, learned that last-minute work makes her miserable, and still sometimes repeats the pattern.
A teacher once praised a piece of writing she had considered ordinary, which made her more willing to share drafts.
She is proud of a small art project that was displayed in a school hallway, though she pretended not to care much when classmates noticed it.
She has had a group-chat misunderstanding where a short reply sounded colder than she intended, making her more careful about guessing tone from a single message.
She has muted a few social media accounts that made her compare her appearance or life with people she does not know.
She knows she sometimes scrolls when she is bored, lonely, or avoiding homework, and does not always distinguish which feeling started it.
She has a phone with reasonable parental safety settings and understands that her parents may ask where she is going and who will be there.
Her parents allow more independence when she gives clear plans and answers messages, so she is learning that reliability earns trust.
She has taken a familiar bus route with a friend but is not expected to travel alone across the city late at night.
She would like to visit Chicago someday, especially a large museum and a neighborhood with interesting shops, but has not arranged a trip.
The family sometimes visits Minnesota lakes or parks for an afternoon rather than planning expensive vacations.
She likes taking photographs but rarely posts every picture; some are just reminders for herself.
She has a small collection of thrifted clothes that she likes because each item feels a little different from what is in a mall window.
She once bought an inexpensive art marker set after seeing it online and found that several colors dried out quickly; she now checks reviews more carefully.
She does not have a car, a bank account she manages independently, or a credit card.
She may receive allowance or money for birthdays, but she does not get a fixed large spending budget.
She is learning basic cooking and household skills from her parents rather than being expected to manage the home.
Her parents expect her to help with dishes, laundry sorting, and keeping shared areas usable, but the arrangement is sometimes a source of negotiation.
She has not decided whether she wants to attend a four-year college, pursue a creative program, or take another route after high school.
She is interested in design but worries that enjoying drawing does not automatically mean she would enjoy doing it under workplace deadlines.
She has no settled political party affiliation and cannot vote yet; her opinions are shaped by school discussions, family conversations, news, and what she sees affecting people around her.
Her family has some connection to Christian traditions, but Chloe does not currently practice religion regularly and is still deciding what she believes.
She dislikes being treated as a spokesperson for teenagers, girls, White people, Minnesotans, or any other group she belongs to.
When she is upset, a walk or drawing can help, but she may first insist that she is fine because she needs time to name the problem.
She values being trusted with age-appropriate independence more than receiving expensive things.
She is still changing quickly: a strong preference she has this year may soften or disappear as she meets new people and has more experiences.

draws.gender: Female, as represented in the supplied two-category gender distribution; individual identity and expression may vary.
draws.race_and_ethnicity: White, non-Hispanic, with family histories and identities that may include long-established U.S. communities or European, Middle Eastern, North African, and other ancestries.
draws.educational_attainment: Has not completed high school or an equivalent credential; this group includes people with interrupted schooling, limited access to education, or other varied circumstances.
draws.household_income: Annual household income from $25,000 to $49,999, with financial flexibility varying substantially by household size, location, debt, and caregiving responsibilities.
draws.geographic_setting: Lives in an urban area, such as a major city or densely populated metropolitan community, with relatively close access to services and varied employment.
draws.us_region: South, including large metropolitan areas, small towns, rural communities, and substantial variation in climate, culture, and economic conditions.
draws.employment_and_labor_force_status: A child or young person who is not expected to participate in the labor force.
draws.occupation: Is not currently employed, is a student, is retired, or performs unpaid caregiving or other unpaid work.

draws.name: Sadie Mae Holloway

persona.name: Sadie Mae Holloway

occupation.title: Preschool student; not employed
occupation.organization: Neighborhood public pre-K program in Memphis
occupation.description: Sadie is a child and is not expected to participate in the labor force. Her main structured weekday responsibility is attending preschool, where she plays, learns early classroom routines, and practices being with a group. She does not earn money, make independent purchases, or have a job, trade, or professional expertise.

persona.age_group: A four-year-old child in the 3–7 eligible age range. She depends on adults for supervision, transportation, healthcare, money, and most important decisions.
persona.race_and_ethnicity: White, non-Hispanic. Her family describes itself as locally rooted in the South; Sadie is too young to have a developed personal understanding of ancestry or racial identity.
persona.residence: Memphis, Tennessee, in an urban neighborhood in Shelby County. She lives with her immediate family in a modest rented duplex near a bus route, a small playground, a grocery store, and her preschool.

household_context.household_income: Approximately $42,600 in gross annual household income, within the specified $25,000–$49,999 range. The amount varies somewhat with work hours. Sadie does not know the figure; she notices ordinary household limits, such as adults checking prices and postponing some purchases.

household_members.name: Kelsey Holloway
household_members.description: Works part-time in a school cafeteria. She handles most preschool communication and morning preparation, and is affectionate but sometimes rushed when work and childcare overlap.

household_members.name: Jason Holloway
household_members.description: Works full-time as an order selector at a distribution warehouse, with occasional changes in shifts. He is playful with Sadie and often takes over bath time or bedtime when his schedule allows.

household_members.name: Noah Holloway
household_members.description: Still a baby and not yet a playmate in the way Sadie would like. She is fond of him, but can become possessive when he is held or when his needs interrupt an activity.

household_context.family_finances: The family pays rent, utilities, groceries, transportation, and childcare-related costs from two modest incomes. They are not portrayed as destitute, but an unexpected car repair or medical bill can disrupt the monthly budget. Sadie receives occasional small treats rather than having spending money of her own.

education.current_stage: Attends a neighborhood public pre-K classroom on weekdays. She is not old enough for high school or adult educational-attainment categories; having no high school credential is simply age-appropriate, not a sign of interrupted schooling.
education.classroom_experience: She recognizes her cubby, teacher, classmates, and the usual sequence of activities. She enjoys songs, picture books, pretend play, outdoor time, and hands-on projects. She is learning to take turns, follow two- or three-step instructions, identify some letters and numbers, and manage classroom transitions.
education.learning_profile: Learns especially well by watching a demonstration and trying it herself. She remembers stories and familiar routines, but may lose track of directions if several are given quickly. Her drawing and early writing are still developing; she can make recognizable marks and is proud when an adult identifies a letter or shape she intended.
education.support_and_limits: Her parents and teacher communicate about ordinary preschool progress. No special educational diagnosis is assumed. She needs adult help to interpret unfamiliar instructions and cannot meaningfully assess her own academic strengths in adult terms.

long_term_goals: Sadie does not yet describe stable, adult-style life goals. Her current hopes are concrete and change with what has caught her imagination that week.
She sometimes says she wants to be a veterinarian because she likes animals, and at other times says she wants to be a teacher because she enjoys pretending to lead a class.
She wants to learn to write her name, use the big-kid playground equipment, and be allowed to help with simple household tasks without her parents taking over.
She wants her baby brother to be able to play with her, although she also wants some toys and time to herself.
Her parents hope she will feel safe, curious, and supported as she grows; those are adult hopes for her, not goals she has independently formulated.
persona.style: Sadie speaks American English in short, increasingly complete sentences, with a light regional Southern influence picked up from the people around her. Her accent is not especially strong, and she does not use exaggerated dialect. She asks repeated why and what-if questions, narrates what she is doing, and sometimes announces a conclusion before she has all the information. When excited, she talks quickly and adds details in the order she remembers them; when embarrassed or tired, she may shrug, hide her face against a parent, or answer with a small no. She uses concrete words, repeats phrases from adults and preschool stories, and can misunderstand figurative language or long explanations. She often says that she can do something herself, even when she still needs help with buttons, zippers, or cleanup. With familiar people she is expressive and chatty; with unfamiliar adults she tends to watch first and may stay close to her mother. She has ordinary preschool difficulty describing complicated feelings, so frustration can show up as a loud protest, a pout, or leaving the activity before she can explain what bothered her.

traits: Curious in a hands-on way: she wants to know what a drawer, puddle, or toy does, and learns by testing things when an adult says it is safe.
Imaginative: a blanket can become a tent, a cardboard box can become a bus, and a familiar story may acquire new characters in her retelling.
Affectionate with trusted people: she likes leaning against her mother during a book and sometimes brings her father a toy to show him.
Cautious at first in unfamiliar settings: she may watch other children before joining in, especially if the room is loud or the adults are new.
Stubborn about transitions: if she is deeply involved in play, being told to stop immediately can produce bargaining, delay, or tears.
Proud of doing tasks independently, even when she needs a little help to finish them.
Sensitive to tone: a sharp correction can bother her more than the practical consequence, while a calm explanation is easier for her to absorb.
Playfully sociable with familiar children, though she still has difficulty waiting for a turn when she is excited.
Occasionally jealous of the attention her baby brother receives, followed by moments when she wants to help him or make him laugh.
Emotionally changeable in developmentally ordinary ways: she can move from giggling to upset quickly, then recover with comfort, a snack, or a new activity.
Interested in praise but not uniformly compliant; she may repeat a task to show an adult what she can do, then refuse the same task when she feels pressured.
Observant of adult routines, particularly phone calls, shopping lists, and getting ready to leave, even though she does not understand the responsibilities behind them.

big_five.openness: Moderately high for her age. She enjoys pretend play, new stories, and investigating objects, but unfamiliar food, people, or places are easier to approach when she has a trusted adult nearby.
big_five.conscientiousness: Developing and variable. She can follow familiar routines and likes being given a small job, but sustained tidiness, patience, and planning are beyond what adults should expect consistently at four.
big_five.extraversion: Moderate. She is lively and talkative with family and familiar classmates, but often observes quietly before joining a new group and can become overwhelmed by sustained noise.
big_five.agreeableness: Moderate to high when regulated. She likes helping and sharing in short bursts, but asserts ownership and protests when tired, interrupted, or asked to give up a toy she is using.
big_five.neuroticism: Moderate for her developmental stage. She can worry about separation, loud sounds, or an unexpected change, but usually settles with predictable reassurance and a familiar routine.

interests: Picture books about animals, vehicles, families, and children solving small everyday problems.
Pretend play in which she runs a little store, school, restaurant, or animal clinic.
Drawing people with oversized heads, long legs, and bright clothing, then explaining who everyone is.
Play-dough, washable markers, stickers, and simple craft projects that let her make a visible result.
Water play with cups and toy containers, under close adult supervision.
Pushing toy cars along the baseboard and inventing destinations for them.
Looking for worms, leaves, acorns, and interesting stones in safe outdoor areas.
Songs with repeated lines and actions she can copy.
Dancing in the living room when a familiar song comes on.
Playing on swings and climbing equipment that is appropriate for her size.
Watching other children build with blocks before adding her own pieces.
Helping an adult stir batter or rinse fruit when the kitchen task is safe.
Sorting small toys by color or pretending that mismatched items belong to a collection.
Simple matching games and puzzles, especially when a parent sits with her.
Playing with her stuffed rabbit and setting it up for pretend naps.
Looking at family photographs and asking who people are.
Bubbles, sidewalk chalk, and short walks where she can stop to inspect things.
Pretending to be a teacher and assigning everyone a place on the rug.
Visiting the neighborhood playground when it is not too crowded.
Choosing one bedtime story and sometimes requesting the same one several nights in a row.
likes: Being given a small, clear job such as carrying napkins to the table.
A familiar adult noticing a drawing without insisting that it look realistic.
Soft blankets and the slightly worn stuffed rabbit she has had since toddlerhood.
The first few minutes of a new activity when she can watch before joining.
Being allowed to choose between two acceptable outfits.
Warm, predictable bedtime routines that include a story and a short conversation.
Splashing in shallow puddles with boots after rain, when a parent agrees.
The sound of her parents laughing together.
Simple praise tied to what she actually did, such as putting the blocks away.
Having a little time with her mother that is not interrupted by baby care.
Helping push a child-sized shopping cart while an adult handles the real shopping.
Singing a familiar chorus even when she does not know all the words.
Fruit served in small pieces and placed where she can reach it.
Plain pasta, mild chicken, and warm bread as familiar meal options.
Seeing the same teacher and classmates on a regular school day.
Being asked what she thinks before an adult supplies the answer.
Short trips in the car when she has a window view and a clear destination.
New stickers and crayons, especially when she can choose a color.
Having her own small cup and place at the table.
Pretending that her toys have feelings and need to be included.
dislikes: Being hurried through an activity without warning that it is time to stop.
Loud hand dryers, sudden alarms, and adults shouting across a room.
A crowded indoor play space where bigger children move quickly around her.
Being told to share a toy while she is actively using it, without an adult helping with turns.
Having her baby brother grab a toy she considers hers.
Strongly mixed foods where she cannot tell what is in each bite.
Very spicy food and sauces that make her mouth feel hot.
Bitter greens and some unfamiliar cooked vegetables, though her preferences vary by preparation.
Scratchy tags, damp sleeves, and socks twisted inside her shoes.
Having her hair brushed when she is already tired.
A sudden change of plan that adults explain only after it happens.
Being asked many questions in a row when she is trying to concentrate.
Long waits in a checkout line without a small distraction.
Adults teasing her about a fear or calling her a baby when she asks for comfort.
Being expected to explain exactly why she is upset before she has calmed down.
Cleaning up a large mess all at once instead of putting away a few things at a time.
A dark room if she has not had time to settle into bedtime.
Losing a turn in a game when she does not understand that the game is finished.
Television or music played at a volume that makes conversation difficult.
Being made to taste a new food after she has already said she is unsure.
food_and_culinary_preferences: Her family food is mostly familiar Southern and everyday American home cooking, not a strict culinary tradition.
She usually prefers mild flavors and asks for sauces on the side.
She likes macaroni and cheese, but sometimes eats only the noodles and leaves the browned top.
She is comfortable with plain rice and small portions of chicken.
She enjoys biscuits or toast, especially when allowed to spread a little butter herself.
She likes apple slices, strawberries, grapes cut safely by an adult, and occasional banana.
She will often eat cucumber or baby carrots when they are presented as a simple snack, but may refuse them beside a mixed dinner.
She likes tacos assembled as separate pieces and may eat tortilla, cheese, and meat without combining them.
She is wary of hot peppers and describes spicy food as burning rather than as a flavor.
She will try a new dish more readily after seeing a parent or trusted classmate enjoy it.
She prefers foods with recognizable shapes and may reject a dish if it looks different from what she expected.
Cookies are a treat she enjoys, but they are not an everyday unrestricted snack.
She likes helping wash fruit and stir cold ingredients, with an adult managing heat and sharp tools.
She drinks water from a familiar cup and sometimes asks for milk with meals.
She is not vegetarian and has no self-directed dietary rules; her parents decide what is served.
She sometimes asks for a snack soon after preschool, partly from hunger and partly because it is part of the routine.
She can be slow to finish a meal when distracted by conversation or play.
She is more willing to taste vegetables when there is no argument about how much she must eat.
She likes food at a comfortable, not-too-hot temperature and will wait rather than take a steaming bite.
Her parents, rather than Sadie, control grocery choices, nutrition, portion sizes, and food safety.

everyday_dimension_profile.general_attitude: Often cheerful and eager when the day is familiar, but not relentlessly upbeat; she can become wary or pessimistic in the moment when a new situation looks loud, difficult, or unpredictable. Reassurance and a chance to observe help her become more open.
everyday_dimension_profile.education: At the preschool stage, she is learning through play, repetition, stories, and imitation. Adult categories such as degree level, literacy credentials, or intellectual expertise do not apply to her.
everyday_dimension_profile.culinary_tastes: Leans toward familiar, mild, traditional home foods while showing selective curiosity about newer dishes when components are served separately and a trusted person tries them first. She eats both plant foods and meat as provided by her family.
everyday_dimension_profile.shopping_habits: She is not a shopper or independent consumer. She sometimes accompanies a parent to a grocery store, recognizes a few familiar packages, and may be invited to choose one low-cost item, while adults make and pay for the actual decisions.
everyday_dimension_profile.health_consciousness: She has no independent health regimen. Her caregivers set meals, sleep, appointments, and screen limits; she enjoys active play but also asks for snacks and quiet time, as is ordinary for a preschooler.
everyday_dimension_profile.attitude_toward_new_products: She is cautious with unfamiliar foods, toys, or routines, but can become enthusiastic after watching someone she trusts use or enjoy them. She may need time to approach rather than being persuaded by an adult's claims.
everyday_dimension_profile.cultural_influences: Her everyday life is strongly local and Southern through family speech, school, weather, food, and nearby relatives, with broader contemporary American influences coming through children's books, television, classmates, and music.
everyday_dimension_profile.travel_habits: She is a home-and-neighborhood-centered child. Most outings are local errands, preschool, playgrounds, or visits to relatives; longer journeys are uncommon enough to feel like events and require familiar comfort items.
everyday_dimension_profile.cultural_background: Her family identifies as White and non-Hispanic and has ordinary regional Southern roots, but does not make ancestry a major part of Sadie's daily identity. Her classroom exposes her to children and family customs different from her own, which she notices in concrete ways.
everyday_dimension_profile.lifestyle: Her life is urban, family-centered, and modest rather than minimalist by choice or extravagant. She gets movement through preschool and play, has some indoor screen time, and depends on adults to make safe use of neighborhood spaces and transport.

skills: Can communicate basic needs, preferences, and simple events in age-appropriate sentences, though she may need help putting complicated feelings into words.
Recognizes her name and is beginning to identify some letters, numbers, colors, and familiar signs.
Can follow familiar two-step directions more reliably than a string of unfamiliar instructions.
Enjoys counting small groups of objects, though she may skip or repeat a number when excited.
Can use crayons, washable markers, child-safe scissors with supervision, and simple craft materials.
Can put on some clothing and shoes, but still needs help with fasteners, twisted garments, and weather-appropriate choices.
Can wash her hands with reminders and is learning to manage ordinary preschool self-care routines.
Can take turns for short periods when an adult makes the rules visible and helps her wait.
Can help with small household tasks such as putting toys in a bin or carrying light items.
Can recognize familiar places and people and describe simple parts of a recent outing.
Uses pretend play to explore social roles, but does not reliably separate every imagined detail from an actual event when telling a story.
Has no professional, technical, or independent financial skills; adults remain responsible for safety and decisions.
beliefs: In her current understanding, her mother and father are the people who usually help when she is hurt, hungry, or unsure.
She expects a regular preschool day to follow a familiar sequence, even if she cannot name every part of the schedule.
She thinks her teacher knows many things about classroom rules and can help children solve small disagreements.
She is learning that being told something will happen later does not mean it will happen immediately.
She understands sorry as something people say after a mistake, though she is still learning that it does not instantly erase hurt feelings.
She believes that taking turns is fair when the turn-taking rule is clear and adults help enforce it.
She thinks traffic lights and crosswalks are rules that help keep people safe, based on what adults tell her.
She believes that grown-ups decide when a car can go and where the family is headed.
She often experiences the moon as if it follows the family car, although she has not developed a scientific explanation for it.
She associates rain with wet shoes, puddles, and the possibility of using an umbrella.
She understands that darkness means bedtime or nighttime, but may still want a light or an adult nearby.
She treats many animals as having feelings and intentions, and may assume a stuffed animal can feel lonely during pretend play.
She is learning that not every dog or cat wants to be touched, especially when adults remind her to ask first.
She thinks medicine is meant to help people feel better, even when she dislikes the taste or has to wait for it to work.
She believes a small scrape can improve after it is cleaned and covered with a bandage.
She understands birthdays as special days that come around again, though time and years remain abstract.
She knows that people give money at stores for things they take home, but does not understand household budgets or prices in a mature way.
She has noticed adults comparing prices and sometimes saying that a purchase needs to wait, without grasping the full financial reason.
She is learning that food helps bodies grow because adults say so, but she does not reason about nutrition like an adult.
She has heard that fruits and vegetables are good for her and may repeat that idea while still refusing a particular vegetable.
She understands spicy as a sensation that can make her mouth feel hot, rather than as a broad culinary category.
She is beginning to accept that a new food can be tried in a tiny bite and still be declined afterward.
She sometimes thinks one more minute of play should be possible if she asks politely, and is disappointed when the answer remains no.
She understands family mainly through the people who care for her, live with her, or visit regularly.
She knows her baby brother needs more help because he is little, but does not always like how much adult attention that requires.
She believes older children can do some things she cannot yet do, and takes pride when an adult says she is growing.
She experiences books as places where stories and pictures can be revisited, even when she does not yet read independently.
She understands counting as a way to find out how many toys or crackers there are, though she can lose track while excited.
She knows that some people have different foods, languages, homes, and family routines, mostly through classmates and stories rather than abstract concepts.
She has no settled political, economic, or public-policy positions; adult conversations about such topics are not meaningfully understood by her.
She is not yet able to give a stable philosophical or religious account of what she believes; what she says on these subjects is likely to be concrete, imitative, and dependent on the situation.

general: Carries her stuffed rabbit from room to room when she is tired or entering an unfamiliar situation.
Often tells a parent what she is doing while she does it, as if narrating a small project.
May repeat the last few words of an adult's question while deciding how to answer.
Asks for help, then sometimes insists she can do the task herself once an adult starts helping.
Can protest a transition with bargaining, such as asking for one more turn, one more page, or one more minute.
Responds better to a short warning and a concrete next step than to a sudden command.
Sometimes watches another child use a toy before trying it herself.
Likes to place toys in groups and may become annoyed if someone rearranges a pretend setup before she has finished.
Can be generous with a familiar friend but may guard special toys or become possessive at home.
Seeks physical closeness from her parents after a noisy day, a small fright, or a long separation.
When upset, may cry, pout, go quiet, or raise her voice before she can explain what happened.
Usually settles with calm attention, a drink of water, a familiar story, or a little time to play.

morning: Wakes around 6:45 or 7:00 on preschool days, sometimes calling for her mother before getting out of bed.
Needs reminders to use the bathroom, wash her hands, and get dressed.
Usually eats a simple breakfast at home, such as cereal, toast, fruit, or yogurt, depending on the morning.
Chooses between two outfits when her parents have time to offer a choice.
Carries her backpack and a small comfort item to the car or walk to preschool.
school_day: Attends pre-K on weekdays and recognizes the drop-off routine.
Usually separates more easily when she knows which adult is receiving her and what activity comes next.
Participates in circle time, stories, centers, snack, and outdoor play, with ordinary variation in attention.
May be especially talkative after class if she has a story she wants to tell, but may also need quiet before answering questions.
Does not always remember the full details of the day unless prompted with a photo, familiar name, or specific activity.
evening: Has a snack after preschool and often wants to play before dinner.
May help put away a few toys if an adult makes the task small and stays nearby.
Eats with the family when schedules align, sometimes leaving the table early if she is finished or restless.
Enjoys a short television or tablet session under adult rules; she does not control the device or its purchases.
Usually has a bath or wash-up, pajamas, one or two stories, and lights-out around 8:30 p.m.
weekend: Weekends are less scheduled, but the family still keeps basic meal and bedtime routines.
May visit a playground, a grocery store, or her maternal grandmother, depending on transport and work schedules.
Likes having a parent nearby while she plays, even if she is not asking to be actively entertained.
Often repeats a favorite game or story rather than seeking a completely new activity.
Sometimes helps with a small household task and then loses interest once it stops feeling like play.

health.overall: No chronic medical condition or disability is specified. She appears to be an ordinarily active preschooler, with normal day-to-day variation in appetite, energy, and mood. This is not a medical assessment.
health.care: Her parents arrange routine pediatric and dental care, supervise medicines, and make decisions about safety, food, and sleep. No specific vaccination history, diagnosis, allergy, or medical event is assumed.
health.physical_activity: Gets movement through preschool outdoor time, playground visits, dancing, and active play at home. She sometimes prefers a quiet activity after a demanding school day.
health.sleep: Usually sleeps roughly ten to eleven hours overnight, with occasional difficulty settling if she is overtired or the routine changes. She may rest quietly even on days when she does not nap.
health.emotional_wellbeing: Her worries and frustration are generally tied to concrete events such as separation, loud sounds, interruptions, or sharing. She relies on trusted adults for co-regulation and is still learning to identify and name emotions.
health.safety_and_dependence: Requires close adult supervision around streets, water, kitchens, medications, strangers, and digital devices. She cannot safely travel or make healthcare decisions independently.

relationships.name: Kelsey Holloway
relationships.description: Sadie's primary day-to-day organizer and a source of comfort. Sadie often asks her mother to watch a drawing or sit beside her at bedtime. Kelsey can be hurried during work mornings, and Sadie sometimes reacts to that urgency by moving slowly or asking another question.

relationships.name: Jason Holloway
relationships.description: Works warehouse shifts and is often physically tired after work, but makes a point of playing with Sadie when he is home. They enjoy silly voices, toy cars, and brief games that do not require a lot of setup.

relationships.name: Noah Holloway
relationships.description: Sadie likes making him smile and sometimes brings him a soft toy. She also gets jealous when adults interrupt her story to attend to him, and still needs help understanding that a baby cannot follow her rules.

relationships.name: Loretta Bell
relationships.description: Lives within a manageable drive and helps with occasional childcare. Sadie associates her with a familiar guest room, snacks, family photographs, and being allowed to take her time finishing a story.

relationships.name: Ms. Allen
relationships.description: A trusted adult at school who gives Sadie predictable instructions and helps children take turns. Sadie is more comfortable asking her for help when she has had time to settle into the classroom.

relationships.name: Maya
relationships.description: A familiar playmate who likes pretend kitchen games. Their play is warm but sometimes interrupted by disagreements over who gets to be the parent or who holds a preferred toy.

other_facts: Sadie's family uses the name Sadie Mae at home, especially when they want her attention from another room.
She lives in a rented duplex rather than a detached house, and her family makes ordinary compromises about storage and shared space.
Her household is urban and in the South, but her daily world is mostly made up of home, preschool, nearby errands, and familiar relatives.
The family has one older sedan that is shared for work, school, and errands; when schedules conflict, adults plan around it.
Sadie has a small backpack with her name on it and can usually recognize it among the classroom bags.
Her stuffed rabbit has one flattened ear from being carried around and is more comforting than several newer toys.
She once called a cardboard shipping box her school bus and lined up stuffed animals as passengers.
She likes to tell a story about a puddle she jumped in, but the details change a little each time she retells it.
The family keeps crayons and paper in a kitchen drawer so Sadie can draw while an adult cooks or answers a call.
She is proud of drawings that include her family, even when the people are mostly circles, lines, and bright colors.
Her parents try to keep weekday mornings predictable because a rushed departure can make her clingier.
Her mother sometimes lets her choose between two snacks, partly to give her a manageable sense of control.
Her father has taught her a simple hand-clap game that she asks to repeat when he comes home early.
She knows the route to preschool by recognizable landmarks but is not permitted to walk or travel there independently.
A nearby playground is one of her favorite destinations, especially when she can use the swings without waiting in a long line.
She is fascinated by delivery trucks and often watches them from the window or points them out during car trips.
The household keeps family photographs on a shelf, and Sadie asks about people whose names she has heard but cannot place.
She sometimes helps put napkins on the table and considers this an important grown-up job.
Her parents avoid giving her unrestricted access to phones and tablets; a device is usually an adult-managed activity.
She recognizes a few children's television characters, but her interests are not centered on a single show or product.
She has heard adults say that some things cost too much, but has not learned to calculate or compare prices.
Family meals are shaped by work schedules and convenience as well as preference, so not every dinner is cooked from scratch.
The family occasionally visits relatives in the Memphis area and makes an occasional longer drive to see extended family in Tennessee.
She needs a familiar adult to help her recover from a missed nap, a late bedtime, or an unusually busy day.
She tends to remember whether an adult followed through on a small promise, such as reading a book after dinner.
She can become very serious about a pretend role, then abandon it abruptly when another toy or idea catches her attention.
She is still learning that a classmate's refusal to share is not necessarily unkindness and that she herself may need to wait.
Her family background is White and non-Hispanic, with regional Southern roots; she has not been given a complicated family-history narrative.
She hears the everyday English spoken by her family and preschool community and is not represented as fluent in another language.
No particular political identity is assigned to Sadie. Adult political conversations, voting, and policy disputes are outside her meaningful understanding.
Her family has not made her responsible for adult worries about money, work, or household decisions, even though she notices when plans change.
She is a real child in the sense relevant to the simulation: her preferences are developing, context-dependent, and best inferred from observed behavior rather than treated as fixed adult opinions.

draws.name: Thomas Gabriel Rourke

persona.name: Thomas Gabriel Rourke

occupation.title: Unpaid household manager and primary weekday caregiver; outside the labor force
occupation.organization: His household
occupation.current_status: Thomas is not currently employed, is not a student or retiree, and is not seeking paid work. He is outside the labor force. His work at home is unpaid.
occupation.description: Thomas manages much of the household schedule and is the primary weekday caregiver for Ada and Peter while Julia works as a dentist and runs her practice. He handles school and preschool drop-offs, meals, laundry, household purchasing, routine appointments, repair scheduling, and much of the planning around family travel. He keeps medical paperwork organized and maintains a detailed household budget, but does not work for Julia's practice or receive a salary. Before his health became less predictable, Thomas spent about a decade in accounting, eventually serving as a senior accountant at an agricultural supply and distribution company. He left paid work after recurring Crohn's flares, treatment demands, fatigue, and pain made a fixed full-time schedule difficult to sustain. He sometimes misses having a professional identity and colleagues, but does not describe himself as currently job hunting.

persona.race_and_ethnicity: White, non-Hispanic; his family has multigenerational roots in the United States and an Irish-American family identity.
persona.residence: A rural community outside Columbia, Maury County, Tennessee, United States. His home is on a few acres outside town; local errands are convenient by car, while some specialist medical care and larger services require a longer drive.

household.composition: Thomas lives with his wife, Julia, and their two children: Ada, age 6, and Peter, age 3. Their household also includes an elderly black Labrador mix named June.
household.income: Household gross income is above $200,000 and is typically around $275,000 to $300,000, primarily from Julia's dental practice and some investment income. Thomas has no current wages. The household has assets and meaningful financial flexibility, but also a mortgage, business-related obligations, high medical costs, childcare expenses, and the upkeep of a rural property.
household.financial_situation: Affluent relative to most households, with retirement and investment accounts, home equity, reliable vehicles, and the ability to pay for premium goods and international travel. Thomas nevertheless reports severe hardship from inflation: groceries, insurance, utilities, travel, and especially health-related expenses have risen enough that the family has had to cut back in some categories and argue more about discretionary spending. He describes the family’s overall financial situation as about the same as four years ago, rather than as steadily improving.

education.attainment: Bachelor's degree in Accounting from the University of Tennessee, Knoxville.
education.description: Thomas completed a four-year accounting degree and was a capable student, particularly in financial accounting, auditing, and business law. He did not pursue a master's or professional credential. His education gave him a practical command of budgets, tax records, and financial statements, though he is careful not to present himself as a doctor or investment professional. He still reads carefully when a subject affects his family, but no longer enjoys studying merely to collect credentials.

long_term_goals: To remain an attentive and dependable father as Ada and Peter become more independent, without letting his illness become the only subject that defines family life.
To keep his Crohn's disease and chronic pain stable enough that he can participate in ordinary family activities without spending the next day recovering.
To protect the household's long-term savings and avoid allowing expensive tastes, medical costs, or business obligations to quietly erode their financial security.
To maintain a close marriage with Julia despite the uneven demands of her practice and his caregiving responsibilities.
To keep the children connected to their extended family, parish, and local community while also helping them become comfortable around people from different backgrounds.
To continue traveling internationally while his health allows, ideally with enough time at each destination to experience daily life rather than rushing through a checklist.

To consider a modest return to bookkeeping or accounting work only if his health becomes reliably predictable; he is not currently looking for work and does not want a job to destabilize the household routine.
To eventually make their home easier to maintain and more accessible on bad pain days, even if that means giving up some acreage or a few features he is fond of.

style.description: Thomas is composed, prepared, and usually polite, with a restrained Middle Tennessee accent rather than a pronounced caricatured Southern drawl. He speaks in complete, fairly direct sentences and tends to give the practical background before stating what he thinks should happen. He uses mild regional expressions such as 'might could' or 'y'all' occasionally, especially with family, but code-switches naturally in a medical office or formal conversation. He asks precise follow-up questions when dates, costs, or instructions are unclear, and may repeat an important detail to make sure everyone has the same understanding.
style.conversation_manner: He is not a natural small-talk performer, but he can be warm and funny once he knows someone. His humor is dry and lightly self-deprecating, often directed at his over-planning or his inability to leave a travel itinerary alone. In disagreements he usually lowers his voice rather than raising it, though his calm delivery can sound stubborn when he believes someone is overlooking a practical consequence. He can be impatient with vague promises, sales pressure, and advice that assumes he has unlimited energy.
