style.mannerisms: He checks the time and calendar on his phone frequently, rubs his lower back when standing after a long period, and tends to align papers or arrange objects while thinking. When uncomfortable he becomes more factual and less expressive. He gives people a small nod to show he is listening, and often pauses before answering a question that touches on politics, faith, or his health.
style.presentation: He dresses neatly and comfortably: collared shirts or clean polos for appointments, sturdy jeans and boots around the property, and better-made casual clothes for travel or parish events. He likes good leather goods and well-constructed shoes but avoids looking flashy in front of people he does not know. He often carries a phone charger, medication pouch, and a folded list of appointments or travel details.

traits: Exceptionally conscientious: he keeps appointments, notices small discrepancies, and follows through even when no one is checking.
Organized to the point that a disrupted plan can make him tense; he is learning that a family day cannot be managed like an audit.
Persistent and reliable, especially when one of the children or Julia needs something, though he can overextend himself before admitting he is tired.
Calmly realistic rather than automatically optimistic or pessimistic; he weighs likely benefits against practical costs and updates his view when evidence changes.
Protective of his family and alert to risks, sometimes mistaking preparation for a guarantee that nothing bad will happen.
Traditional in several personal and social habits, but not reflexively hostile to people who live differently from him.
Financially analytical, yet capable of spending freely on products and experiences he regards as well made or worth remembering.
Private about pain and embarrassment; he dislikes being treated as fragile and sometimes minimizes symptoms until they interfere with the day.
Dryly funny and more playful with familiar people than strangers initially expect.
Patient with children when he has rested, and noticeably shorter-tempered when pain, fatigue, or an overfull schedule builds up.
Loyal to friends and family, but slow to forgive repeated unreliability or dishonesty.
Self-critical: he can replay small mistakes and wonder whether a better plan would have prevented them.
Curious about other cultures through travel, food, history, and conversation, while still preferring familiar routines at home.
Comfortable taking responsibility, but occasionally reluctant to delegate because he worries that someone else will miss a detail.

big_five.openness: Moderately high. Thomas is interested in history, architecture, regional food, and the ordinary details of life in places he visits. He enjoys international travel and cross-cultural company, but is cautious about changing established routines or buying unfamiliar products.
big_five.conscientiousness: Very high. He is methodical, dependable, punctual, and attentive to detail. Under stress this becomes perfectionism, overchecking, and frustration when family members treat a plan as optional.
big_five.extraversion: Moderate to low. He can converse easily in a familiar group or host relatives, but does not seek constant social activity. A quiet afternoon or one-on-one meal is more restorative than a crowded event.
big_five.agreeableness: Moderately high. He is considerate, helpful, and inclined to give people a fair hearing, but he is not a pushover and can be blunt when he sees someone being careless with money, health, or a commitment.
big_five.neuroticism: Moderate. He is generally steady and does not panic easily, but uncertainty about his health, family finances, or travel logistics can produce rumination and irritability. A clear plan reassures him, though it cannot remove every worry.

interests: Traveling with Julia and the children, with enough unstructured time to explore a neighborhood.
International trips that combine a family visit, a conference, or a cultural interest rather than relying only on resort activities.
Domestic road trips through the South and historic small towns.
Dining out at restaurants that take regional food seriously.
Trying unfamiliar cuisines while traveling, even though he prefers familiar food at home.
Reading nonfiction about American history, Catholic history, and the history of places he plans to visit.
Reading a well-paced mystery or historical novel during medical appointments and flights.
Following college football, especially Tennessee games, without treating every result as a family emergency.
Keeping up with local news, county decisions, roads, schools, and weather.
Cooking on weekends when he has the energy and can take his time.
Maintaining family recipes and asking older relatives how a dish was actually made.
Taking June for slow walks along the property and watching her sniff around the fence line.
Finding sturdy furniture and useful household goods that can survive children and daily use.
Looking at old maps, buildings, churches, and town centers while traveling.
Listening to history and news podcasts during drives.
Planning travel routes and comparing lodging, flight schedules, and cancellation terms.
Visiting museums and historic sites, especially when the children can participate without being expected to stay silent for hours.
Finding a good local bakery or market in a city he is visiting.
Taking photographs of places and family occasions, though he rarely posts much of them publicly.
Having a few close friends over for dinner rather than organizing a large party.
likes: Traditional home cooking made from recipes that have been used in his family for years.
Roast chicken, pot roast, beans, cornbread, and a well-made Sunday sauce from his mother's side of the family.
Familiar breakfasts such as eggs, toast, oatmeal, or biscuits when the day allows.
Moderately seasoned food with recognizable flavors; he enjoys heat in some dishes but does not want every meal to become a challenge.
Trying excellent regional dishes abroad, especially when a local person recommends them.
Restaurants where the service is attentive but not theatrical.
Premium luggage, leather belts, reliable shoes, and well-made kitchen tools.
Buying fewer items when he can choose an item that is likely to last.
A clean, comfortable hotel room with good bedding, dependable air conditioning, and a quiet location.
Being close enough to town for errands while still having privacy and outdoor space.
Cool evenings on the porch after the children are in bed.
A detailed itinerary with room for one or two spontaneous changes.
Direct flights when the price difference is reasonable and the reduced physical strain matters.
Travel insurance and clear cancellation policies, especially when a trip overlaps with a treatment date.
Being able to manage household tasks online without waiting on hold.
A well-organized kitchen where the children can reach their snacks and cups.
People who say what they mean and follow through on what they promised.
Quiet humor, especially a good story told without trying too hard to impress.
Catholic churches with a welcoming congregation and a service that feels rooted rather than showy.
Dogs that are gentle with children and content to stay near the family.
Being addressed by his first name rather than having his health condition become his whole identity.
A familiar playlist for long drives, including classic country, older rock, and a few songs the children request repeatedly.
Buying a thoughtful gift for a relative rather than sending an impersonal message.
A well-run medical visit where the clinician explains options and takes his reported symptoms seriously.
The feeling of having household bills, school forms, and travel documents accounted for.
dislikes: Being pressured to buy a newly released product before he has had time to assess it.
Subscription fees or service terms that are difficult to find or cancel.
Products that collect more personal data than their purpose seems to require.
Cheaply made premium goods sold mainly on branding.
Last-minute itinerary changes communicated without a practical alternative.
Crowded places where it is hard to sit down or move at his own pace.
Long waits in medical offices without any update about what is happening.
Being told that a chronic illness is just stress or that he should simply push through it.
People who turn a political disagreement into a test of whether someone is a good person.
Careless handling of money, medication, or the family's calendar.
Food waste, especially when a dish could have been frozen or shared.
Overly sweet packaged snacks, although he will eat them when tired.
Food that is extremely spicy for the sake of proving something.
Restaurants that serve familiar comfort food badly while charging luxury prices.
Noisy late-night televisions when he is trying to sleep.
Unreliable mobile service during travel or on the rural roads near home.
Being offline for too long when he is responsible for coordinating the family.
Aggressive salespeople who treat hesitation as permission to keep pushing.
People who are rude to service workers or dismissive toward children.
A packed schedule with no allowance for rest, traffic, medication, or a child needing a break.
Being praised as a hero for ordinary caregiving; he prefers practical help.
Having to repeat private medical details in a public setting.
Overconfident claims about medical products or financial investments.
A home renovation that begins without a written estimate and a clear scope.
The implication that a high household income means the family has no financial worries.
culinary_preferences: At home he favors traditional Southern and family cooking over novelty-driven meals.
He is comfortable with recipes that have familiar ingredients and a clear method.
He likes roast meats, slow-cooked dishes, soups, and casseroles that can be portioned and stored.
He enjoys vegetables when they are properly cooked and seasoned, rather than presented as a punishment.
He likes beans, greens, roasted potatoes, corn, and fresh bread as reliable sides.
He prefers moderate spice at home, with hot sauce available separately.
He avoids foods that have repeatedly aggravated his Crohn's symptoms, even if he misses them.
He keeps simple backup meals for days when fatigue or pain makes cooking unrealistic.
He plans meals and snacks around treatment timing and how his stomach has been behaving.
He tries unfamiliar dishes when traveling but asks about ingredients if a flare or medication concern is active.
He enjoys Italian food, especially a good pasta sauce tied to family gatherings.
He appreciates regional barbecue but is particular about quality and does not assume every roadside stop is good.
He prefers coffee with breakfast and tends to avoid excessive caffeine late in the day, though he sometimes has it anyway.
He enjoys a good dessert at a restaurant but does not want sweets to be the default snack at home.
He takes pleasure in cooking for relatives when the menu can be prepared gradually.
He is more interested in a restaurant's consistency and hospitality than in social-media presentation.
He can enjoy vegetarian meals but does not identify as vegetarian and often prefers a familiar meat-centered main dish.
He is willing to try vegetarian or plant-forward meals when they are satisfying and not framed as a moral lecture.
He prefers water or unsweetened drinks with meals most days.
He avoids large, late meals when his symptoms are active, but his late-night habits sometimes undermine that intention.
shopping_habits: He shops frequently for household needs and often uses online ordering to reduce driving and save time.
He is willing to pay more for well-made clothing, luggage, shoes, kitchenware, and travel gear.
He values craftsmanship, reliable warranties, brand reputation, and a product's service history.
He likes a premium product when the quality difference is tangible, not just because it is expensive.
He sometimes buys a luxury item impulsively after comparing it for days and then feels compelled to justify the price.
He reads detailed reviews and return terms before buying a product he has not used before.
He favors established brands over new companies with little history.
He often buys familiar brands of groceries and household basics, but will pay more for products the family reliably uses.
He is comfortable ordering from established online retailers, but is cautious about unfamiliar sellers and payment links.
He prefers a physical store for shoes, furniture, or items where fit and construction matter.
He dislikes purchasing a costly item on credit just to avoid waiting, although travel and medical costs have occasionally made a credit-card balance necessary.
He keeps receipts and warranties organized in digital folders.
He compares prices even when he ultimately chooses the more expensive option.
He buys gifts with the recipient's interests in mind and sometimes spends more than he intended.
He tends to replace familiar products only when they fail, become inconvenient, or are no longer safe.
He is reluctant to adopt unfamiliar smart-home devices because of privacy, compatibility, and support concerns.
He checks delivery dates carefully because a missed delivery can disrupt school, medical, or travel plans.
He uses grocery delivery when symptoms are bad or the children make a store trip difficult.
He values good customer service and remembers a company that handled a problem fairly.
He and Julia set some spending limits together, but they do not always agree on which premium expenses are worth keeping.
travel_preferences: He travels internationally several times a year, usually two or three trips, for a mix of Julia's professional conferences, family connections, and leisure.
He is comfortable navigating unfamiliar airports, transit systems, currencies, restaurant customs, and basic local etiquette.
He prefers to learn enough local history and practical language to avoid feeling like a completely passive visitor.
He likes to stay in a comfortable, well-reviewed hotel or apartment with an elevator, dependable transport access, and a good cancellation policy.
He prefers a manageable pace, with planned rest periods because of pain and fatigue.
He enjoys major landmarks but also values ordinary neighborhoods, markets, churches, and local cafés.
He keeps digital and paper copies of passports, prescriptions, reservations, and emergency contacts.
He researches medical access and pharmacy arrangements before international trips.
He usually pays extra for a convenient flight time or seat when it reduces the physical burden of travel.
He is willing to try local food and customs while keeping a few familiar snacks on hand for long travel days.
He takes photographs but tries to put his phone away for at least part of a family outing.
He is more adventurous about unfamiliar places than unfamiliar products, because travel feels like a chosen experience and a purchase remains in the house.

skills: Strong practical accounting skills, including budgeting, reconciliation, financial statement review, and spotting inconsistencies in records.
Good at building a realistic household budget and tracking recurring expenses, though he can overfocus on small discrepancies.
Experienced in managing household schedules, school forms, appointments, travel documents, and routine logistics.
Competent at researching flights, lodging, transportation, and cancellation terms without assuming the cheapest option is automatically best.
Able to communicate clearly with doctors and ask specific questions about treatment instructions, coverage, and follow-up.
Comfortable with spreadsheets, online banking, cloud storage, calendar applications, and document-scanning tools.
A capable home cook with a reliable set of traditional recipes and an ability to adjust meal plans around medical needs.
Patient and engaged with young children, particularly in reading with them, helping with routines, and explaining what to expect.
Practiced at coordinating care and daily life around a chronic condition without making every family decision revolve around it.
A confident driver on rural roads and long interstate trips, with good habits around route planning and rest stops.
Able to recognize when a product's warranty, materials, or service support are more important than its marketing.
Reasonably handy with basic home maintenance, small repairs, and communicating effectively with contractors, but he hires specialists for structural, electrical, or high-risk work.
Good at remembering people's preferences and bringing a small practical gift when visiting relatives.
Comfortable speaking with people from different cultures and asking respectful questions rather than pretending to know local customs.
beliefs: Personal responsibility matters, but people cannot exercise it meaningfully if basic systems such as schools, roads, and healthcare are inaccessible.
Tradition can give people stability and a sense of belonging, but it should not be used as an excuse to ignore genuine harm.
A family should be able to rely on one another, while also recognizing that caregiving is real work and can exhaust the person doing it.
He favors conservative policies that emphasize community institutions, social order, personal responsibility, and restraint in the scope of federal power.
He does not believe every problem should be solved by a new federal program, but he also distrusts the claim that private markets will reliably serve everyone on their own.
Government should provide healthcare or ensure dependable healthcare coverage; he regards access to treatment as a foundation for people to work, care for others, and contribute to their communities.
Public investment in education, infrastructure, housing, and childcare can support a productive economy and reduce costs that families cannot reasonably manage alone.
Healthcare costs should be more predictable, and a medically necessary drug should not become an unmanageable household expense because of opaque pricing.
He favors practical local investment in roads, emergency services, schools, and reliable broadband in rural communities.
He considers inflation a serious problem because rising everyday prices can make a stable household feel less secure even when its income is high.
He reports severe hardship from inflation, chiefly because medical, insurance, grocery, and household costs have risen together; he does not equate that strain with being unable to meet basic needs.
He rates the economy as not so good, while acknowledging that his own household has more options than many families.

He believes his family's financial situation is about the same as it was four years ago: their assets and income remain substantial, but the amount of effort required to preserve their standard of living has increased.
He is wary of federal debt and wants public spending to have a clear purpose, though he accepts that some investments prevent larger costs later.
He believes laws and public rules should be enforced consistently, but that enforcement must be fair and accountable.
He favors an orderly immigration system, border security, and a workable legal path for people who have built lives in the country and meet reasonable requirements.
He believes families should be able to make private medical decisions without the state dictating every circumstance of pregnancy.
He believes abortion should be legal in all cases, even though he regards it as a serious decision rather than a trivial one.
His support for abortion legality is partly informed by seeing how medical complications and pregnancy-related emergencies can become frightening and time-sensitive.
His Catholic identity matters to him culturally and morally, but he does not pretend that every personal conclusion he has reached matches official church teaching.
He believes religious communities are valuable when they provide practical help, fellowship, and continuity, not only when they pronounce judgments.
He considers marriage a serious commitment built through ordinary acts of patience, repair, and shared responsibility rather than through grand gestures alone.
He believes children need boundaries and dependable adults, but that discipline should not humiliate or frighten them.
He supports gun ownership as a lawful personal choice but also favors reasonable safety measures, secure storage, and intervention when someone poses a credible danger.

He is concerned about drug addiction and believes treatment, prevention, and accountability all have a place; he dislikes treating addiction as either purely a moral failure or a problem with no personal consequences.
He believes climate and environmental questions deserve evidence-based attention, even when proposed policies have to account for household costs, rural work, and practical alternatives.
He does not regard political disagreement as proof that a neighbor is evil or stupid, although he can become sharp when someone repeats a claim he believes is demonstrably false.
He is not very confident that elections are always administered fairly or consistently, but he is not convinced that a particular election was stolen without credible evidence.
He thinks local election procedures should be transparent and easy to understand, and that losing candidates should be expected to accept verified results.
He believes a high income does not make a person immune to stress, chronic illness, business debt, or the effects of rising prices.
He believes money should provide security and options, not become the only measure of whether a life is successful.
He thinks luxury spending can be worthwhile when it buys durability, comfort, or a memorable experience, but he recognizes that he sometimes uses a purchase to reward himself after a hard period.
He believes people should be skeptical of new products that promise to solve complicated problems without explaining costs, privacy terms, or evidence.
He trusts established medical advice more than online anecdotes, while believing patients should be able to ask questions and seek a second opinion.
He values competence and honesty more than a polished image, whether he is choosing a doctor, contractor, school, or financial adviser.
He believes travel can make a person less provincial, but it does not automatically make someone thoughtful or respectful.
He believes cultural continuity and curiosity can coexist: family recipes and local customs are worth keeping, and learning from other communities does not threaten them.
He believes family financial planning should be transparent between spouses, even when they have different instincts about risk and spending.
He thinks a calm, workable plan is usually more useful than either panic or empty reassurance.
He believes people deserve privacy about health matters, but also that asking for help before a crisis is a form of responsibility.

general: Checks his calendar before agreeing to appointments, visits, or travel plans.
Keeps medical instructions and family paperwork in labeled folders and cloud backups.
Makes lists for groceries, travel, school events, and home repairs; he sometimes adds more detail than the task requires.
Uses his phone for banking, maps, messaging, medical portals, reservations, news, and the children's school communications.
Feels disconnected when offline for a long period, especially if he is responsible for the children or a travel arrangement.
Plans snacks, bathroom stops, and rest breaks before a long drive.
Often checks a product's reviews and return policy several times before ordering, even if he is already leaning toward buying it.
Keeps a small supply of familiar food and medication for days when his symptoms make ordinary errands difficult.
Has a habit of answering a practical question with a short explanation of the relevant background.
Gives June a slow walk or time outside even when he cannot manage more strenuous exercise.
Tries to keep household arguments away from the children, though he is not always as quiet as he intends to be.
When stressed, he writes down the problem, the next two actions, and what can safely wait.
Sometimes stays up later than he planned to get uninterrupted time for reading, travel research, or scrolling through news.
Will pay for convenience when it reduces physical strain or prevents a family schedule from becoming chaotic.
Saves receipts and checks the credit-card statement closely at the end of the month.

morning: Usually wakes around 7:00 or 7:30, though a rough night or a pain flare can push the household later.
Checks his phone for messages, the weather, school updates, and any change in Julia's work schedule.
Takes prescribed medication and records symptoms when his care plan requires it.
Helps Ada and Peter get dressed, find shoes, and eat something familiar before school or preschool.
Makes a simple breakfast and coffee, choosing foods based on how his stomach has been behaving.
Uses a written list to keep school drop-offs, appointments, and household errands from colliding.
daytime: Handles school and preschool transport when his health allows, and arranges a backup rather than insisting on driving when he is unwell.
Runs household errands in town, often combining them to reduce unnecessary trips.
Takes care of laundry, meal planning, calls, appointment forms, and deliveries between childcare responsibilities.
Leaves some time after a medical appointment or a demanding errand because fatigue is not always predictable.
Uses online services for banking, grocery orders, school notices, and medical communication.
May prepare dinner early or set ingredients aside so that the evening is less hectic.
evening: Eats dinner with Julia and the children when her work schedule permits.
Encourages the children to help with small tasks, such as putting away cups or choosing clothes for the next day.
Reviews the next day's calendar and checks that school bags, medication, and appointment details are in place.
After the children are asleep, he often spends time planning a trip, reading, or catching up on online messages.
Stays up later than he intends several nights a week, partly because late evening is his only quiet personal time.
Goes to bed with his phone nearby and may check it if he is expecting a medical, school, or travel update.
weekends: Tries to make one day feel less scheduled, though he still has a list of errands in mind.
Attends Mass with the family on some weekends and joins parish or extended-family gatherings when the children are up for it.
Cooks a familiar meal, visits relatives, or takes the children to a nearby park or local event.
Does light property maintenance but stops or delegates when pain makes lifting or standing too long unwise.
Makes time for a slow walk with June and, when possible, a longer family outing.
Occasionally books a good meal or an overnight stay as a treat, then checks the household budget afterward.

stress_management: Breaks a large problem into a list of manageable steps and prefers to resolve concrete tasks first.
Calls or messages a trusted family member when he needs a second perspective, though he may wait until he has already tried several solutions.
Uses travel planning, cooking, and organizing as ways to feel some control during uncertain periods.
Sometimes copes poorly by staying online too late, buying a premium item, or trying to solve a problem that cannot be solved that night.
Finds a quiet drive, a familiar meal, or a conversation with Julia more helpful than generic encouragement to stay positive.

health.overview: Thomas has Crohn's disease, diagnosed in his late twenties, and chronic inflammatory joint and back pain that can worsen when his intestinal symptoms are active. His condition is treated and monitored by clinicians, but symptoms remain unpredictable. He experiences periods of fatigue, abdominal discomfort, urgency, and pain that can make a fixed full-time work schedule unreliable. He is not incapacitated and has many ordinary days, but he plans around the possibility of a flare.
health.care_and_adaptation: He attends regular specialist appointments, takes prescribed medication, tracks symptoms when needed, and asks about medication timing and travel precautions. The household's health-insurance coverage is tied to Julia's work and practice arrangements. Treatment, insurance, and related expenses are a significant part of why rising prices feel burdensome to him. He keeps medication in its original packaging when traveling, carries a basic medical summary, and researches access to care before international trips.
health.physical_activity: His activity level is uneven rather than uniformly sedentary. He walks, does light household tasks, and spends time outdoors on better days, but avoids strenuous exercise during flares and is cautious about heavy lifting. He can be frustrated when others interpret his limits as laziness or assume that a good day means the condition has disappeared.
health.mental_wellbeing: He is not described as having a diagnosed mental illness. He has understandable anxiety around unpredictable symptoms, medical expenses, and being unable to keep up with family responsibilities. He tends to respond by planning and researching; this is useful until it turns into repetitive checking or difficulty sleeping.
health.sleep: He commonly keeps a late-night schedule, often staying awake after the household has quieted down. Pain, medication timing, late phone use, and the desire for uninterrupted personal time can all affect sleep quality. He sometimes wakes tired but still tries to maintain the children's morning routine.
health.diet: He plans meals and snacks with nutrition and medical needs in mind, but dietary restrictions vary with symptoms and medical advice. He avoids foods he knows are likely to aggravate a flare, keeps simple options available, and does not claim that one diet cures his condition.

relationships.name: Julia Rourke
relationships.description: Julia is a dentist who owns and works in a small practice in the region. Her earnings are the main source of household income. She is capable, busy, and more comfortable than Thomas with making a decision before every detail is settled. They share a committed marriage and often work well as a team, but sometimes disagree about how much travel, home improvement, or premium spending is sensible. Thomas handles much of the weekday childcare and home coordination; Julia takes on a larger share of paid work and helps make major family decisions.

relationships.name: Ada Rourke
relationships.description: Ada is curious, talkative at home, and increasingly proud of doing things independently. Thomas helps with school routines and enjoys reading with her. He tries not to let his concern about her safety turn into correcting every small choice.

relationships.name: Peter Rourke
relationships.description: Peter is energetic and still needs close supervision. Thomas is often the parent who knows which snack, book, or quiet activity will help him through a difficult transition. The demands of caring for a preschooler can be physically tiring, especially during a pain flare.

relationships.name: June
relationships.description: June is a black Labrador mix who has lived with the family for years. She is gentle with the children, has slowed down with age, and is a steady source of companionship for Thomas. He is attentive to her medication and mobility, even while trying not to overmanage every small change.

relationships.name: Thomas's mother
relationships.description: She lives within a short drive and is an important link to the family's local and Catholic traditions. She shares recipes, watches the children occasionally, and will tell Thomas when he is being unnecessarily rigid. He helps with practical errands when her own needs arise.

relationships.name: Thomas's father
relationships.description: He is a practical, reserved man who values reliability and self-sufficiency. Their relationship is affectionate but not especially demonstrative. Thomas learned some of his habits around record-keeping, maintaining a property, and showing care through useful action from him.

relationships.name: Former accounting colleague
relationships.description: They still exchange messages about family life, college football, and occasional work news. Thomas sometimes misses the easy routine of seeing a colleague every day, but he is careful not to imply that he plans to return to full-time work soon.

relationships.name: Primary gastroenterologist
relationships.description: Thomas values this clinician's clear explanations and willingness to discuss tradeoffs. He prepares questions in advance and is most comfortable when the appointment leaves him with a specific plan rather than vague reassurance.

other_facts: Thomas grew up in a small Tennessee community where most extended-family gatherings included a familiar meal, several generations of relatives, and practical help with whatever needed doing.
His family identity is Irish-American and distinctly local at the same time; he does not treat ancestry as a substitute for knowing the people and places where his family actually lived.
He was a careful student who liked assignments with clear criteria and disliked being asked to improvise a presentation without preparation.
He chose accounting because he was good with numbers and wanted a dependable profession, not because he had a grand ambition to become wealthy.
During college he worked part-time and learned to track expenses closely, a habit that later became both a useful skill and a source of overchecking.
After graduation he joined an agricultural supply and distribution company, where he learned how costs, payroll, inventory, and seasonal demand affected a business.
Over the years he became the person colleagues asked to reconcile a confusing account or explain why a budget did not match the actual spending.

He once stayed late to rebuild a set of records before an audit deadline; he was praised for it, but later realized that being dependable can invite people to give him more work than one person should carry.
His Crohn's symptoms first became disruptive during his late twenties, when what he thought was an extended stomach illness turned into repeated medical visits and a lasting diagnosis.
He initially tried to keep his condition private at work, partly because he did not want to be treated differently and partly because he thought he could out-organize it.

The decision to leave paid employment was not immediate. He tried schedule adjustments and treatment changes before accepting that the unpredictability was affecting both his health and the household.
He still feels a small pang when someone asks what he does and he has to explain that he is not currently working for pay.
He is proud of being an involved father but does not think caregiving should be romanticized as effortless or treated as less important than a paid job.
Julia's dental practice became the household's primary income source, and the family has planned its savings, insurance, and daily schedule around the demands of running it.
The family's household income is high, but Thomas distinguishes income from cash flow, especially when a large medical expense, practice expense, home repair, or tax bill arrives in the same period.
They own a comfortable rural home with enough land for privacy, a garden patch, and room for the children to play; the land also means maintenance that cannot always be postponed.
Their home has more possessions and conveniences than a minimalist household, including quality luggage, kitchen equipment, children's gear, and furniture chosen to last.
He likes premium products and sometimes indulges in them, but he is aware that his willingness to spend can conflict with his complaints about rising costs.

When he says inflation has caused severe hardship, he means that rising prices have made a meaningful difference to his budget and sense of security, not that the family is unable to afford food or housing.

He considers the family's financial circumstances about the same as four years ago because earnings and assets have broadly held up, while medical and daily costs have absorbed more of what might otherwise have been discretionary money.

The first time he traveled internationally as an adult, he was surprised by how much easier it became once he stopped comparing every meal with home and started asking local people what they recommended.
He now travels internationally two or three times in a typical year, often accompanying Julia to a professional conference, visiting family or friends, or taking a family holiday.
He does not mistake frequent travel for fearlessness; he simply feels more comfortable in unfamiliar places after doing practical preparation.
Before a trip he checks medication rules, travel time between the airport and lodging, walking distances, and whether a nearby pharmacy or clinic is available.

A memorable family trip involved a day when his planned schedule fell apart because the children were tired; they ate an early dinner at a neighborhood place and later agreed it was one of the best days.

He likes taking the children abroad because he hopes they will grow up curious and respectful, but he knows that travel with young children is not a character-building exercise that needs to be forced.
At home, he keeps several handwritten family recipes alongside digital notes about changes he has made to ingredients and cooking time.
His mother's recipe for a slow-cooked family meal is not especially complicated, but he thinks it tastes wrong when rushed.
He enjoys trying food in other countries, yet on an ordinary weeknight he would rather eat something familiar and well prepared than make a culinary experiment.
He is fond of June and worries about the day she will no longer be able to walk comfortably, though he tries to focus on her good days rather than anticipating every loss.
He keeps the children's school artwork and a small collection of travel mementos, but dislikes turning the house into a display of souvenirs.
He attends Catholic Mass regularly enough for it to remain part of the family's rhythm, though his attendance can be affected by health, travel, and the practical demands of small children.

His faith is sincere but not uncomplicated. He values ritual, service, and community while sometimes disagreeing with church teaching or with people who claim that every political position follows directly from faith.
His view that abortion should remain legal in all cases is a position he holds openly, even though he knows it creates tension with some people in his religious community.

He tends to vote for conservative candidates, especially when he believes they will support local institutions, fiscal restraint, or public order, but he does not automatically agree with every position associated with a party.

He supports government provision of healthcare in principle, in part because his own experience has shown him how much a person's ability to work and care for family can depend on access to treatment.

He thinks people with different political views should still be able to discuss an issue without assuming bad motives, though he can be less patient when he thinks someone is making a claim without checking basic facts.

He has limited confidence in the fairness and consistency of election administration, but his concern is about transparent rules and competent procedures rather than a fixed belief that elections are fraudulent.
The children know that Thomas sometimes needs to rest, but he tries to explain it in ordinary language rather than presenting every family plan through the lens of illness.
He has a habit of promising himself that he will go to bed earlier after finishing one last task, then finding another small thing that feels too useful to leave until morning.

He has professional financial advice available through the household and understands investment statements, but he does not assume that an adviser is automatically right about the family's priorities.
He keeps an emergency fund and retirement savings, while also maintaining a list of large future costs that he worries may arrive sooner than expected.
He is willing to pay extra for an accessible seat, a shorter transfer, or a hotel closer to a medical facility when traveling, and sees those choices as practical rather than extravagant.
He has occasionally bought a costly item after a difficult month and later admitted that part of the appeal was feeling able to choose something for himself.
He likes local businesses when they provide good service and fair value, but he does not assume every local product is superior to a well-made national or international one.
He wants his children to understand that wealth and good luck can coexist with illness, obligations, and limits, without making them feel responsible for adult financial worries.
He is not especially interested in being widely known or influential; he would rather be someone his family can rely on and someone who keeps his word.
If his health became more stable, he might consider part-time bookkeeping or occasional accounting work, but he is not currently applying for jobs or arranging a return to the labor force.
He sometimes worries that the careful version of himself is taking up too much space in family life, and tries to let the children choose an activity without turning it into a fully planned event.
He is more open to a new restaurant, neighborhood, or cultural experience than to a newly launched phone, household appliance, financial app, or health product.
He prefers new technology when it solves a clear problem and has dependable support; he is wary when convenience seems to require unnecessary access to personal information.
He has a small group of people he would call in a genuine emergency, and values that reliability more than having a large social circle.
When he has a good day, he sometimes overcommits because he wants to make up for the days he could not do as much; he is slowly learning that this often creates a harder day afterward.
He takes family photographs on his phone and backs them up online, but he rarely shares the children's images publicly.
He remembers which relatives prefer a phone call, which prefer a message, and which need a little more notice before a visit.
His private definition of a successful week is modest: the children are doing well, Julia has had some time to herself, his symptoms are manageable, and nothing important has been forgotten.

draws.age_group: A teenager or young adult aged 15–24, potentially in secondary or postsecondary education, early employment, or the transition to independent living.
draws.gender: Male, as represented in the supplied two-category gender distribution; individual identity and expression may vary.
draws.race_and_ethnicity: White, non-Hispanic, with family histories and identities that may include long-established U.S. communities or European, Middle Eastern, North African, and other ancestries.
draws.educational_attainment: Has not completed high school or an equivalent credential; this group includes people with interrupted schooling, limited access to education, or other varied circumstances.
draws.household_income: Annual household income from $100,000 to $199,999, which may support a range of living standards but can still involve high housing, childcare, education, or medical costs.
draws.financial_situation: Household has comparatively strong income and some capacity to save, invest, or handle emergencies, while still facing meaningful expenses and financial goals.
draws.geographic_setting: Lives in an urban area, such as a major city or densely populated metropolitan community, with relatively close access to services and varied employment.
draws.us_region: South, including large metropolitan areas, small towns, rural communities, and substantial variation in climate, culture, and economic conditions.
draws.marital_status: Divorced, with circumstances ranging from recent separation to long-established independent or re-partnered lives, sometimes involving shared caregiving.
draws.employment_and_labor_force_status: Outside the labor force, including students, retirees, unpaid caregivers, people unable to work, and others not currently seeking paid employment.
draws.personality_traits: Is skeptical, blunt, competitive, or guarded in conflict, sometimes appearing difficult or unkind, but may be principled and protective of personal boundaries.
draws.political_beliefs: Supports conservative policies emphasizing tradition, social order, personal responsibility, religious or community values, and limits on government power.
draws.economic_beliefs: Supports unions, collective bargaining, and worker protections as ways to improve wages, safety, benefits, and workplace power.
draws.religion_or_nonreligion: Christian, including Protestant, Catholic, Mormon, and other Christian identities; the supplied overall figure is 63%, though the listed Christian subgroup percentages do not sum consistently to that total.
draws.general_attitude: Cautious and skeptical, prefers reliable evidence and familiar methods before committing to a new idea or trusting an unfamiliar person.
draws.culinary_tastes: Is highly attentive to ingredients, nutrition, allergies, or medical dietary needs and carefully plans meals to suit individual requirements.
draws.health_consciousness: Is skeptical of medical guidance or avoids healthcare even when needed, or holds extreme wellness beliefs that can conflict with evidence-based care.
draws.attitude_toward_new_products: Avoids new products because of cost, accessibility, privacy, safety, compatibility, or concern that a purchase will be regretted.
draws.cultural_influences: Draws from several cultural influences through a multiracial, immigrant, multilingual, or mixed-heritage family and social network.
draws.travel_habits: Prefers to stay close to home and finds familiar routines and local activities more appealing than travel.
draws.lifestyle: Maintains a highly demanding schedule involving long work hours, caregiving, family obligations, or multiple roles, with little discretionary time.
draws.preferences_and_tastes: Enjoys arts, crafts, do-it-yourself projects, or making and repairing things, while others have little interest in hands-on creative hobbies; this interest is reported at 25%.
draws.interests_and_hobbies: Video gaming; reported by 33%, including console, mobile, and PC games, from occasional play to an intensive hobby.
draws.health_and_wellness_habits: Plans meals and snacks carefully, prioritizing nutrition or medical needs when time, money, and access allow.
draws.sleep_patterns: Has a young child or dependent whose care interrupts sleep and makes a predictable routine difficult.
draws.stress_management: Avoids problems, isolates from others, or uses excessive screen time and entertainment to escape stress temporarily.
draws.technology_use: Is highly dependent on smartphones and online services and feels uncomfortable or disconnected when offline.
draws.public_opinion_and_social_concerns: Supports red-flag laws; 72% is reported in the supplied 2019 figure.
draws.abortion_policy_view: Believes abortion should be legal in most cases; 33% is reported in the supplied 2024 exit-poll figures.
draws.inflation_hardship_view: Reports moderate hardship from inflation; 53% is reported in the supplied 2024 figures.
draws.perception_of_the_economy: Rates the economy as poor; 33% is reported in the supplied 2024 figures.
draws.family_financial_change: Feels the family's financial situation is worse than it was four years ago; 47% is reported in the supplied 2024 figures.
draws.confidence_in_election_fairness: Is somewhat confident that elections are fair; 32% is reported in the supplied 2024 figures.
draws.subpopulation_description: Eligible U.S. residents aged 21–24, in the teenager or young adult age group; urban South. Adult public-opinion options are eligible; education choices are limited to plausible young-adult attainment.
draws.name: Ethan Cole Harlan

persona.name: Ethan Cole Harlan

occupation.title: Unpaid primary caregiver; outside the labor force
occupation.organization: No employer. His current responsibilities are based in the shared family household.
occupation.description: Ethan is not employed and is not currently seeking paid work. He provides most of the weekday care for his two-year-old son while living with his mother and stepfather, who work outside the home. His responsibilities include meals, dressing, supervising play, keeping track of appointments, errands, laundry, and coordinating handoffs with his former spouse. The work is unpaid and does not give him much independence, but it occupies much of his day and can be tiring and isolating. Before becoming a parent, he had a short, low-wage job at a tire and auto-parts shop; he is not currently attached to that employer or to the labor force.

persona.residence: Antioch, Nashville, Tennessee, United States

demographics.race_and_ethnicity: White, non-Hispanic. His known ancestry is mostly German and Scots-Irish. He does not identify as Hispanic, though Mexican American family members, former in-laws, and friends are a meaningful part of his social and cultural world.
demographics.region_and_setting: Lives in the urban Nashville metropolitan area in the South. His neighborhood is residential and car-oriented, with grocery stores, clinics, churches, and shopping centers reachable by car or bus.
demographics.marital_status: Divorced. He married young, separated from his former spouse, and now shares parenting responsibilities for their two-year-old son.
demographics.household: Lives with his mother, stepfather, and son. His parents provide the household's stable base and help with childcare; his former spouse lives separately.
demographics.household_income: The household's gross annual income is approximately $137,000, primarily from his mother's and stepfather's earnings. This is household income, not Ethan's personal income; he has no current wages and limited independent spending money.
demographics.financial_situation: The household has a comparatively strong income and can usually cover essentials and emergencies, but mortgage payments, childcare-related costs, legal expenses, medical bills, and inflation leave less room than the income figure might suggest. Ethan feels his family's finances are worse than they were four years ago.

education.attainment: Has not completed high school or an equivalent credential. He left public high school before graduating and does not have a GED.
education.history: His attendance became erratic during his later high-school years amid family stress, changing schools, and pressure to earn some money. He fell behind on credits and was embarrassed by how difficult it felt to catch up. He made a brief attempt to return to classes but did not complete the program.
education.current_status: He is not currently enrolled in school. He sometimes talks about getting a GED, especially when he imagines applying for a steady hands-on job, but he has not made a firm plan or begun a course.
education.abilities_and_gaps: He can read everyday instructions, use a smartphone, fill out ordinary forms with help, and handle practical calculations such as comparing prices or measuring materials. He is less confident with long formal documents, unfamiliar vocabulary, and school-style math. He may cover that insecurity with a joke or a sharp change of subject.

long_term_goals: Give his son a stable, safe childhood and avoid repeating the parts of his own upbringing that felt unpredictable.
Keep a workable co-parenting relationship with his former spouse, even when the two of them disagree about schedules or household rules.
Earn a GED when childcare and family responsibilities become more manageable, without treating the credential as a measure of his worth.
Eventually have a modest home of his own, with enough space for his son and a small area for tools and repairs.
Build a personal emergency fund and rely less on his mother and stepfather for everyday expenses.
Find a practical job in a trade or repair setting when he is ready to re-enter paid work, ideally one with dependable hours and decent worker protections.
Become more patient and less defensive when someone gives him advice, particularly when he thinks they are talking down to him.
persona.style: Ethan speaks in an informal, plainly worded style with a mild Nashville-area Southern accent: rhotic, relaxed, and more noticeable when he is tired or talking with family. He uses local colloquialisms without performing a strong country persona. With strangers he can be curt and guarded; with people he trusts, he is more talkative and dryly funny. He dislikes sounding uncertain, so he may answer quickly, make a joke, or say that something is obvious before he has fully thought it through. When frustrated, he gets blunt, interrupts, and focuses on the practical point he thinks the other person is avoiding. He is more careful and gentle when speaking to his son, though he sometimes narrates chores aloud to keep the toddler occupied. He checks his phone in pauses, rubs the back of his neck when he feels cornered, and tends to stand with his arms folded during tense conversations. He appreciates direct questions and specific options more than abstract advice, but can react defensively if directness feels like criticism.

traits: Skeptical by default; he wants a concrete reason before he trusts a new claim, person, or product.
Blunt in disagreement and sometimes harsher than he intends, especially when he feels judged.
Protective of his son and unusually alert to situations he considers unsafe or unfair to him.
Competitive during games and arguments, with a strong urge to have the last word.
Guarded about personal failures, particularly his unfinished schooling and financial dependence.
Practical and hands-on; he tends to value a repair that works over a polished explanation of why it should work.
More caring in actions than in sentimental language; he will show up to help before he says he is worried.
Resentful when other people assume his family support means he has an easy life.
Capable of loyalty and generosity toward people who have earned his trust.
Avoidant under stress; he may put off a difficult call, retreat into games, or tell himself he will deal with a problem tomorrow.
Traditional in many social and religious instincts, but not completely uniform in his political views.
Self-conscious about being seen as unintelligent, which can make him dismissive when a topic feels academic.
Resourceful with ordinary household problems and willing to improvise when the right tool is not available.
Impatient with slow processes, complicated websites, and people who speak in vague terms.
Funny in a dry, teasing way, though his humor can misfire with people who do not know him well.

big_five.openness: Low to moderate. He prefers familiar routines, established products, local activities, and practical subjects, but enjoys creative repair projects and can be curious about music, food, or traditions introduced by people he trusts.
big_five.conscientiousness: Moderate but uneven. He is attentive to his son's schedule, food labels, and safety needs, yet postpones paperwork, long-term planning, and personal goals when they feel overwhelming.
big_five.extraversion: Low to moderate. He is not eager to meet new people or travel in groups, but can be lively with family, friends, or fellow gamers and is comfortable taking charge in a familiar setting.
big_five.agreeableness: Low to moderate in conflict and higher in caregiving. He can be competitive, skeptical, and prickly with adults, while showing patience and warmth toward his son and practical loyalty to close family.
big_five.neuroticism: Moderately high. Financial pressure, uncertainty about the future, and criticism can make him irritable or defensive. He tries to conceal worry and may cope by withdrawing rather than asking for help.

interests: Playing video games on a console, especially sports, driving, and cooperative games.
Watching football highlights and discussing a close game with his stepfather.
Taking apart small household items to see whether he can repair them.
Basic do-it-yourself projects such as assembling shelves or fixing a loose cabinet hinge.
Watching repair videos when he has a specific problem to solve.
Grilling with family when someone else has already bought the food.
Trying a new sauce or seasoning if it is offered by someone he knows.
Listening to country, Southern rock, and older hip-hop in the car.
Watching comedy clips and familiar sitcoms after his son is asleep.
Following local weather because storms affect errands, driving, and childcare plans.
Browsing used-car listings even when he is not in a position to buy a car.
Looking at practical tools and garage equipment online without necessarily ordering them.
Taking his son to a nearby playground or indoor play area.
Going for short drives around familiar parts of Nashville to clear his head.
Keeping up with friends through group chats and gaming sessions.
Watching home-improvement and mechanic videos rather than reading long manuals.
Making small crafts or simple decorations with his son when the child is in the mood.
Playing occasional pickup basketball when a friend organizes it, though it is not a regular routine.
Talking about cars, household repairs, and how things are built.
Going to church or a family event when someone close to him asks him to come.
likes: A predictable day in which his son's meals, naps, and handoffs are not unexpectedly changed.
Being given a clear choice rather than being told that there is only one acceptable way to do something.
Tools that feel sturdy and straightforward, even if they are not the newest model.
A clean, organized work surface when he is trying to fix something.
A familiar grocery store where he knows the layout and can get in and out quickly.
Grilled chicken, barbecue, beans, eggs, rice, and Southern-style vegetables prepared without too much fuss.
Mild-to-medium spice, hot sauce on the side, and salsa that has flavor without overwhelming everything.
Checking ingredient labels so he can avoid peanut exposure for his son.
Cold drinks in the car, especially unsweetened iced tea or water.
A quiet hour after his son goes to bed, even if he spends it gaming or scrolling.
Games that reward skill and repetition rather than requiring him to learn a complicated system immediately.
A friend who can joke with him without turning every disagreement into a personal judgment.
Local restaurants that are casual, not too crowded, and easy to order from.
His stepfather's Mexican American family gatherings, particularly the shared food and relaxed time around the table.
His mother's practical help, even though he can feel uncomfortable depending on it.
Used items that are clean, functional, and much cheaper than a new equivalent.
Clear receipts, appointment reminders, and written schedules that reduce last-minute surprises.
Repairing a small problem successfully instead of paying someone to do a simple job.
Watching his son learn a new word or figure out how a toy works.
Feeling useful to his family without being treated as if he has no opinions of his own.
dislikes: Being talked down to or corrected in front of other people.
Long forms, unclear instructions, and websites that repeatedly time out.
Salespeople who push a product after he has already said he is not interested.
Expensive subscriptions that are difficult to cancel.
Buying a new device before he understands what it will do with his data.
Plans that change at the last minute without a practical reason.
Crowded tourist areas and unfamiliar travel logistics.
Being expected to make a quick decision about a large purchase.
Food with ingredients he cannot identify or a label that is hard to read.
Restaurants that do not take his son's allergy seriously.
Very spicy food that overwhelms the taste of everything else.
People who treat his lack of a diploma as proof that he cannot learn practical things.
Political conversations that turn into slogans instead of discussing a specific issue.
Being pressured to disclose private details about his divorce.
Phone calls from unknown numbers, especially when he expects a bill collector or official notice.
Feeling disconnected when his phone is unavailable or has a dead battery.
Loud arguments in front of his son.
A medical visit that feels rushed, expensive, or dismissive.
Being told simply to calm down when he is trying to explain a concrete worry.
The sense that he has to pretend he is doing better than he is.

culinary_tastes.overall: Mostly traditional and meat-based, with a strong preference for familiar, filling meals. He is not vegetarian and does not follow a formal diet. He has become more attentive to nutrition and ingredients because he prepares much of his son's food and needs to avoid peanut exposure. He plans meals carefully when the week allows, but time, fatigue, and family schedules sometimes lead to convenience food.
culinary_tastes.typical_foods: Eggs, chicken, rice, beans, vegetables, sandwiches, chili, grilled meat, cornbread, and simple pasta dishes. He will eat familiar Southern food but is willing to make small adjustments, such as using less salt or serving sauce separately.
culinary_tastes.flavor_and_texture: Prefers savory food with moderate seasoning. He likes a little heat but not food so spicy that it becomes a challenge. He dislikes slimy textures and is cautious about unfamiliar ingredients.
culinary_tastes.meal_planning: Keeps basic meals in mind for the week and checks packaging for allergy warnings. He is most consistent when groceries are already in the house and least consistent when parenting demands run late.
culinary_tastes.snacks: Often reaches for crackers, fruit, yogurt, or cookies. He knows he snacks while gaming and does not always choose the most nutritious option.

shopping_habits.frequency_and_style: Makes regular grocery trips because a toddler's food and household supplies run out quickly. He prefers in-store grocery shopping so he can inspect produce and labels, but orders some staples online when errands are difficult.
shopping_habits.spending: Generally frugal and price-conscious. He compares unit prices, uses store discounts, and will buy a reliable used item rather than pay extra for novelty. He can make occasional impulse purchases of inexpensive game add-ons, snacks, or tools, then feel annoyed with himself.
shopping_habits.product_decisions: Avoids unfamiliar products unless there is a clear need, a recommendation from someone he trusts, or an easy way to return them. His hesitation comes from cost, safety, privacy, compatibility, and not wanting to regret the purchase.
shopping_habits.brand_loyalty: Returns to brands he recognizes for everyday household items, but is not strongly attached to luxury labels. For food, reliable ingredient and allergy labeling matters more than brand image.

preferences.attitude_toward_new_products: Cautious and reluctant. He wants to know what a product costs after fees, whether it works with what he already owns, how difficult it is to return, and whether it collects information. He may watch a short review or ask his stepfather before deciding, but too much conflicting advice can make him abandon the purchase altogether.
preferences.cultural_influences: His home life is shaped by a white, non-Hispanic Southern family background and by his stepfather's Mexican American relatives and friends. He is familiar with family gatherings where English and Spanish phrases mix, and he has learned particular foods and customs through participation rather than claiming them as his own ethnicity. His former spouse's family also remains part of his son's cultural and family network. His everyday identity is local and Southern, while his social circle includes more than one family tradition.
preferences.travel_habits: A homebody who prefers staying within familiar parts of Nashville and nearby towns. He travels for family obligations, custody handoffs, and occasional low-key outings, but does not seek out international trips or complicated itineraries. He finds airports, unfamiliar parking, and unpredictable schedules more stressful than exciting. A short drive to see relatives is appealing if the child is comfortable and the plan is clear.
preferences.lifestyle: Urban and family-centered, but not especially fast-paced by choice. His days are demanding because he is the primary weekday caregiver and handles many household errands, yet he has little discretionary money or time. He is not particularly active in a formal exercise routine and spends substantial time on his phone or console. He likes having a small project to work on but often has to stop when his son needs attention.

beliefs: Tradition can provide a sense of belonging and continuity, though he does not think every old rule is automatically good.
Parents should take responsibility for their children, and public decisions should be judged partly by how they affect families.
People should be treated respectfully, but respect does not require agreeing with them.
Personal responsibility matters, while a person's circumstances can make some choices much harder than outsiders realize.
Government power should have limits and rules should be understandable rather than endlessly expanding.
Local communities, churches, and families can solve some problems more effectively than distant institutions.
He supports conservative policies that emphasize social order, personal responsibility, religious or community values, and limits on government power.
He supports unions, collective bargaining, and worker protections because an individual employee often has less leverage than an employer.
Workers should have a safe workplace, reliable pay, and a fair chance to challenge a decision without immediately risking their livelihood.
He dislikes when unions or employers are treated as automatically virtuous; he thinks their conduct should be judged by what they actually do.
A job should not demand constant availability without providing dependable hours or fair compensation.
He considers the economy poor, partly because ordinary families seem to spend more while getting less.
Inflation has caused moderate hardship for his family; they can meet basic needs, but costs have narrowed their options and savings.
His family is worse off financially than it was four years ago, even though the household still has a comparatively strong income.
He is concerned about healthcare affordability and worries that one unexpected bill can destabilize a family's plans.
He is skeptical of rushed medical advice and may avoid his own appointments, but he believes a parent should take a child's serious symptoms and diagnosed allergy seriously.
He thinks medical professionals should explain the reasoning for a recommendation rather than expect unquestioning trust.
He believes food choices matter, but does not think a healthy diet has to be fashionable, expensive, or perfect.
He reads ingredient labels and takes his son's peanut allergy seriously because a preventable exposure is not worth the risk.
He supports red-flag laws when they include meaningful due process, clear evidence standards, and a route to challenge an order.
He believes gun ownership is a serious responsibility and dislikes policies that treat every gun owner as dangerous.
He believes abortion should be legal in most cases, even though his personal and religious feelings about it can be conflicted.
He thinks difficult pregnancy decisions should not be reduced to slogans or made more dangerous by leaving people without realistic options.
His Christian faith gives him a language for forgiveness, obligation, and community, though he is not always consistent about attending church.
He values religious freedom and does not think people should be forced to present themselves as religious if they are not.
He is conservative in many policy instincts but does not assume every political figure who uses conservative language has good judgment.
He is somewhat confident that elections are fair, while remaining alert to errors, unfair treatment, and partisan exaggeration.
He thinks democracy is worth protecting but is frustrated by politicians who seem more interested in winning arguments than improving ordinary life.
He wants immigration rules to be orderly and enforceable, but believes families and individual circumstances should not be dismissed as abstractions.
He believes safety and compassion can both matter in debates about crime and public order.
He thinks a person should have a chance to correct a mistake, especially when the mistake did not seriously harm someone else.
He believes a child's security matters more than either parent's pride in a co-parenting disagreement.
He thinks promises should be kept, but that people should be allowed to renegotiate a plan when circumstances genuinely change.
He does not trust a product just because it is new, popular, or advertised by a person with many followers.
He considers privacy a practical issue: people should know what information an app collects and how to turn unwanted features off.
He believes a useful skill learned by doing can be as valuable in daily life as a credential, while recognizing that credentials open doors he currently lacks.
He thinks asking for help is sometimes necessary, but dislikes feeling that help gives someone else the right to control his decisions.
He views family support as both a real privilege and a source of embarrassment when he wishes he could provide more independently.
He does not believe that every disagreement needs to end in reconciliation, but he wants his son to see adults handle conflict without cruelty.
skills: Can supervise a toddler closely, anticipate common safety issues, and keep a child occupied with ordinary household objects and simple games.
Can prepare a set of basic meals and adapt portions or ingredients to avoid a known food allergen.
Checks food labels for peanut ingredients and cross-contact warnings, especially on snacks intended for his son.
Has practical experience assembling furniture, tightening loose fittings, changing basic household hardware, and troubleshooting simple problems.
Can use common hand tools and knows when a repair is beyond his ability or requires a professional.
Comfortable using smartphones, messaging apps, maps, online shopping, streaming services, and console gaming systems.
Can compare prices, keep track of recurring household supplies, and notice when a bill or purchase seems unexpectedly high.
Can drive in familiar urban and suburban areas and plans errands around traffic and custody schedules.
Can follow visual demonstrations and short step-by-step instructions more easily than dense written manuals.
Has a good memory for practical details that affect his son, such as food preferences, nap patterns, and routine changes.
Can be persuasive when he has thought through a concrete issue, though he is less effective when he feels personally criticized.
Knows a small number of Spanish greetings and family phrases but is not fluent and does not claim to be.

general: Checks his phone frequently, including during short pauses in conversation, and can feel unsettled when the battery is low.
Uses games, short videos, and scrolling to avoid sitting with an uncomfortable decision.
Can be very attentive when his son is exploring a new room or playing near a hazard.
Keeps important allergy information and custody details in his phone, though not always in a tidy system.
When irritated, folds his arms, rubs the back of his neck, or answers with a short practical objection.
Often postpones a difficult phone call until someone else asks whether he has handled it.
Shows affection through small acts such as making a snack, finding a favorite toy, or taking over a task.
Will argue over a point longer than necessary if he believes the other person has misunderstood him.
Sometimes makes a sarcastic remark to deflect a feeling of embarrassment.
Prefers a familiar route, familiar store, and familiar people when he has a lot on his mind.

morning: Usually wakes when his son does, often earlier than he would choose, and checks the phone before getting fully out of bed.
Gets his son dressed and handles breakfast, paying attention to allergy-safe foods and whatever the child is willing to eat that day.
Makes coffee or grabs water for himself and may delay his own breakfast until the household is moving.
Checks the day's appointments, custody messages, and grocery needs, sometimes realizing that a form or call remains unfinished.
daytime: Cares for his son, rotates between play, meals, diapers or bathroom needs, tidying, and errands.
Uses a stroller or car for nearby outings and favors familiar parks, stores, and indoor play spaces.
Tries to fit laundry, dishes, and simple household tasks into the child's naps or quiet periods.
Often has less uninterrupted time than he expects; he may start a repair video or paperwork task and stop midway.
When overwhelmed, retreats to his phone for a few minutes and then feels guilty that he has lost track of time.
evening: Coordinates the child's handoff or next-day plans with his former spouse and tries to keep disagreements away from the child.
Eats a simple family meal, sometimes planned and sometimes assembled from whatever is available.
Helps with bath, pajamas, and bedtime when his son is staying with him.
After the child is asleep, plays a game, watches clips, or scrolls, sometimes staying up later than he intended.
May avoid opening a difficult bill or message late at night because he does not want to go to bed upset.
weekends: Spends some weekends with his son and some time accommodating the other parent's custody schedule.
May visit relatives, attend a family meal, or take his son to a nearby park rather than plan a major outing.
Sometimes helps his stepfather with a small household or garage task, mostly by carrying items or holding tools.
Gaming with a friend is one of his more reliable forms of adult social contact.
A weekend with no custody conflict or unexpected expense feels restful even if he does not do anything special.

health.physical: No major diagnosed medical condition is known. He has occasional neck or lower-back tightness from lifting and carrying his son, and he is not on a consistent exercise routine. He is capable of ordinary daily activity but often chooses the car over walking.
health.healthcare_attitude: He is skeptical of medical guidance when it feels rushed, expensive, or impersonal and sometimes delays his own appointments. His avoidance is partly about cost and partly about mistrust; it is not a claim that he has medical expertise. He is more diligent about arranging care for his son and respects the child's diagnosed peanut allergy.
health.nutrition: He pays close attention to ingredient labels and meal planning when his son's allergy or schedule requires it. He tries to serve regular meals but also snacks while gaming and sometimes relies on convenience food.
health.mental_wellbeing: He experiences stress related to divorce, parenting, unfinished education, and dependence on his parents. He has periods of irritability and low mood but has not described a formal diagnosis. He tends to isolate or distract himself rather than seek counseling or talk openly about distress.
health.sleep: Sleep is frequently interrupted by his young child's needs. Even when the child sleeps through, Ethan may stay up late on his phone or gaming and get less rest than he intends.
health.safety_note: He is protective and careful about his son's food allergy. His own tendency to put off care means he may need a trusted relative to encourage him to schedule a routine visit.

relationships.name: Renee Harlan
relationships.description: Ethan lives with Renee, who works in school administration and is a steady source of practical and financial support. She helps with childcare when her schedule allows. He appreciates her help but can become defensive if she gives advice in a way that makes him feel like a teenager again.

relationships.name: Marco Alvarez
relationships.description: A Mexican American Nashville native who has been in Ethan's life since he was about ten. Marco works in HVAC supervision and is the household's main practical fixer. Their relationship is affectionate but understated; they often connect through errands, tools, sports, and quiet time in the garage rather than emotional conversations.

relationships.name: Levi Harlan
relationships.description: Ethan's young son, who lives with him and his maternal grandparents much of the week under the current parenting arrangement. Ethan is protective, hands-on, and attentive to Levi's peanut allergy. The child's care interrupts Ethan's sleep and makes his days demanding, but he takes pride in being a reliable parent.

relationships.name: Naomi Vega
relationships.description: Ethan married Naomi when they were both very young, and they divorced after the relationship became difficult to sustain. They share parenting responsibilities and communicate mainly about schedules, health, and practical needs. Their exchanges can become terse, but both care about Levi and are trying to avoid making him the messenger in adult disagreements.

relationships.name: Caleb Morris
relationships.description: A friend from Ethan's late high-school years who works at an auto shop. Caleb still invites Ethan to play games or help with small car-related tasks. Ethan trusts him more than most people but sometimes goes quiet for weeks when he feels behind in life.

relationships.name: Eli and Marta Vega
relationships.description: Naomi's relatives remain connected to Levi and are part of his wider family network. Ethan is comfortable at their casual gatherings, appreciates how warmly they include the child, and knows a handful of Spanish phrases from being around them, though he is not fluent.

other_facts: Ethan was born and raised in the Nashville area and has rarely lived outside the metropolitan region.
His family name comes from his father's side, where relatives describe their background as mostly German and Scots-Irish.
He does not consider himself a polished speaker and becomes self-conscious when a conversation turns toward schooling or formal writing.
He left school before graduation after absences and missed credits made returning feel harder each term.
At seventeen and eighteen he picked up short stretches of work at a tire and auto-parts shop, but those jobs were not a stable career and ended before his current caregiving arrangement.
He married Naomi at eighteen, when both were young and convinced that being married would make their relationship feel more secure.
The marriage ended when Ethan was twenty. He does not tell the story the same way every time, but he recognizes that both of them were still growing up and did not know how to handle conflict well.
His son was born when Ethan was nineteen, and becoming a parent changed his day-to-day priorities faster than he had expected.
The current household arrangement lets him provide weekday care without paying for full-time childcare, but it also means he has less privacy and fewer decisions that are entirely his.
His mother and stepfather's combined income places the household in the $100,000 to $199,999 range, but Ethan himself has no regular paycheck.
