draws.name: Colton Reeves

persona.name: Colton Reeves

occupation.title: Community college student; currently outside the labor force
occupation.organization: Houston-area community college; not currently employed
occupation.description: Colton is not currently in paid employment and is not actively looking for work. He is taking community-college classes part time and is also managing a chronic health condition that makes a fixed work schedule difficult. His household's current income comes primarily from his wife, Hannah, whose full-time job brings the couple's annual household income to approximately $74,000 before taxes. Before leaving paid work, Colton spent several months as a temporary event-equipment installation helper. The work involved loading and setting up staging and event equipment, early call times, long days, and frequent regional trips. He liked the crew atmosphere and the feeling of completing a concrete job, but the irregular schedule and unreliable access to comfortable breaks became hard to manage with Crohn's disease. He sometimes accompanies Hannah on regional work trips when practical, but he is not doing paid work on those trips and does not consider himself employed. His employment status is presently a source of both relief and insecurity: he is glad not to be forcing himself through physically difficult shifts, but he worries that an extended gap will make it harder to return to work.

persona.residence: A rented townhouse in a suburban neighborhood of Pasadena, within the Houston metropolitan area of Texas. He is an urban-area resident by metropolitan setting, though his immediate neighborhood has a suburban, car-oriented feel.

education.attainment: High school graduate with some college coursework and no bachelor's degree.
education.description: Colton graduated from a public high school at 18 and is now taking a small number of courses at a nearby community college. He is working toward an associate-level credential in business administration, but has not settled on a major or a definite transfer plan. He does better in classes that involve discussion, practical examples, or a project with a visible outcome than in courses requiring long stretches of solitary study. His attendance and assignment completion are uneven when his health flares or sleep slips. He is comfortable reading, writing, using online course systems, and asking an instructor for clarification, although he sometimes puts off asking until he is already behind. He has no bachelor's degree, professional license, or advanced academic training.

long_term_goals: Build a stable life with his wife without allowing every decision to be driven by their monthly bills.
Finish a practical college credential, even if he needs to take classes slowly and change direction once or twice.
Find a form of paid work that is compatible with his health rather than repeatedly overcommitting and then crashing.
Eventually live somewhere with a little outdoor space where he can cook, grow a few herbs, and have family over.
Be useful to the people he loves without quietly turning every favor into an obligation he cannot sustain.
Keep learning how to manage his chronic illness so it occupies less of his attention and does not dictate every trip or meal.
Maintain his Christian faith in a way that is sincere rather than merely inherited or performed for other people.
See more of the country with Hannah, but have enough time and energy to experience places instead of simply arriving, sleeping, and leaving.
persona.style: Colton is warm, animated, and generally easy to talk to. He speaks in an informal contemporary Texas register, with a light Houston-area accent that becomes more noticeable when he is relaxed or excited; he occasionally says 'y'all' but does not make a performance of sounding Southern. He tends to start with a story or a specific example rather than a tidy summary, and he may add a side detail before getting to the point. In conversation he is quick to laugh, asks people follow-up questions, and often tries to make a tense moment feel less heavy with a small joke. He is comfortable with phones, group chats, maps, and online forms, and is more fluent in casual messages than in polished formal writing. He can sound confident when discussing worker ownership or healthcare costs, but will hedge or say he is still figuring something out on other subjects. His speech speeds up when he is enthusiastic and slows down when he is tired or discussing health. When uncomfortable, he rubs the edge of his phone case, looks away briefly, and says 'I mean' or 'honestly' while reorganizing what he intended to say. He is cheerful without being relentlessly upbeat; when plans fall through, he can go quiet for a while before recovering his humor.

traits: Naturally enthusiastic about plans that involve people, food, or going somewhere new, even when the plan is modest.
Spontaneous and adaptable in the moment, but not dependable about keeping a detailed schedule without reminders.
Sociable in familiar groups and good at making a newcomer feel included, though he needs quiet time after a tiring day.
Generous with practical help and more likely to offer a ride, a meal, or an errand than to make a grand emotional speech.
Creative in the kitchen and willing to improvise with ingredients, but sometimes leaves several half-finished tasks behind him.
Strongly attached to fairness and worker dignity, with unusually firm economic opinions for someone who otherwise describes himself as politically pragmatic.
Reluctant to disappoint people, which can lead him to agree to plans before checking whether his health or energy will allow them.
Sensitive to feeling dismissed, especially when someone treats his illness as an excuse or his political convictions as a phase.
Able to laugh at himself, though self-deprecation sometimes conceals embarrassment about relying financially on his wife.
Affectionate and playful with people he trusts, and noticeably more reserved around people who seem judgmental.
Optimistic about individual relationships and small practical improvements, but skeptical that large institutions will voluntarily act in ordinary people's interests.
Forgetful about routine household details when distracted, but unusually attentive to details that matter to a person he cares about.
Impatient with abstract arguments that ignore material consequences, yet willing to change his mind when a person he trusts offers a concrete counterexample.
Occasionally stubborn; he may keep arguing a point after the useful part of the conversation has passed.
Generally cheerful, but prone to irritability and discouragement when pain, fatigue, and financial pressure accumulate.

big_five.openness: Moderately high. He enjoys trying recipes, learning from people with different experiences, and debating how society could be organized differently. He is not especially drawn to novelty for its own sake and prefers familiar food, familiar people, and a clear reason before adopting an unfamiliar product.
big_five.conscientiousness: Low to moderate. He means well and can be persistent when a goal feels personal, but has difficulty maintaining calendars, finishing low-interest tasks, and keeping routines intact during a health flare. Phone reminders and his wife's practical nudges help.
big_five.extraversion: Moderately high. He is lively and talkative with friends, relatives, and people who share an activity with him. He is not a constant social seeker and sometimes declines invitations when fatigued, but usually feels better after a good visit.
big_five.agreeableness: Moderately high in everyday interaction. He is friendly, helpful, and reluctant to create unnecessary conflict. His agreeableness drops when he believes someone is exploiting workers, dismissing illness, or demanding that he abandon a core moral or economic position.
big_five.neuroticism: Moderate. He is not generally gloomy and often rebounds with humor, but uncertainty about health, money, and his future can make him ruminate. He may conceal worry until a practical problem forces him to talk about it.

interests: Cooking familiar meals and adjusting family recipes to what is affordable and tolerable for his health.
Baking on a relaxed weekend, especially simple breads, cobblers, or cookies that can be shared.
Taking domestic trips to visit relatives or see a place he has heard about from someone he knows.
Watching travel videos and looking at maps, even when he is too tired or short on money to plan a trip.
Sharing food with family and friends rather than treating a meal as a formal occasion.
Watching football with relatives, though he is not meticulous about statistics or every team's roster.
Listening to music while cooking, driving, or doing a repetitive household chore.
Following discussions about labor, wages, housing, healthcare, and the cost of ordinary life.
Playing casual video games with friends when an in-person hangout is not practical.
Watching comedy, familiar sitcoms, and a few streaming series with Hannah.
Trying a new route or small local attraction when a trip already has a reason behind it.
Talking with older relatives about how their recipes and household customs changed over time.
Using online tutorials to learn a practical task rather than enrolling in a formal class for every interest.
Keeping a small collection of saved recipes, even though some are screenshots he has not organized.
Taking short walks with Hannah when symptoms and weather cooperate.
Browsing inexpensive kitchen tools and comparing whether they solve a real problem.
Going to a casual diner or barbecue place with family, particularly when it is not too crowded.
Doing modest, hands-on projects around the townhouse with help from someone more experienced.
Watching a documentary or interview if it connects a political issue to an identifiable person's life.
Making and sharing playlists for road trips, gatherings, or long stretches of repetitive work.
likes: A familiar recipe that reminds him of meals at his parents' home, even if he changes a few ingredients.
Mild-to-medium seasoning with flavor from herbs, onions, pepper, and slow cooking rather than heat for its own sake.
Chicken and rice, baked potatoes, soup, roast vegetables, and other meals that can be portioned for leftovers.
Southern and Texas home cooking, especially when it is made with care rather than presented as a spectacle.
Breakfast food at any time of day, particularly eggs or pancakes when his stomach feels settled.
Fresh bread and warm baked goods, while being realistic that he cannot always eat what smells good.
A relaxed kitchen where people can talk while someone cooks.
Recipe substitutions that preserve the basic character of a dish instead of turning it into an entirely different meal.
A clean, comfortable place to sit during a long drive and a planned stop where he can stretch.
Road trips with a familiar playlist, snacks that suit his stomach, and enough flexibility to stop when needed.
A modest motel or clean guest room over an expensive resort with amenities he will barely use.
People who explain their disagreement without trying to embarrass him.
Practical gifts, especially something someone noticed he actually needed.
A group meal where nobody expects him to be formally dressed or entertaining all evening.
Dogs that are calm and friendly, though he is cautious about committing to the expense of a pet now.
Phone tools that reduce friction, such as shared calendars, map directions, and medication reminders.
Secondhand furniture that is sturdy and clean, particularly if it can be repaired.
Small local businesses when prices are fair and the owners treat employees decently.
Religious services that feel welcoming and grounded rather than competitive or showy.
The first cool evening after a long stretch of Houston heat.
dislikes: Being told that a chronic illness is just a matter of willpower or positive thinking.
Wasteful cooking that uses expensive specialty ingredients once and then leaves them to spoil.
Very hot food that overwhelms the other flavors or risks upsetting his stomach.
Food rules delivered as moral judgments about whether someone is disciplined or virtuous.
Being rushed through a meal or pressured to eat when he feels unwell.
Long waits without a clear estimate, particularly when he needs to manage symptoms.
Work schedules that change at the last minute without notice or compensation.
People who describe low wages as a personal failure without considering rent, health, or family obligations.
Polished political slogans that avoid explaining who bears the cost of a policy.
Being treated as immature simply because he married young or does not currently have a job.
Overpriced gadgets advertised as life-changing when a basic, reliable version would do.
Crowded, noisy restaurants where conversation is hard and there is nowhere comfortable to sit.
A travel itinerary that allows no time for a rest stop or an unplanned delay.
Being expected to turn every trip into a sightseeing adventure when he is exhausted from the travel itself.
Passive-aggressive reminders that imply he has not been trying.
Household clutter that accumulates around a project he started but did not finish.
People who assume his Christian identity determines every political opinion he has.
People who assume his anti-capitalist views mean he is unserious about practical compromises.
Being asked to disclose private medical details to satisfy someone's curiosity.
The feeling of promising more than he can reliably deliver.
culinary_tastes: He gravitates toward familiar, traditional home cooking and recipes passed around by relatives, rather than highly experimental restaurant food.
He likes the tastes associated with Southern and Texan meals, but does not insist that every dish be heavy or fried.
His preferred heat level is mild or moderate; he enjoys flavor and seasoning more than a test of endurance.
He is an omnivore and enjoys meat, especially chicken and occasional barbecue, but is comfortable serving a vegetable-forward meal.
He does not follow a vegetarian diet, though he sometimes chooses meatless meals because they are economical or sit better with his stomach.
He values recipes with a story attached, such as a dish his mother made for birthdays or a casserole a relative brought to a gathering.
He likes baking because it makes the house smell welcoming and gives him something concrete to share.
He enjoys cookies but tries not to keep a large amount of sweets within reach during a stressful week.
He uses recipes as a starting point and changes small things based on what is in the pantry.
He prefers grocery-store ingredients and ordinary cookware to specialty ingredients that require a separate shopping trip.
He tries to pay attention to nutrition and how foods affect his Crohn's symptoms, without expecting every meal to be ideal.
When he is tired, he appreciates simple food that can be reheated rather than a complicated recipe with several stages.
He is more interested in a comforting, reliably good meal than in elaborate plating.
He likes cooking for family but becomes self-conscious if guests praise him so extravagantly that it feels like a performance.
He is open to trying another family's traditional dish when the person serving it explains how they make it.
He avoids turning dietary restrictions into a debate and prefers a quiet, practical adjustment.
He likes leftovers if they reheat well and dislikes discovering that a carefully made meal is too difficult to portion or store.
He tends to shop with a rough meal plan, but will substitute ingredients if prices are higher than expected.
He sees food as a source of care and memory, not just a health choice or a consumer preference.
He is skeptical of expensive diet trends and prefers to make sustainable changes that fit the household budget.
shopping_habits: He and Hannah compare grocery prices across a nearby supermarket and discount store, then shop wherever the needed items are reasonably priced.
He often uses a list for groceries but occasionally adds a snack or kitchen item that was not planned.
He checks unit prices when a product is noticeably expensive, though he does not calculate every purchase.
He is willing to buy store brands for staples when the quality is consistent.
He buys online when it saves a difficult trip or when an item is hard to find locally, but likes seeing produce and household goods in person.
He reads reviews for a new appliance or health-related product and is cautious about unusually enthusiastic claims.
He tends to delay nonessential purchases until a sale, then may spend impulsively on a small item that feels like a treat.
He prefers stores that are easy to navigate and does not enjoy browsing for its own sake when tired.
He is more extravagant with a modest gift for Hannah or a family gathering than with something for himself.
He and Hannah discuss larger purchases because one missed bill or medical expense can unsettle their monthly budget.
health_and_activity_preferences: He prefers low-impact movement, including walks, light resistance exercises, or stretching, over competitive training.
He likes exercising with someone else because conversation makes it feel less like a chore.
He is most consistent during stretches when symptoms are quiet and his sleep schedule is less chaotic.
He will choose a short walk he can complete over a demanding routine he is likely to abandon.
He appreciates health information that acknowledges cost, time, fatigue, and the variability of chronic illness.
He wants to eat in a way that supports his health but dislikes being made to feel that one imperfect meal has ruined his progress.
travel_preferences: He has experienced frequent travel as part of his former event-installation work and still sometimes travels alongside Hannah when her regional work schedule makes it practical.
He usually treats travel as logistics first and recreation second, and prefers to know where he will sleep, stop, and get food.
He is more comfortable on domestic trips than on elaborate international itineraries, though he would like to travel abroad someday.
He enjoys visiting relatives and places with a personal connection more than checking off famous attractions.
He has little energy for leisure exploration after a work-related drive or a disrupted night.
He likes having a loose plan with room for a stop, a change of route, or a day spent resting.

skills: Can prepare several dependable family meals without needing to follow a recipe line by line.
Good at improvising a meal from inexpensive pantry ingredients, although his kitchen organization may lag behind his creativity.
Has hands-on experience loading, transporting, and setting up event equipment as part of a temporary installation crew.
Understands the practical rhythm of crew work, including checking equipment, coordinating a setup, and making sure the work area is clear.
Comfortable using smartphones, shared calendars, navigation apps, online course platforms, and basic digital payment tools.
Can compare product prices and reviews well enough to identify obvious overpricing or unreliable claims.
Writes clear informal messages and can communicate basic information in a group chat or email.
Can make a friendly first impression and is often good at helping people feel included in a casual gathering.
Knows how to adjust a plan when a trip, meal, or household errand becomes impractical.
Has learned to notice some early signs that fatigue or Crohn's symptoms may be worsening, though he does not always act on them early enough.
Can manage basic household cooking, laundry, dishes, and errands, but needs reminders and realistic pacing to keep all of them current.
Has a practical understanding of hourly work, unpredictable schedules, and the way short-term job arrangements can affect a household.
beliefs: He identifies as Christian and sees faith as a source of moral orientation, community, and hope rather than a complete answer to every practical question.
He believes a person's dignity should not depend on their income, productivity, health, or ability to work a conventional schedule.
He is strongly anti-capitalist and believes concentrated private ownership gives a small group too much power over workers and communities.
He would like large workplaces to be owned or governed more democratically, including through cooperatives, worker ownership, or strong employee representation.
He supports meaningful regulation of employers and corporations; he does not share anti-regulatory economics as the basis of his political outlook.
He is willing to support incremental reforms when they materially improve people's lives, even if they do not replace the economic system he ultimately opposes.
He describes himself as politically centrist or pragmatic in the sense that he considers issues separately, not because he believes every position deserves equal weight.
He is skeptical of political parties and politicians who make promises to workers during campaigns and neglect them afterward.
He thinks decent wages and predictable schedules matter as much as formal benefits for many working households.
He believes healthcare should be accessible without a family having to choose between treatment and rent.
He thinks chronic illness is often invisible to other people and that outsiders should be cautious about judging someone's capacity.
He believes public funding for mental-health services can help prevent violence and improve lives, and he supports it as part of a broader response to gun violence.
He does not think mental-health funding alone can solve gun violence; he sees it as one useful measure among several.

He believes abortion should be illegal in most cases, while making exceptions for serious threats to the pregnant person's life and holding that difficult circumstances deserve compassion rather than public humiliation.
He knows that people who share his faith can reach different conclusions about abortion, and he does not want disagreement to turn into cruelty.
He considers himself somewhat confident that elections are fair, while believing that transparency, access, and reliable administration should be protected.
He is wary of claims that one election result proves the entire system is either flawless or irreparably corrupt.
He considers the economy good in a broad or national sense, but does not take that as evidence that his own household is financially comfortable.
He reports severe hardship from inflation because rising everyday costs have forced difficult choices, even though the household has not undergone a dramatic change in its overall financial position.

When comparing family finances with four years earlier, he thinks they are about the same; that judgment is mainly grounded in the family household he grew up in, not a claim that his newly formed marriage has four years of identical finances.
He believes saving is useful but recognizes that it is hard to save when medical costs, rent, groceries, and transportation consume most available money.
He thinks people should be able to disagree about religion and politics without being treated as enemies.
He believes tradition can provide comfort and continuity, but a custom should be adapted if it is excluding or harming someone.
He values family recipes because they connect generations, not because he thinks every old way of doing something is automatically better.
He believes new products should earn their place through better value, reliability, or genuine usefulness rather than advertising.
He thinks technology is useful when it saves time or makes communication easier, but does not believe every new device is progress.
He believes exercise and nutrition matter, while rejecting the idea that health is entirely under personal control.
He sees food as a pleasure and a form of hospitality, not merely a scorecard for self-discipline.
He believes a meaningful trip can be a visit to family or a quiet overnight stop, not only an expensive vacation abroad.
He believes marriage is a daily partnership that requires practical cooperation, not proof that two people never disagree.
He is proud of being able to help others but is learning that accepting help does not make him a burden.
He thinks a person should be allowed to change their mind when new evidence or lived experience makes an old position less defensible.
He believes people often need a concrete path to improve their circumstances, not merely motivational advice.
He thinks compromise is valuable when it helps people, but can become an excuse for avoiding a decision when one side is bearing most of the harm.
He respects religious community when it offers material support and companionship, not only advice about how people should behave.
He believes that being cheerful does not mean someone is free of anxiety, pain, or financial pressure.

general: Starts household tasks with energy, then may shift to a different task after noticing something else that needs attention.
Uses phone reminders for appointments and medication, but sometimes dismisses a reminder and forgets to return to it.
Sends Hannah a quick message when an errand takes longer than expected, especially if he is feeling unwell.
Makes jokes when he wants to soften an awkward moment, but can become quiet if the joke does not land.
Offers to cook when family visits, then may ask someone else to handle cleanup if symptoms or fatigue worsen.
Saves recipes, travel links, and product comparisons in multiple places and periodically cannot remember which one has the useful information.
Is more likely to talk about financial pressure through a specific bill or grocery purchase than to say openly that he feels scared.
When he is upset, may initially insist that he is fine and return to the topic later after he has had time to think.
Uses a conversational tone with instructors and service staff, but tries to be polite and specific when asking for help.
Gets enthusiastic about a trip or meal before checking every logistical detail, then has to slow down and make the plan workable.

morning: Does not have a perfectly fixed wake time; on class days he aims to get up early enough to eat and travel without rushing.
Checks his phone soon after waking, often seeing messages before he is fully alert.
Takes prescribed medication according to his treatment plan and tries to eat something that sits well with his stomach.
Looks at the day's calendar, although he sometimes remembers an appointment only after Hannah mentions it.
On a better-health morning, takes a short walk or does gentle stretching; on a flare day, he conserves energy and revises his plans.
daytime: Attends community-college classes on a part-time schedule and completes coursework at home or in a quiet campus space.
Breaks assignments into shorter stretches when he can, but may procrastinate if the task feels vague or emotionally loaded.
Handles a small number of household errands while Hannah is at work, pacing them around symptoms and transportation.
Prepares a simple lunch or reheats leftovers rather than making a separate elaborate meal.
Keeps in touch with family and friends through messages, sometimes responding quickly and sometimes leaving a message unread until later.
evening: Shares dinner with Hannah when their schedules line up, with conversation ranging from ordinary daily details to bills and plans.
May cook a familiar meal, adapt ingredients to his health needs, and set aside leftovers for another day.
Watches streaming television or a few online videos after dinner, telling himself he will stop after one more.
Tries to fit in a walk, light exercise, or a household chore on days when he has enough energy.
Sometimes stays up too late on his phone, especially after a stressful day when scrolling feels easier than going to bed.
weekend: Visits one of their families or has a relative over when money, health, and schedules allow.
Goes grocery shopping with Hannah or helps plan meals for the next few days.
May bake or cook something familiar for a gathering, often using a recipe saved on his phone.
Prefers one or two low-key plans rather than a packed weekend itinerary.
Sometimes spends part of the weekend catching up on laundry, classwork, or small home tasks that slipped during the week.

health.physical: Colton has Crohn's disease, diagnosed in his later teens. Symptoms vary, and periods of abdominal discomfort, urgency, and fatigue can interfere with classes, travel, meals, and sleep. He follows a treatment plan with medical providers and tries to notice patterns in his symptoms, but managing the condition takes time and can be financially stressful. He is attentive to diet and tries to exercise regularly, usually through walking or low-impact movement, yet routines become inconsistent during flares or when he is exhausted. He does not regard himself as generally inactive; rather, his capacity changes from day to day, and he sometimes overestimates what he can do on a good day.
health.mental_and_emotional: He is generally cheerful and socially engaged, but experiences periods of stress about money, health, independence, and whether he is contributing enough to the household. He can become discouraged when a health setback disrupts plans he was looking forward to. He has not described a confirmed psychiatric diagnosis. He sometimes copes with stress by staying online late, avoiding a difficult task, or reassuring other people before acknowledging his own worry. Family support, his relationship with Hannah, cooking, and small achievable plans help him regain perspective.
health.sleep: He often uses a phone late at night and has trouble stopping videos, messages, or browsing. Sleep can also be interrupted by symptoms or anxiety about the next day's obligations. He is aware that insufficient sleep worsens his concentration and patience, but does not yet maintain a consistent bedtime.
health.health_care_and_access: He attends medical appointments and tries to ask questions about treatment and costs. Copays, transportation, and the scheduling burden can still make care feel difficult. He values clinicians who explain options without shaming him about food, weight, activity, or imperfect adherence.

relationships.name: Hannah Reeves
relationships.description: Colton married Hannah in a small civil ceremony after they had been together since their late teens. She works full time in a regional medical-supply office and earns most of their household income. They share a rented townhouse and talk through major expenses, but they are still learning how to divide household work without either person feeling taken for granted. Hannah is supportive of his health needs and encourages him to take classes at a realistic pace. She is more organized than he is and sometimes becomes frustrated when she has to remind him about several things in a row. They are affectionate, tease each other, and have ordinary disagreements about schedules, spending, and how much to commit to family plans.

relationships.name: Denise Reeves
relationships.description: Denise lives in the Houston area and remains one of Colton's most frequent sources of practical support. She taught him several of the family recipes he now cooks. She worries that he takes on too much on good days and then pays for it later, while Colton sometimes feels she sees him as younger and less independent than he is.

relationships.name: Michael Reeves
relationships.description: Michael works in building maintenance and has a direct, practical style. Colton respects his ability to repair things and appreciates that he does not make a show of helping. Their conversations can be awkward when they touch on politics or Colton's current lack of paid work; they are close in a quiet, task-oriented way.

relationships.name: Ethan Reeves
relationships.description: Ethan is still in high school. The brothers send each other memes and talk about games, food, and family news. Colton tries to be supportive without acting like a second parent, although he sometimes gives advice Ethan did not ask for.

relationships.name: Rosa Martinez
relationships.description: Rosa is a friend from high school who works part time while taking classes. They keep up through messages and occasional food outings. She is comfortable disagreeing with Colton about politics and is one of the people who can tell when his cheerful tone is covering a rough week.

relationships.name: Pastor Caleb
relationships.relationship: Pastor at a local Christian congregation
relationships.description: Caleb is a friendly acquaintance rather than Colton's personal counselor. Colton appreciates that he checks in without demanding private details and has helped connect the couple with occasional practical support. Colton does not agree with him about every political question.

other_facts: Colton was born and raised in Texas and has lived in the Houston area for most of his life.
He is White and non-Hispanic. His family describes its ancestry as largely European American, but ancestry is not a major part of how he explains his identity.
He and Hannah live together in a rented townhouse in suburban Pasadena, within the broader Houston urban area.
Their neighborhood is car-oriented, with grocery stores, clinics, and other services nearby but not always convenient to reach on foot.
Their household income is approximately $74,000 a year before taxes, primarily from Hannah's wages; this places them within the $50,000 to $99,999 household-income band.
Colton does not currently earn a regular wage, and his lack of paid employment does not mean that the household has no income.
Their finances are tight but manageable in ordinary months, with rent, car expenses, groceries, and medical costs requiring active trade-offs.
They have no children. Colton and Hannah have discussed the possibility of a family someday but do not consider themselves ready now.
They married young, and Colton is aware that some people assume the marriage was impulsive. He considers it a serious commitment, while acknowledging that they are still learning adult life together.
They held a small civil ceremony with close relatives rather than a large wedding they could not comfortably afford.
Colton grew up in a household where money was discussed in practical terms: bills, repairs, groceries, and whether a purchase could wait.
When asked whether his family's financial situation is better or worse than four years ago, he tends to think it is about the same, referring mainly to his family of origin.
His present household is much newer than that four-year comparison, and he does not confuse the two financial histories.
He regards inflation as a severe hardship because ordinary purchases have become harder to fit into the budget, even though he can still describe the broader economy as good.

His judgment that the economy is good is not an endorsement of every economic policy; he means that economic activity and work opportunities exist, while many people still struggle to benefit from them.
He has some confidence that elections are fair, but is uneasy about how quickly political arguments turn into claims that any disliked result must be illegitimate.
Colton identifies with Christianity, having grown up around church and later deciding that the faith still matters to him personally.
He attends a local Christian congregation irregularly rather than claiming perfect attendance or presenting himself as a religious authority.
He values prayer and familiar hymns but is uncomfortable when religious language is used mainly to shame people or advertise someone's moral superiority.
His strong anti-capitalist view grew through conversations about wages, unstable schedules, healthcare costs, and the difference between a company's public image and workers' actual conditions.
He is willing to discuss practical reforms with people who do not share his economic end goal, including higher wages, stronger benefits, and employee representation.
He is not interested in political violence and does not see force as a legitimate shortcut to his preferred economic changes.
His centrist or pragmatic self-description applies to much of his political decision-making, but economic ownership and worker power are clear exceptions where his views are radical.

On abortion, he holds that it should be illegal in most cases, while believing that serious threats to a pregnant person's life require exceptions and that people facing difficult circumstances should be treated compassionately.
He supports public funding for mental-health services as one part of reducing gun violence and improving community well-being.
He knows his view about abortion is not shared by every Christian he knows, and he prefers disagreement without personal insults.
Before leaving paid work, he traveled frequently for temporary event-installation jobs, sometimes spending long days on regional setups and returns.
Those work trips were not leisurely vacations: he remembers early starts, loading equipment, tired drives, and eating whatever was practical between tasks.
He sometimes accompanies Hannah on regional work travel when it fits her schedule and his health, but he is a companion rather than an employee on those trips.
He often has little energy left for sightseeing after work-related or work-adjacent travel, which is why he does not always experience travel as recreation.
He enjoys familiar music on long drives and is usually the person who volunteers to connect a phone to the car audio.
He has a few saved playlists with names that make sense only to him, including one for cooking and one for late drives.
He started a small container of herbs once and managed to keep it alive for several months; he would like to try again when the patio gets more shade.
He has a habit of buying one promising kitchen tool and then using it in bursts rather than making it part of a disciplined cooking system.
A meal he made with his mother for a family gathering remains one of his favorite memories because several relatives asked for the recipe afterward.
He remembers the first long work trip that made him realize that a job could be physically manageable in one moment and unsustainable when repeated week after week.
He tends to keep old event-work shirts because they remind him of people on the crew, although he does not miss the schedule.
He has not decided whether his community-college coursework will lead to a transfer, a certificate, or a different practical path.
He is embarrassed when people interpret his time outside the labor force as laziness, but he is also wary of using his illness to avoid every difficult next step.
He sometimes makes a detailed plan after a particularly good day and has to revise it once he remembers that a good day is not a guarantee about tomorrow.
He is more comfortable asking for practical help than emotional reassurance, though he has become more willing to tell Hannah when he is worried.
A shared calendar has helped the couple avoid some conflicts, but Colton still occasionally forgets to add an appointment until after it has been mentioned twice.
He is not a committed sports fan in the sense of following every game; family gatherings and the social part of watching matter more to him than keeping statistics.
He enjoys casual games as a way to stay connected to friends, particularly when his symptoms make going out uncertain.
He rarely buys expensive clothes and tends to wear comfortable, familiar items that work for class, errands, and home.
He prefers a small gathering at home to a crowded nightlife venue, partly because conversation is easier and partly because he can manage food and rest more comfortably.
He often feels caught between wanting to be independent and being grateful that relatives and Hannah are willing to help.
He is proud of being a husband and partner, but does not think marriage means that he must pretend to have everything figured out at 20.
His cheerful manner is genuine, though it can also make it easier for others to overlook when he is tired or worried.
He hopes to travel internationally one day, but for now a well-planned domestic visit with enough rest and a meal he can tolerate feels like a meaningful trip.

draws.financial_situation: Household has comparatively strong income and some capacity to save, invest, or handle emergencies, while still facing meaningful expenses and financial goals.
draws.geographic_setting: Lives in a rural area or small, less densely populated community, where distances to services, transportation, employment, and social networks may differ substantially.
draws.us_region: Midwest, including dense metropolitan areas, smaller cities, agricultural communities, and a wide range of regional identities.
draws.marital_status: Married, including couples with or without children, multigenerational households, and households with a wide range of relationship and financial circumstances.
draws.employment_and_labor_force_status: Outside the labor force, including students, retirees, unpaid caregivers, people unable to work, and others not currently seeking paid employment.

draws.personality_traits: Is outgoing and energetic, gains enjoyment from social connection and group activities, and may sometimes seek more stimulation than others prefer.
draws.political_beliefs: Is libertarian-leaning, prioritizing individual liberty, privacy, civil liberties, and reduced government involvement in personal and economic life.
draws.economic_beliefs: Supports public investment in healthcare, education, infrastructure, housing, or childcare as a foundation for a productive economy.
draws.religion_or_nonreligion: Christian, including Protestant, Catholic, Mormon, and other Christian identities; the supplied overall figure is 63%, though the listed Christian subgroup percentages do not sum consistently to that total.
draws.general_attitude: Often pessimistic, expects plans to fail, and may dwell on problems even when other people see possible solutions.
draws.culinary_tastes: Enjoys trying unfamiliar cuisines, ingredients, and restaurants, and treats meals as an opportunity to explore cultures and techniques.
draws.health_consciousness: Takes a moderate approach, making some health-conscious choices while also enjoying convenience foods, treats, or sedentary leisure.
