draws.name: Megan Hollis

persona.name: Megan Hollis

occupation.title: Full-time library assistant and learning-program coordinator
occupation.organization: A small regional public library serving several rural Maine towns
occupation.description: Megan works full time at a public library. She handles circulation and holds, helps patrons use computers and online forms, prepares children's and adult literacy activities, maintains displays, answers routine reference questions, and helps keep the building welcoming and orderly. She often becomes the person who remembers which patrons need large-print books, which child is nervous about reading aloud, or which local group needs the meeting room set up early. She does not have a librarian's graduate degree and does not present herself as a subject specialist; when a question needs deeper research, she finds reliable sources or refers it to the appropriate staff member. The library's small staff means she alternates between desk work, program setup, troubleshooting printers, and practical errands. She enjoys being useful and talking with patrons, but can be worn down by being expected to stay cheerful through a long stream of small requests. Her personal salary is substantially below the household's combined income; the broader education-and-library wage figure in the demographic description is not her individual pay.

persona.residence: A rural community outside Farmington, Maine, in the Northeast region of the United States. She lives in a converted upstairs area of her mother's older farmhouse, several miles from the town center and about a twenty-minute drive from most routine services.

identity_and_household.population_eligibility: A 31-year-old U.S. resident in the 25–54 adult age group. She is a White, non-Hispanic woman who lives in a rural Northeastern community, has never married, and is employed full time in education and library services.
identity_and_household.race_and_ethnicity: She identifies as White and non-Hispanic. Her family describes its roots as multigenerational in Maine, with English and French-Canadian ancestry in older branches of the family; she does not claim that ancestry makes her an expert on either culture.
identity_and_household.marital_and_parental_status: She has never married and has no children. She has had a few serious relationships, but none became a marriage or a shared-parenting arrangement.
identity_and_household.household_income_and_finances: The three-adult household has a gross annual income of approximately $132,000, placing it in the $100,000–$199,999 range. That total combines Megan's earnings, her mother's wages, and her stepfather's pension and occasional seasonal work; it is not Megan's individual salary. The household can save and has an emergency fund, but old-house repairs, medical and dental bills, vehicle costs, and higher grocery and heating expenses make money feel tight. Megan says inflation has caused severe hardship and that the family's finances are worse than four years ago.

persona.education: Megan finished high school in her home county and later earned an associate degree in library and information services at a community college. She has no bachelor's degree. Her coursework covered cataloguing, basic information technology, children's literacy, research support, and public-facing service. She is comfortable learning through practical demonstrations, short courses, and asking knowledgeable colleagues questions, but she can feel self-conscious in conversations where people treat a four-year degree as the only mark of intelligence. Her writing is clear and competent, though she proofreads carefully when preparing formal material. She has taken occasional workplace trainings in digital privacy, first aid, and supporting beginning readers, and has considered taking more classes without deciding whether the cost and time are worthwhile.
long_term_goals: Keep her job stable, become more confident in coordinating library programs, and earn a modest raise or a role with more responsibility without taking on unmanageable debt.
Build her savings enough that an unexpected car repair, medical bill, or household emergency does not immediately unsettle the family budget.
Improve her sleep and stamina in small, realistic ways; she does not imagine that she will suddenly become a fitness enthusiast, but she would like ordinary days to feel less exhausting.
Have a comfortable, private place of her own someday, ideally a small apartment or cottage within driving distance of her mother rather than a move to a city she does not know.
Take a few well-organized trips with dependable transport and lodging, including one visit to coastal Maine that is more than a hurried day trip.
Stay connected to her family and long-standing local friendships while becoming less dependent on the familiar routine that sometimes makes her feel stuck.
persona.style: Megan is lively and conversational in person, especially when she is welcoming someone or telling a story she knows well. She has a broadly recognizable Maine/New England accent, not a theatrical one; local place names and family expressions come out more strongly when she is relaxed. She speaks in a friendly, quick rhythm, uses contractions, asks follow-up questions, and will fill a silence with a small anecdote. At work she is warm and capable with children and older patrons, and she can make an unfamiliar person feel included in a group activity. She often smiles before she has decided whether she is actually in a good mood. When discouraged, her voice gets flatter and her answers shorter, though she may still keep up the social performance out of habit. She uses dry humor about rural driving, library printers, and the cost of groceries, but does not like being teased about her education or told that her sadness is simply a matter of attitude. She is more direct with family than with patrons, sometimes saying, "I know, I know," when she feels nagged. She does not use elaborate professional jargon in ordinary conversation and prefers a clear explanation over an impressive-sounding one. In unfamiliar social or cultural settings she is polite but watchful, and tends to relax once she recognizes the customs and knows what is expected.

traits: Outgoing and socially energetic in familiar settings; she enjoys group activities and can carry a conversation even when her private mood is low.

Persistently discouraged at times, with a low sense of hope that makes chores and personal plans feel heavier than they look from the outside; this is a description of her experience, not a diagnosis.
Practical and resourceful when a concrete problem has to be solved, particularly at work or around the house.
Friendly and attentive to people who are new, shy, elderly, or unsure how to ask for help.
Strongly attached to familiar routines, places, and local relationships, and slower to feel at ease in unfamiliar social environments.
Curious about new consumer products and willing to try new features, even though she is cautious about paying full price.
Opinionated on moral and public questions; she can listen to other views, but does not always soften her own position to avoid disagreement.
Financially careful, with a tendency to compare prices and save consistently even while feeling that everyday costs are squeezing the household.
Sensitive to criticism about her ability, education, or perceived lack of ambition; she may joke first to protect herself.
Generous with practical help, such as covering a desk, bringing food to a family gathering, or helping someone use a computer, but not always good at asking for help in return.
More comfortable with clear plans and dependable arrangements than with improvising a trip or walking into an unfamiliar situation without preparation.
Sometimes avoids difficult tasks when tired, then feels guilty and tries to compensate with a burst of effort.
Can be stubborn once she believes an issue is a matter of right and wrong.
Enjoys being noticed and included, but may need a quiet evening after an animated day with patrons or family.

big_five.openness: Moderate. She is eager to explore new household products, apps, entertainment, and practical features, but prefers familiar customs and a relatively homogeneous local social environment. Her curiosity is stronger around useful or enjoyable novelties than around rapid changes in her community's culture or daily expectations.
big_five.conscientiousness: Moderately high in dependable responsibilities and money management: she shows up for work, remembers patrons' needs, plans purchases, and contributes to savings. It is lower in self-care routines, especially sleep, exercise, and finishing personal tasks when her mood is low.
big_five.extraversion: High. She gains energy from conversation, community events, and working with people, and often takes an active role in a group. This outgoing behavior can coexist with sadness and does not mean she feels cheerful or energized every day.
big_five.agreeableness: Moderate to high in ordinary interactions. She is helpful, courteous, and accommodating at work, though she can become firm or judgmental when a subject touches a deeply held moral belief or when she thinks someone is being irresponsible.
big_five.neuroticism: Moderately high. She worries about expenses, family stability, and whether she is falling behind in life; stress can disrupt her sleep and make minor setbacks feel disproportionately discouraging. She can still function reliably and sometimes uses humor or social connection to get through a hard day.

interests: Reading novels in short bursts, especially family dramas, mysteries, and accessible historical fiction.
Reading nonfiction when it connects to a practical question, a local story, or a subject she has been discussing with someone.
Following local news and weather updates because road conditions and town decisions affect her daily life.
Watching television and streaming shows after work, particularly drama, comedy, reality competitions, and familiar series she can leave on while folding laundry.
Listening to music in the car, often choosing familiar pop, country, soft rock, or older songs she remembers from family gatherings.
Helping with library reading events and seeing a child become more comfortable reading in front of other people.
Talking with patrons and coworkers during a calm shift, especially when the conversation turns into a funny local story.
Browsing product reviews and trying a new app or household gadget when it seems useful or entertaining.
Taking scenic drives through western Maine, provided she knows where she is going and has enough fuel.
Going to a local fair, community supper, craft sale, or library program where she is likely to recognize someone.
Keeping up with a few friends through text and social media, even during stretches when she does not have the energy to arrange a visit.
Reading online articles about everyday health, cooking, home repairs, and local history.
Doing occasional low-pressure crafts or seasonal decorating with her mother, without wanting it to become a demanding hobby.
Watching cooking videos or home-organization clips without reliably following the healthier or more ambitious suggestions.
Enjoying familiar small-town events more than crowded concerts or large city festivals.
Playing simple word, puzzle, or trivia games on her phone during breaks.
Looking through travel brochures and organized-tour itineraries, even when a trip is only a possibility.
Sharing funny clips and pictures with her sister and two close friends.
Listening to coworkers recommend books and sometimes borrowing one she would not have chosen herself.
Taking part in group activities when she can arrive with someone she knows or has a clear role.
likes: A warm, lively room where people are talking but she can still hear the person next to her.
Being greeted by name by regular library patrons.
A book with an engaging plot that does not demand that she keep track of a dozen complicated subplots.
A familiar television series that makes an evening feel less empty.
Sweet iced coffee or a flavored coffee drink as an occasional treat.
Soft cookies, packaged snack cakes, chips, and other convenient snacks she can keep in a desk drawer or the car.
Fried potatoes, diner breakfasts, casseroles, and rich comfort foods associated with family meals.
A clear itinerary that tells her where she will sleep, how she will get there, and when meals are available.
A new device or household product that is easy to set up and does something visibly useful.
Discounts, coupons, store-brand versions, and sale prices that let her enjoy a purchase without feeling foolish afterward.
A quiet drive through familiar rural roads with music on and no urgent errand at the other end.
Local fairs and craft sales where she can browse without committing to an expensive purchase.
Having a private room or corner of the house where she can shut the door and watch something by herself.
People who explain things plainly rather than making her feel ignorant for asking.
A short, friendly conversation with an older patron who is glad someone remembered a detail from last week.
Fiction and news articles she can read in ten- or fifteen-minute stretches.
A well-made winter coat, dependable boots, and other purchases that last through Maine weather.
An organized group outing where someone else has handled the driving and logistics.
Small household improvements that make an old room more comfortable without turning into a full renovation.
Feeling that she has put some money aside even if the amount is modest.
dislikes: Being told to "just cheer up" or that everyone is tired, as if that settles what she is describing.
People who mock small towns or speak as though rural residents are ignorant by default.
Feeling pressured to spend money because everyone else is buying something.
Unexpected travel changes, missed connections, or being left to solve transportation in an unfamiliar place.
Very spicy food that overwhelms the taste of everything else.
Complicated recipes that require specialty ingredients, several pans, and a clean kitchen afterward.
A cold, bare waiting room or a loud public space where she cannot follow a conversation.
Being corrected publicly in front of patrons or coworkers.
People who treat a bachelor's degree as proof that someone is automatically more competent.
A long list of wellness advice that assumes she has unlimited time, money, and motivation.
Unfamiliar social situations where she cannot tell what people expect of her.
Last-minute household repairs that arrive before payday or consume money she had set aside.
The taste and smell of cigarettes lingering on clothes, even though she smokes when stressed.
Trying to sleep while worrying about bills, family issues, or what she forgot to do at work.
A patron being rude to a coworker who is trying to help.
Food that is presented as a moral test, with people lecturing her about what she should eat.
Being asked to take on unpaid extra responsibilities indefinitely because she is "good with people."
Long, unstructured travel days with no reliable meal or restroom plan.
A new product that is difficult to set up, has hidden costs, or requires an account for every feature.
Feeling that people assume her political views, religion, or intelligence from where she lives.
culinary_preferences: She generally prefers familiar American comfort food to experimental tasting menus.
She enjoys rich, sweet, fried, and processed foods and does not routinely count calories or follow nutritional guidelines.
Cookies are a frequent favorite snack, with chocolate chip and oatmeal-raisin both acceptable depending on what is available.
She also keeps chips, crackers, snack cakes, and candy around for convenience, especially during busy workweeks.
She likes fried chicken, burgers, pizza, baked pasta, and diner-style breakfasts.
She likes food with flavor but prefers mild or moderate seasoning and usually avoids very hot peppers.
She will try a new packaged snack if it is inexpensive, has appealing reviews, or is offered by someone she trusts.
She eats meat and does not identify as vegetarian; meatless meals are fine when they are familiar and filling.
She is more likely to eat vegetables when they are part of a casserole, soup, or side dish than when served as a large plain salad.
She often relies on convenience foods, leftovers, and inexpensive staples because of limited energy and time after work.
Her meals can be irregular; she may skip a proper lunch and snack at the desk, then eat a large dinner late.
She likes sweet drinks and flavored coffee more than unsweetened beverages, though she keeps water in the car.
At family gatherings she gravitates toward familiar dishes rather than being the person who asks for a special menu.
She enjoys a good homemade pie or cake but does not bake on a regular schedule.
She sometimes buys a healthier-looking item with good intentions and then reaches for the easier snack when tired.
shopping_habits: She compares prices across nearby stores and checks digital flyers before larger grocery trips.
She uses coupons when they are easy to redeem and does not want couponing to become a second job.
She plans essential purchases and postpones nonessential ones when household bills are due.
She is frugal about clothing and household goods but will spend more on durable boots, a warm coat, or a reliable phone.
She is careful with online orders and checks shipping costs, return policies, and reviews before buying.
She prefers to shop in person for groceries and items where color, fit, or quality is hard to judge online.
She will try a new product early if it is discounted, easy to return, or available in a low-cost version.
She sometimes makes an unplanned small purchase when stressed, usually food or a modest comfort item, then feels annoyed with herself.
She contributes regularly to savings and has an emergency fund, but may use it for household or car costs rather than a purely personal emergency.
She finds household budgeting reassuring in principle but can feel discouraged when careful planning does not prevent costs from rising.
preferences.health_consciousness: She has limited physical activity, irregular sleep, and inconsistent meal timing. She knows these habits are not helping her energy, but she often prioritizes getting through work and family obligations over making a major lifestyle change. She is more receptive to one manageable change than to a strict diet or exercise plan.
preferences.attitude_toward_new_products: She is an early and enthusiastic tester of new consumer products, especially phone features, small kitchen devices, personal-care products, and practical household items. Novelty appeals to her, though she controls the financial risk by checking reviews, waiting for a sale, or choosing a cheaper version.
preferences.cultural_comfort_and_influences: She feels most at ease in familiar local settings with customs and viewpoints she recognizes. She values her family's Maine traditions and local institutions and can be cautious around unfamiliar social norms, but this preference is not a claim that she has no interest in outside entertainment, products, or information.
preferences.travel_habits: She is an occasional traveler rather than a frequent one. She prefers organized tours, familiar hotel chains or well-reviewed inns, a clear schedule, reliable transportation, and known options for food and medical access. She is more comfortable visiting a new place when the logistics are handled and someone she trusts is going with her.
preferences.reading_and_entertainment: She reads fiction, nonfiction, news, and educational material in uneven bursts. She watches a substantial amount of television and streaming entertainment, including drama, comedy, reality programming, and familiar comfort shows; she is not a film or television critic and does not need every choice to be intellectually ambitious.

beliefs: She generally identifies as an Independent and prefers to judge candidates and proposals issue by issue rather than treating a party label as a full description of her views.
She values compromise when it produces a workable result, but does not believe compromise is automatically virtuous if it means abandoning a moral conviction.
She thinks individual effort, persistence, useful skills, and prudent decisions are major contributors to financial success and mobility.
She also recognizes that illness, family obligations, local job options, housing costs, and bad luck can limit what effort alone can accomplish.
She considers inflation a severe problem in her household because groceries, heating, vehicle expenses, and ordinary bills have risen faster than the family feels able to absorb.
She describes her family's finances as worse than they were four years ago, despite steady employment and careful spending.
She rates the economy as poor from the perspective of everyday household costs, even though she understands that national economic statistics may tell a more complicated story.
She believes illegal immigration is a very big problem and favors meaningful enforcement of immigration law and a controlled process for entry and legal status.
Her concern about immigration is tied in her mind to fairness, enforcement, and pressure on public resources; she does not want people treated cruelly or blamed solely for seeking safety or work.
She believes abortion should be illegal in all cases because she regards unborn life as morally significant even in circumstances where many people would favor exceptions.
She knows that her abortion position is a strong and unpopular one in some settings and does not pretend that the issue is easy for every person affected by it.
She is not affiliated with a religion, does not identify as Christian, and is best described as agnostic rather than actively religious.
She does not pray as part of a regular routine, though she understands why family members find comfort in prayer and religious community.
She thinks religious institutions can offer belonging and practical help, while also believing that no one should be pressured into faith.
She is somewhat confident that elections are fair, but would not say that every election is free of mistakes or that every official is beyond criticism.
She worries about political hostility and possible post-election violence, partly because national arguments now reach people through phones even in a small rural town.
She dislikes the way partisan conflict makes ordinary conversation feel like a loyalty test.
She favors a pragmatic approach to public policy and is more persuaded by a proposal's concrete costs and effects than by a slogan.
She believes public libraries should remain welcoming public places, including for people who cannot afford books, computers, or a quiet place to work.
She thinks education matters, but rejects the idea that people without bachelor's degrees are incapable of learning or making informed decisions.
She believes children benefit from patient adults who make reading feel safe rather than embarrassing.
She thinks a person's work deserves respect even when it is not prestigious or highly paid.
She believes steady saving is worth doing even if it cannot guarantee security against every emergency.
She does not equate a high combined household income with feeling wealthy, especially when several adults share expenses and the house needs repairs.
She thinks it is reasonable to be frugal about ordinary purchases while still enjoying occasional treats.
She believes health matters, but finds advice unrealistic when it ignores fatigue, stress, local access, and the cost of food and care.
She considers healthcare affordability a serious concern and dislikes delaying necessary care because of cost or uncertainty about the bill.
She believes substance misuse and drug addiction affect rural communities as well as cities, and that public responses should include treatment and accountability.
She values familiar community traditions, but accepts that local life changes as younger residents, new families, and new ideas arrive.
She feels more comfortable with familiar customs and viewpoints than with rapid cultural change, but tries not to assume that an unfamiliar person is unkind or dishonest.
She thinks new products can make daily life easier, though advertising often exaggerates what a product can actually do.
She trusts a recommendation more when it comes from someone who has used the product and will mention its drawbacks.
She believes travel is worthwhile when it gives people a change of scene without making the whole experience stressful or financially reckless.
She thinks family members should help one another, but that help should not become an unspoken expectation that one person will carry every burden.
She values being dependable and dislikes letting people down, even when that tendency leads her to accept too much.
She believes local public services matter more when people live far from larger towns and cannot easily replace them with private options.
She thinks feeling sad for a long time is real and burdensome even when a person is still working, joking, and showing up for other people.
She would rather have someone listen without immediately offering a lecture or a simple fix.
skills: Experienced in circulation desk work, placing holds, checking materials in and out, and helping patrons navigate basic library systems.
Able to explain simple computer tasks patiently, including printing, email access, scanning, and filling out common online forms.
Good at remembering returning patrons' preferences and making a practical suggestion without making the interaction feel formal.
Capable of planning small literacy events, setting up a room, preparing supplies, and adjusting when attendance is higher or lower than expected.
Comfortable finding reliable introductory information and distinguishing a basic reference question from one that needs specialist research.
Competent with email, word processing, spreadsheets at a basic level, shared calendars, and everyday smartphone functions.
Strong customer-service instincts and a good ear for whether someone needs detailed help or a quick answer.
Able to keep several routine tasks moving during a busy shift, though interruptions can make paperwork take longer.
Practical about household spending, sale comparisons, and maintaining a modest savings plan.
Knows local roads and services well and can give useful directions to nearby towns, clinics, schools, and community events.
Good at making new participants feel included in a group, particularly children and adults who are embarrassed to ask for help.
Can learn new consumer technology quickly when she can try it hands-on and does not feel judged for asking basic questions.

general: She talks easily with patrons and coworkers, often beginning with a question about someone's day or a small local detail.
She tends to use snacks as a quick comfort when she feels depleted, especially during a long shift or a late evening.
She checks product reviews and sale prices before spending, but may still buy an inexpensive novelty item because trying it sounds fun.
She saves a set amount when the household budget allows, then feels frustrated when repairs or medical expenses take money back out.
She uses her phone throughout the day for work messages, directions, local news, entertainment, and contact with family.
She sometimes avoids responding to a message when she feels low, then sends an enthusiastic reply later as though no delay occurred.
She can be animated in a group and then prefer to spend the evening alone in her room with a familiar show.
She smokes when stressed despite disliking the smell and knowing it is not good for her health.
She makes lists for errands and work tasks but is more likely to complete them if the first step is very clear.
She is quick to help someone else with a practical problem and slower to say that she herself is struggling.

morning: Her sleep varies considerably. On an ordinary workday she aims to get up around 6:15 a.m., but after a restless night she may hit snooze more than once.
She gets dressed quickly, checks the weather and road conditions, and has coffee or a sweetened drink rather than preparing a substantial breakfast.
She drives to work because the rural distance and limited public transportation make walking or transit impractical.
If she has time, she takes a snack or leftovers with her; if not, she assumes she can find something at work or on the way.
workday: She starts by checking the desk, returns, program calendar, and any messages that need an early response.
She moves between patron service, computer help, shelving, program preparation, and short administrative tasks.
She is sociable through much of the day and often remembers details of prior conversations with regular visitors.
She may eat at an irregular time and snack while handling quieter desk work.
After a demanding interaction she usually returns to the next task rather than taking a formal break to process it.
evening: She drives home and may stop for groceries or a household errand if it can be combined with the trip.
Dinner is often a convenience meal, leftovers, or something familiar prepared by her mother; she sometimes eats later than she intended.
She watches television or streaming content, scrolls through her phone, and messages family or friends.
If she is worried or overstimulated, she may smoke or snack rather than take a walk or use a relaxation routine.
She intends to go to bed at a reasonable time but can remain awake for hours, moving between her phone, a show, and anxious thoughts.

weekends: She may sleep late after a short or fragmented workweek night, then feel annoyed that part of the morning has passed.
She helps with groceries, laundry, or small household tasks and often accompanies her mother on an errand.
She is more likely to attend a local fair, family gathering, community supper, or friend's home if she knows at least one person there.
She occasionally takes a scenic drive or visits a nearby town, usually with a specific destination rather than setting off without a plan.
She sometimes spends a weekend afternoon watching a run of familiar television episodes and postponing a personal task she has been avoiding.
sleep_and_stress: Her sleep is highly irregular: some nights she gets only a few hours, while other times she stays awake very late and sleeps substantially during the day off that follows.
She does not maintain a consistent wind-down routine and often uses a screen close to bedtime.
Stress tends to produce comfort eating, smoking, and inactivity rather than exercise or meditation.
Social contact can lift her mood temporarily, but she does not treat a pleasant evening as proof that the longer-running sadness has disappeared.
financial_habits: She checks household costs and saves consistently when income and bills permit.
She avoids unnecessary subscriptions and compares prices, but is not an extreme couponer.
She keeps a modest emergency reserve and sees it as protection against car, heating, or home repairs.
She sometimes feels that careful saving is being undone by prices and shared household expenses she cannot fully control.

health.physical_wellbeing: Megan reports low physical activity, irregular meals, frequent snacking, and inconsistent sleep. Rural driving and desk-based library work mean she gets little incidental exercise. She has no stated major chronic diagnosis, and no specific medical history is established here. She knows that her habits could be healthier but has difficulty sustaining changes during periods of low energy.
health.mental_and_emotional_wellbeing: She experiences persistent sadness, discouragement, and low hope, and at times ordinary tasks feel unusually difficult. This is a description of her reported state, not a clinical diagnosis. She can still be outgoing, funny, and responsive to other people while feeling low internally. She has considered talking with someone about her mood but has not established a regular mental-health care routine.
health.sleep: Her sleep pattern is extreme and irregular rather than reliably restful. She can have nights of very short sleep or prolonged wakefulness and then catch up with substantial daytime or weekend sleeping. No sleep disorder diagnosis is asserted.
health.coping_and_risk_habits: When stressed she is more likely to smoke, eat for comfort, stay inactive, or spend a long time on a screen. These behaviors bring short-term relief but can leave her feeling more tired or dissatisfied later. She does not present herself as someone who has everything under control.
health.healthcare_access: She can reach routine services by car, though the distance and cost make appointments inconvenient. She is concerned about healthcare affordability and tries to plan for bills, but an unexpected expense can still cause significant strain.

relationships.name: Ellen Hollis
relationships.description: Ellen shares the farmhouse with Megan and works in school transportation scheduling. They are close and routinely coordinate meals, errands, and household responsibilities. Ellen is warm and practical but sometimes expresses concern about Megan's sleep and mood in a way Megan experiences as nagging.

relationships.name: Mark Hollis
relationships.description: Mark lives in the household and receives a municipal pension, supplemented by occasional seasonal work such as plowing. He is steady, reserved, and more comfortable fixing a practical problem than talking about feelings. He and Megan get along, though they do not confide in each other as much as she and her mother do.

relationships.name: Tara
relationships.description: Tara lives in another Maine town and works in a dental office. They trade messages and funny videos, and Tara sometimes encourages Megan to take a day trip or make an appointment she has been putting off. They care about each other but have different political instincts and can stop short of arguing when a conversation becomes heated.

relationships.name: Jenna
relationships.description: Jenna is a former classmate who lives within driving distance. They meet for coffee or a diner meal every few weeks and share candid complaints about work and money. Megan is more likely to tell Jenna she is feeling low than to bring it up in a large group.

relationships.name: Ruth
relationships.description: Ruth is a trained librarian who trusts Megan with day-to-day patron service and program logistics. Their working relationship is cordial and direct. Ruth encourages Megan's strengths but can unintentionally add responsibilities because Megan is reliable and sociable.

relationships.name: Caleb
relationships.description: Caleb is an ex-boyfriend from a relationship that ended several years ago. They are not currently involved, though occasional contact can stir up regrets about whether Megan has been too cautious in her personal life. The relationship ended without marriage or children.

other_facts: Megan grew up in the same broad part of Maine where she lives now and recognizes many local family names, roads, and school histories.
Her childhood home was not affluent, but she remembers it as stable because adults worked, repaired things when possible, and expected children to help.
She was a sociable student who was more confident speaking in class than writing long papers under time pressure.
A high school librarian encouraged her to consider library work after noticing that Megan was patient with younger students who needed help finding books.
She initially attended community college part time while working, then completed her associate degree after several years rather than following a direct four-year route.
She is proud of finishing the degree but occasionally compares herself unfavorably with coworkers who have advanced qualifications.
Her first library job was temporary, and she was relieved when the full-time role became available.
She likes the moments when a patron returns to say that a book, computer session, or form of practical help made a difficult day easier.
She has learned that being friendly at work can lead people to assume she is always available for extra tasks.
The farmhouse has character and family history, but its age brings recurring maintenance problems, heating costs, and rooms that are harder to keep warm.
The household's three incomes make the combined annual income comparatively strong, but the money belongs to a shared household with several adults and shared obligations.
Megan contributes to groceries and household expenses and tries to set aside money of her own; the arrangement is practical rather than a sign that she has no wish for independence.
She keeps an emergency fund, though some of it has gone toward vehicle repairs, dental expenses, and work on the house.
A few years ago the family could save more reliably; higher prices and successive repairs have made that feel less true.
She does not think of herself as poor, but she also does not feel financially secure enough to ignore costs.
Her car is essential to her work and social life. A breakdown would be a financial and logistical problem, not just an inconvenience.
She checks the weather forecast before driving in winter and keeps basic supplies in the car, partly from habit and partly because rural roads can be slow to clear.
She has a small collection of books she has actually reread and a much larger collection of library books she means to get to.
She sometimes borrows books for herself after recommending similar ones to patrons, then returns them unread when work or sleep problems take over.
Her social ease is genuine, but it can conceal how discouraged she feels once she is alone.
She is not consistently pessimistic about every outcome; she can be hopeful about a specific plan while feeling doubtful about her life more generally.
She likes new technology when it works intuitively and becomes irritated when a basic device requires multiple accounts, updates, or paid add-ons.
She will often ask a coworker or family member for a quick demonstration rather than spend an hour searching through technical instructions.
Her interest in novelty is strongest for products and entertainment; in community life she tends to prefer familiar people and customs.
She enjoys seeing a new place but wants the travel itself to feel manageable, not like a test of her independence or adaptability.
A well-organized tour appeals because it reduces decisions about transport, lodging, and meals while still giving her something new to see.
She has never been married and sometimes feels behind when friends discuss spouses, mortgages, or children, but she does not want to marry simply to meet a milestone.
She has no children and does not currently make parenting plans; she sometimes helps with children's programs at the library without treating that work as a substitute for having a family of her own.
Her family has longstanding local connections, but she does not assume that every person in town shares her beliefs or background.
She can be uncomfortable when people dismiss her town as backward, and she can also recognize that familiarity sometimes makes her less curious than she would like to be.
Her position on abortion is firm and rooted in a moral belief about unborn life; she does not treat it as a casual political talking point.
Her view of immigration is also firm, but she distinguishes enforcement policy from contempt for individuals and dislikes cruelty being presented as a solution.
She is more confident discussing practical local issues than highly technical national policy, and will say when she does not know enough to answer.
She considers herself unaffiliated and agnostic. She has attended church events with relatives but does not regard herself as Christian or as a member of another faith.
She sometimes wishes she could sleep normally for a week and see what her mood feels like with more rest, but has not yet built a dependable routine.
Her smoking is a stress habit she would rather not have, and she may become defensive if someone treats quitting as a simple matter of willpower.
She responds better to specific, nonjudgmental suggestions than to a lecture about discipline or self-improvement.
A good day for her is usually not dramatic: work goes smoothly, someone makes her laugh, the car behaves, dinner is easy, and she gets a little time alone.
She can be grateful for a stable job and a supportive family while still feeling disappointed by how constrained her life sometimes seems.
She hopes that greater confidence, better sleep, and a few practical changes will gradually make her world feel less narrow, even though she does not always believe that progress will be quick.

draws.age_group: A teenager or young adult aged 15–24, potentially in secondary or postsecondary education, early employment, or the transition to independent living.
draws.gender: Female, as represented in the supplied two-category gender distribution; individual identity and expression may vary.
draws.race_and_ethnicity: Black or African American, including people with multigenerational U.S. roots and people or families with Caribbean, African, or other diasporic backgrounds.
draws.household_income: Annual household income from $25,000 to $49,999, with financial flexibility varying substantially by household size, location, debt, and caregiving responsibilities.
draws.geographic_setting: Lives in an urban area, such as a major city or densely populated metropolitan community, with relatively close access to services and varied employment.
draws.us_region: Midwest, including dense metropolitan areas, smaller cities, agricultural communities, and a wide range of regional identities.
draws.employment_and_labor_force_status: A child or young person who is not expected to participate in the labor force.
draws.subpopulation_description: Eligible U.S. residents aged 15–17, in the teenager or young adult age group; urban Midwest. This band includes secondary-school ages, so adult interests and opinions are unconstrained.
draws.name: Aaliyah Brooks

persona.name: Aaliyah Brooks

occupation.title: High school student; not employed
occupation.organization: Chicago public high school
occupation.description: Aaliyah's primary responsibility is attending school, completing assignments, and learning how to manage the greater independence expected of a high school student. She is not in the labor force and does not have a paid job. At home she sometimes helps with ordinary chores, watches her younger brother for a short time while her mother is nearby or on her way home, and runs small errands with permission. Those family contributions are not a job and do not make her financially independent. She has not yet chosen a career and does not present herself as an expert in any professional field.

persona.residence: South Shore, Chicago, Illinois, United States; an urban neighborhood in the Midwest.

demographic_profile.race_and_ethnicity: Black or African American. Her family has multigenerational roots in the United States, including maternal relatives who moved from Mississippi to Chicago several decades ago.
demographic_profile.household_income: Her household's approximate gross annual income is $42,600, within the specified $25,000–$49,999 range. The money generally covers essentials, but unexpected school costs, medical copays, or a car repair can make the month difficult.
demographic_profile.household: She lives with her mother and younger brother in a rented two-bedroom apartment. Her father lives elsewhere and is part of her life, though contact and practical support are not perfectly regular.
demographic_profile.labor_force_status: She is a minor and is not expected to participate in the labor force. She has no paid job and is not looking for one; school and family responsibilities take up her time.

education.current_status: Aaliyah is a 10th-grade student at a Chicago public high school. At 15, she is among the younger students in some of her classes, but she has settled into high school routines and knows how to ask a teacher for help when she feels comfortable.
education.academic_profile: Her grades are usually a mix of Bs and Cs, with stronger results in English, art, and assignments where she can explain an idea in her own words. Algebra takes her longer, especially when a lesson moves quickly and she is reluctant to ask for a second explanation in front of the class. She can do careful work when she understands the purpose of it, but she sometimes delays longer assignments until the deadline feels real.
education.school_experience: She likes having a few teachers who recognize her and greet her by name. She finds crowded hallways, noisy lunch periods, and group projects with uneven workloads tiring. She participates in an occasional art-room activity and helps with a school display when a friend asks, but she has not committed to a demanding club or leadership role.
education.attitude_toward_learning: She wants school to lead to choices later, though she does not yet know whether that means college, a two-year program, or learning a practical skill after graduation. She is more engaged when lessons connect to actual situations, books, art, or people she can relate to than when material feels like a list to memorize.

long_term_goals: To finish high school with enough confidence and good enough grades to have several real options afterward, rather than feeling pushed into a path she has not chosen.
To find out whether she would enjoy studying illustration, interior design, nursing, or another field before making a costly commitment.
To earn money as an adult without having to feel anxious every time an ordinary bill arrives.
To help her mother and younger brother when she is able, while still building a life that belongs to her.
To travel beyond the Midwest at least once with people she trusts, and eventually visit a place she has only seen in books or online.
To keep a few close friendships through the changes that come with high school and growing up.
To become more comfortable speaking up when she needs clarification or thinks something is unfair.
To have a home that feels peaceful and personal, with enough room for books, art supplies, and people she cares about.
persona.style: Aaliyah is observant before she is talkative, especially around adults or people she has just met. With friends she speaks in relaxed, current teenage language, sometimes using expressions such as 'for real,' 'that's wild,' or 'I don't know, maybe,' but she does not force slang into every sentence. Her Chicago-area accent is generally subtle; it becomes more noticeable in quick, casual conversation and in the rhythm of certain words rather than in any exaggerated pronunciation. She can explain herself clearly in class when she has had time to think, but may answer a personal question with a shrug or a short 'I'm good' until she decides the person is safe to talk to. In texts she uses short messages, reaction images, and occasional voice notes; when annoyed she may leave a message unread rather than say something she will regret. She tends to look at people while listening, then glance away when she is embarrassed or trying to find the right words. She fidgets with a sleeve cuff, twists a pencil, or smooths the edge of a notebook when nervous. Her humor is dry and affectionate, and she likes noticing small absurdities in school life. She does not enjoy being talked down to, especially when someone assumes that being young means she has not thought about something. In unfamiliar situations she is polite and measured; with trusted people she is more animated, teasing, and willing to disagree.

traits: Observant: she notices shifts in a friend's mood, changes in a teacher's tone, and small details in rooms, although she does not always mention what she has noticed.
Caring in practical ways: she will save a seat, share a snack, or check whether her brother has his things rather than make a grand speech about being supportive.
Somewhat guarded: she takes time to trust people and does not immediately share family worries or private opinions.
Quietly funny: she makes understated comments and can be playful with people who understand her humor.
Imaginative: she thinks in pictures and often mentally changes the colors, arrangement, or details of things she sees.
Easily embarrassed: public correction or being singled out can make her go quiet, even if the correction was not harsh.
Fairness-minded: she pays attention to whether rules are applied consistently and can stay bothered by something she sees as a double standard.
Inconsistent with follow-through: she can focus intently on a drawing or a topic she likes, then put off a routine assignment until the last minute.
Cautious about change: she wants to know what a new activity or product will actually be like before she commits, but curiosity can overcome that hesitation.
Proud: she dislikes asking for help when she thinks she should already know something, though she is gradually learning that questions are not a weakness.
Family-oriented without being endlessly patient: she loves her family and can still get irritated by chores, interruptions, or being expected to act older than she feels.
Emotionally perceptive but not always verbally expressive: she often recognizes what she is feeling after she has had time alone.
Sensitive to criticism: she can take a blunt comment personally at first, then reconsider it later if it came from someone she respects.
Socially selective: she enjoys a small group of friends more than a large gathering where she has to keep introducing herself.
Resilient in ordinary, unshowy ways: after a disappointing grade or awkward day she may feel bad for a while, then return to the next task without treating the setback as the end of everything.

big_five.openness: Moderately high. She is receptive to art, unfamiliar music, stories, and other people's experiences, but prefers a little time to get used to major changes. Her curiosity is strongest when she can connect something new to a person, image, or practical example.
big_five.conscientiousness: Moderate to low-moderate. She cares about doing well and is capable of careful work, but planning ahead and keeping every school task organized are genuine challenges. External reminders help, while being nagged tends to make her defensive.
big_five.extraversion: Low-moderate. She is not afraid of people and can be lively with friends, but crowded social settings tire her. She usually prefers one-on-one conversation or a small group to being the center of attention.
big_five.agreeableness: Moderately high. She is considerate and often tries to avoid embarrassing others, but she is not automatically compliant. If she thinks someone is being unfair or disrespectful, she may become blunt or withdraw rather than smooth things over.
big_five.neuroticism: Moderate. School pressure, family money worries, and uncertainty about fitting in can stay on her mind. She is not in constant distress, and familiar routines, trusted people, and time to herself usually help her settle.

interests: Sketching outfits, hairstyles, room layouts, and faces in the margins of notebooks, even when she does not intend to turn the drawings into finished art.
Looking through illustrated books and online images for color combinations, lettering, and small design details.
Reading realistic young-adult fiction when the characters sound like people rather than perfect role models.
Watching comedy and coming-of-age shows with her mother or brother, though she often watches a few episodes alone on her phone.
Listening to R&B, pop, and rap playlists, choosing different music for the bus, homework, and getting ready in the morning.
Taking photos of interesting signs, murals, clouds, window displays, and food, mostly to keep rather than post.
Making simple bead bracelets or decorating inexpensive notebooks when she has the supplies and patience.
Going to the public library when a friend is free, especially to browse rather than follow a strict reading list.
Trying a new snack or drink if a friend recommends it and it costs little enough not to feel like a waste.
Watching short cooking videos and occasionally trying one easy step at home, such as mixing a sauce or arranging toppings.
Following a few creators who share drawing ideas, school humor, or affordable outfit combinations.
Looking at room-decorating ideas and imagining how she could improve a small bedroom without buying expensive furniture.
Playing casual mobile games with her brother, especially games that do not require a long competitive session.
Walking around a familiar shopping area with a friend when they have permission and a clear plan for getting home.
Helping choose music for a family car ride, while accepting that her mother may change it after a few songs.
Watching basketball highlights or a school game occasionally, more for the atmosphere and friends than for statistics.
Learning small facts about cities, landmarks, and food through videos and school assignments.
Keeping a private notes-app list of ideas, things to remember, and phrases she finds funny.
Making cards or small drawings for birthdays when she has time, even if she gets the gift ready later than planned.
Spending quiet time by a window or outside on a mild day when the apartment feels busy.
likes: Rice bowls, baked chicken, and vegetables when the meal is familiar but can be adjusted with a sauce or topping.
Macaroni and cheese at family meals, particularly when it is homemade and not too dry.
Mildly seasoned food with the option to add hot sauce herself rather than having the whole dish made very spicy.
Strawberries, grapes, and watermelon when they are washed and ready to eat.
Soft hoodies, roomy jeans, and clothes that feel comfortable through a long school day.
Thrifted clothes when she finds something clean and in good condition that does not look exactly like what everyone else has.
Small gold-colored earrings and simple accessories that do not snag on her clothes or need careful maintenance.
Fresh stationery, especially smooth pens, colored markers, and notebooks with sturdy covers.
A bedroom that is tidy enough to relax in but still has her drawings and belongings visible.
A calm conversation where nobody rushes her to answer immediately.
Friends who can joke around without turning every conversation into a competition.
Teachers who explain what a good assignment looks like instead of saying only that she should try harder.
Streaming a familiar show while folding laundry or doing an easy chore.
Cold water and fruit after walking home or being active at school.
Finding a low-cost item that is genuinely useful rather than a trendy purchase she will stop using.
Rain against the window when she is safely indoors and does not have to travel in it.
Window seats on buses or trains, where she can look outside without needing to fill every quiet moment.
Simple skincare products that do not sting, smell strongly, or promise impossible results.
Family meals where people can talk without everyone needing to agree about everything.
Being trusted with a small responsibility and having the chance to show she can handle it.
dislikes: Being told to 'calm down' when she is trying to explain why something bothered her.
People reading her private messages over her shoulder or taking her phone without asking.
Being expected to choose an answer instantly when she has not had time to think.
Group projects where one person does most of the work and everyone receives the same credit.
Teachers announcing a mistake in front of the whole class when a quiet correction would work.
Very spicy food that overwhelms the rest of the flavor.
Greasy food that leaves her feeling uncomfortable during the school day.
Being pressured to buy something because a friend says everybody has it.
Online shopping photos that make an inexpensive product look much better than it is.
Crowded, echoing rooms where she cannot hear the person next to her.
Long waits without knowing whether a bus is delayed or coming soon.
People making assumptions about what she can afford based on her clothes or phone.
Being called lazy when she is overwhelmed or has lost track of several assignments.
Waking up already behind schedule and having to rush through getting ready.
Strongly scented products, especially lotions or sprays that linger in a small room.
Shoes that look good online but rub her heels after a short walk.
Being compared with a sibling or a classmate as if they should have the same temperament.
A sudden change in plans when nobody tells her why or what the new plan is.
Adults discussing her as if she is not present when the conversation is about her.
Arguments that get loud quickly and leave everyone acting as if nothing happened afterward.

beliefs: Doing well in school can create options, but one bad grade does not decide a person's whole future.
Some subjects feel hard because the explanation or pace does not work for everyone; struggling is not proof that a student is unintelligent.
Asking for help is useful, although she still finds it embarrassing to do in front of a whole class.
People should be held to the same rules, and adults should explain why a rule exists when it affects young people.
Being young means she is still learning, not that her feelings or observations are automatically silly.
A person can love their family and still need privacy, quiet, and time alone.
Money matters because it affects ordinary choices, but having less money does not tell you whether a family is loving or responsible.
It is better to check a claim before repeating it, especially when a post is designed to make people angry.
She does not trust every polished online recommendation; a creator may be entertaining and still be trying to sell something.
A new product is not automatically better because it is popular, expensive, or described as a must-have.
A cheap product that works reliably is more impressive to her than an expensive one with clever packaging.
Food should taste good and make a person feel reasonably well; she does not think every snack needs to be judged as virtuous or bad.
Cooking at home can be comforting and less expensive, but people should not be shamed when they are tired or lack time.
Health advice should be understandable and practical rather than making people feel guilty for not having perfect habits.
Getting enough sleep matters, even though she sometimes stays up later than she planned using her phone.
Walking and ordinary movement count as activity; exercise does not have to look like an intense sports routine.
She thinks trying unfamiliar food can be fun when there is a familiar option too and nobody mocks her for hesitating.
Family traditions can be meaningful without every younger person having to observe them in exactly the same way.
She feels connected to Black history and culture, while recognizing that Black people do not all share one personality, taste, or opinion.
Her family's Chicago roots matter to her, but she does not want people to reduce the whole city to one neighborhood or one story.
Music, clothes, language, and ideas move across places; liking something from somewhere else does not mean rejecting where she comes from.
Travel sounds exciting, but safety, cost, timing, and who is going with her are real considerations rather than minor details.
She likes the idea of seeing other places but is also comfortable with familiar routes and a quiet day at home.
Being kind is important, but kindness does not require agreeing with someone who is disrespectful.
A sincere apology includes changed behavior, not just saying the right words to end an argument.
Adults should take gun violence seriously because young people should be able to go to school and spend time in public without constant fear.
She has not settled on a political party and is skeptical when adults insist that every issue has an easy answer.
Government decisions can affect whether families can afford healthcare, school supplies, and safe places to live, even when politics feels distant.
Healthcare should not become impossible to access just because a family has limited money, though she does not know the details of how the system should work.
People who move to the United States should not be treated as a single group or blamed for every problem; individual situations are different.
She thinks people should be able to make personal decisions about their lives, but some subjects are complicated and she is still learning how she feels about them.
Climate and pollution matter because they affect the places people live, but she wants adults to explain practical solutions rather than only argue.
Online disagreements can become cruel quickly, and she would rather leave a conversation than keep trying to win it.
A close friend should be able to disagree without using a private insecurity as ammunition.
A good life does not have to look rich or impressive from the outside; feeling safe, having choices, and being treated with respect matter more.
skills: She can draw recognizable faces, clothing details, and simple room layouts, especially when she has a reference image.
She has a good eye for color combinations and can spot when a design feels crowded or unbalanced.
She writes clearly when the topic interests her and can revise a paragraph after a teacher points out a specific issue.
She remembers small personal details friends mention, such as a test date or a food they cannot eat.
She is comfortable using a smartphone for messaging, school portals, photos, maps, and basic online research.
She can compare prices and notice when a sale is not actually much cheaper than the regular price.
She knows familiar CTA routes in her area and follows her mother's rules about where she may travel alone.
She can prepare a few basic snacks and simple foods with permission, and understands that the kitchen needs to be left clean.
She can help her younger brother organize his backpack or find something he has misplaced, though she may complain if asked at the last minute.
She is good at noticing when a friend is unusually quiet and asking a low-pressure question rather than demanding an explanation.
She can use school presentation tools and basic word-processing features, but is not an advanced computer user.
She knows how to look for a library book, school resource, or public information page, while still needing help judging complicated or conflicting sources.
She can keep track of a small amount of spending money if she has a clear purpose for it, but is still learning to plan for several purchases at once.
She is learning to speak up with teachers and adults, particularly when she can prepare what she wants to say beforehand.

general: When she comes home, she usually puts her backpack down before taking off her shoes, then checks her phone for school messages or friend notifications.
She sometimes starts homework at the kitchen table and moves to her room when household noise makes it hard to concentrate.
If a task seems too large, she may postpone it by doing a smaller chore or looking for a reference image; a short checklist helps her restart.
She likes to know the basic plan before leaving home, including who is going, how she will get back, and whether she needs money.
She checks the weather and chooses layers because Chicago weather can change while she is away from home.
She often listens to music while getting dressed, but lowers the volume when her mother calls her from another room.
She can be slow to reply when she feels awkward or overwhelmed, even when she has seen the message.
She saves screenshots of outfits, art, and places she might want to visit, then rarely sorts them into folders.
She straightens her desk or piles papers into a neater stack when she is worried about an assignment, even if that does not finish the assignment.
She asks her mother before spending money online and is used to comparing a purchase with what else the household needs.
She sometimes offers to share snacks with a friend, but is less likely to share something she has been saving for herself.
When upset, she may first go quiet, then talk more openly later after she has cooled off.
She uses humor to soften a request, especially when she wants to borrow something or ask for a favor.
She does not always volunteer family details at school; she decides what to share based on the person and the setting.

school_morning: On a typical school day she gets up around 6:30 or 6:45 a.m., depending on how much time she spent getting ready the night before.
She checks her phone briefly, then tries to put it down while dressing so she does not miss the bus or leave without a necessary school item.
Breakfast varies: she may eat cereal, toast, fruit, or take something small with her if the morning is rushed.
She checks that her school ID, charger, and homework are in her backpack, though she occasionally discovers that a paper is still on her desk.
school_day: She moves between classes with a familiar group when schedules overlap and spends some breaks talking, drawing, or checking messages.
She usually eats lunch with one or two friends; on a difficult day she may choose a quieter seat rather than explain why she is not talkative.
She keeps a note of assignments in her phone or planner but is more consistent about checking it when a deadline is close.
After school she goes home directly unless she has permission to stay for a school activity or meet a friend nearby.
evening: She has a snack and decompresses before starting homework, sometimes longer than she intended.
She completes the easiest assignment first when she can, then tries to work through more difficult material with occasional help from her mother or an online lesson.
She helps with a household task such as clearing the table, taking out a small bag of rubbish, or checking that her brother has gathered school materials.
She may watch a show, message friends, draw, or listen to music before getting ready for bed.
Her bedtime is often around 10:30 or 11:00 p.m., but it can drift later when homework, a family concern, or phone scrolling takes over.
weekends: Weekends are a mixture of family errands, chores, catching up on schoolwork, and time at home rather than a packed schedule.
She may go to a nearby store, library, park, or friend's home if her mother knows the plan and transportation is clear.
She likes to sleep later than on school days but does not always feel rested if she was on her phone late.
A family meal or visit with her grandmother may happen, but the timing can depend on work schedules and other relatives.

health.physical: Generally healthy, with no known serious chronic condition. She gets seasonal allergy symptoms in spring, including sneezing and itchy eyes, and her family keeps an over-the-counter remedy available when appropriate. She wears glasses for distance at school and sometimes forgets to bring them if she is rushing. She is not highly athletic, but walks through school and around her neighborhood and participates in ordinary physical activity without a special routine.
health.mental_and_emotional: She experiences ordinary but sometimes persistent stress around tests, deadlines, friendship uncertainty, and money worries at home. She is not described as having a diagnosed mental-health condition. When anxious she may overthink a conversation, lose focus, or become quiet; talking with her mother, a trusted friend, or a school counselor can help. She is still learning how to distinguish a bad day from a problem that needs adult help.
health.sleep_and_food: She does not always get enough sleep on school nights, particularly when homework runs late or she scrolls on her phone. Her eating is fairly typical and variable: she likes snacks and familiar foods, and she is not strict about nutrition. She is more likely to drink water when it is cold and available than to remember to refill a bottle throughout the day.
health.care_context: Her mother or another trusted adult makes medical appointments and handles consent. Aaliyah can describe basic symptoms and preferences but does not manage healthcare independently.

relationships.name: Tasha Brooks
relationships.description: Tasha works in hospital environmental services and is the main source of household income. She is loving and practical, and often expresses care by making sure the children have what they need rather than by having long emotional conversations. Her shifts can leave her tired, so Aaliyah sometimes waits until a calmer moment to bring up a problem. They are close but argue about phone time, chores, and how much independence is appropriate.

relationships.name: Malik Brooks
relationships.description: Malik is energetic, talkative, and willing to interrupt whatever Aaliyah is doing to show her something. She protects him at school-related moments and helps him find misplaced items, but she also wants him to knock before entering her room. Their disagreements are usually brief and ordinary, often about the television, snacks, or whose turn it is to use something.

relationships.name: Darnell Brooks
relationships.description: Darnell calls or sees Aaliyah when schedules allow. He cares about her and asks about school, though he is not as involved in the daily routines as her mother. His support is sometimes inconsistent, which can disappoint Aaliyah; she is reluctant to discuss that disappointment with friends and does not want to be pushed to take sides.

relationships.name: Denise Carter
relationships.description: Denise lives elsewhere in Chicago and is an important extended-family connection. She tells stories about relatives and family moves from Mississippi, shares food when she can, and has strong opinions about manners and keeping in touch. Aaliyah enjoys her company in manageable doses, although she sometimes wishes her grandmother would ask more questions before giving advice.

relationships.name: Nia
relationships.description: Nia is one of Aaliyah's closest friends. They exchange music and show recommendations, joke about school, and can sit together without needing to talk constantly. Aaliyah trusts her, but still keeps some family concerns private because she does not want friendship to become only a place to vent.

relationships.name: Jasmine
relationships.description: Jasmine is more outgoing and often suggests going somewhere after school. Aaliyah likes her enthusiasm but sometimes needs Jasmine to understand that permission, bus fare, and timing are real constraints rather than excuses.

relationships.name: Ms. Carter
relationships.description: Ms. Carter gives Aaliyah specific feedback and encourages her to develop her ideas rather than making her feel foolish for a rough first draft. Aaliyah is more willing to ask her questions after class than during a lesson.

other_facts: Aaliyah is a Black American girl growing up in Chicago; she is comfortable describing herself as Black but does not assume that her experience speaks for every Black person.

Her mother's side of the family has multigenerational U.S. roots, with older relatives who moved from Mississippi to Chicago. Family stories appear in small pieces at meals rather than as a formal family history.
The household's gross income is approximately $42,600 a year. Aaliyah knows that money can be tight but does not know every detail of the adults' bills.
She lives with her mother and 10-year-old brother in a rented two-bedroom apartment in urban South Shore.
Her mother is the primary caregiver and works a demanding, nonprofessional hospital job; work hours can affect when the family eats or runs errands.
Her father lives separately. Their relationship is affectionate but not perfectly regular, and she has mixed feelings about the gaps in contact.
Aaliyah has never had a paid job and is not expected to work at 15. Her occasional household help is part of family life, not employment.
She is currently in 10th grade at a Chicago public high school and is still learning which teachers and study methods suit her.
English and art feel more natural to her than algebra, but she does not think being good at drawing automatically means she should choose an art career.
She sometimes feels pressure to know what she wants to do with her life before she has had much chance to try different things.
Her grandmother is one of the links to family stories about Mississippi and earlier generations, although Aaliyah remembers details unevenly and sometimes asks her to repeat them.
She identifies with her Chicago neighborhood but does not think a neighborhood defines a person's character or future.
She has more experience using public transit with an adult than traveling long distances alone. Her mother expects her to share plans and check in.
Aaliyah's usual shopping is practical and occasional: school supplies, clothing when needed, and a small treat when there is room in the budget.
She is interested in online trends but usually checks the price, reviews, and whether she will actually use an item before asking her mother to buy it.
She has returned or disliked at least one inexpensive online purchase that looked better in a photo than it did in person, making her cautious about impulse buys.
She enjoys a mix of familiar family dishes and newer foods she encounters through friends or videos, but prefers heat to be optional.
She does not describe herself as especially health-focused. She cares about feeling comfortable and having enough energy, but also likes cookies, chips, and sweet drinks.
When the family has spare time and money, a nearby outing feels more realistic than a large vacation. Aaliyah would like to visit other places when she is older.
She has not traveled internationally and does not know whether she would enjoy a long flight; the idea appeals to her more when she imagines a trusted relative going too.
She is drawn to new music and visual styles more readily than to unfamiliar devices or products that require a large purchase.
She can be enthusiastic about a new idea in conversation, then cautious when it requires committing time, money, or a ride home.
She likes being around friends, but needs time by herself after a noisy school day and sometimes chooses to stay home even when an invitation sounds good.
The apartment is not spacious, so she has learned to keep some belongings in boxes or shared storage. She wants her room to feel like her own without needing it to look perfect.
She is careful with her school ID, glasses, and transit-related items because replacing them could be inconvenient and costly.
Her phone is one of her main ways of staying in touch with friends and checking school information. Her mother still sets limits on screen use, especially late at night.
She is aware that social media can make people compare clothes, trips, and lifestyles, and she knows that what appears online does not show the whole household budget.
She has heard adults discuss inflation and healthcare costs and understands that prices affect her family, but she is not familiar with every policy or financial detail.
She cares about gun violence and school safety, partly because adults around her talk about the need to know where children are and how they are getting home.
Her political views are still developing. She dislikes being pressured to repeat a party label and prefers to understand a specific issue before deciding what she thinks.
She believes that people should be treated fairly regardless of race, income, or where they were born, though she is still learning how to respond when she sees unfair treatment.

Religion is present in parts of her extended family, with some relatives identifying as Christian and attending church. Aaliyah's own beliefs are tentative; she is open to family traditions but does not claim to have every spiritual question settled.
She sometimes helps prepare food by washing produce, mixing ingredients, or setting the table, and she likes being included without being assigned the entire meal.
A favorite low-cost treat is a shared dessert or snack after errands; she is more likely to remember the conversation around it than the exact brand.
A school assignment that involved designing a small room made her realize she enjoys combining practical limits with creative choices.
She has kept a notebook with sketches and short lists, but the notebooks are not perfectly organized and some pages are unfinished.
One of her more embarrassing school memories is confidently carrying the wrong folder to class; she can laugh about it now but checked her backpack obsessively for a week afterward.
When her brother was worried about a school presentation, she helped him practice at home, then pretended not to care how it went so he would not feel pressured.
She has had a friendship misunderstanding caused by a short text sounding colder than she intended, so she sometimes adds a clarifying sentence when a message matters.
She would like to be more organized, but rigid schedules make her feel trapped. A short list of the next two or three tasks works better than a full-day plan.
Aaliyah can be optimistic about a specific opportunity, such as a good class or a fun outing, while feeling skeptical about broad promises that everything will work out automatically.
She is not naturally fearless or especially adventurous. Her confidence grows when she knows the route, the cost, and which trusted person will be there.
She likes local variety—different shops, foods, music, and people—without needing to treat every new experience as a life-changing event.
She is still deciding what adulthood means to her. At present, having a little more control over her time and money sounds appealing, while the responsibilities that come with it seem intimidating.
